Why two-layer skills

A tau skill is two files in a directory: SKILL.md (the prompt) and tau.toml (the manifest). This isn't an obvious choice — most agent frameworks embed both in a single file. This page explains why tau picked the two-layer split, what trade-offs it locked in, and how it interacts with the broader Anthropic Agent Skills ecosystem.

For the surface details, see Reference: skill manifest schema. For the design history, see ADR-0025.

The reframing that produced Option D

When Skills-1 was designed, four shapes were on the table:

  • A: Typed [skill] block in tau.toml, with the system prompt embedded as a TOML triple-quoted string.
  • B: External SKILL.md referenced by relative path from tau.toml, with a tau-specific filename convention.
  • C: Adopt the Agent Skills spec format verbatim (just SKILL.md, no tau.toml — drop tau-specific packaging).
  • D: Two-layer: Anthropic-compatible SKILL.md (frontmatter + body) PLUS tau.toml for packaging metadata + capabilities.

Option D won. The reframing: Anthropic's skill format already defines the prompt layout we want. We don't need to compete with it on prompt encoding; we need to extend it with packaging.

The result is a skill directory that's simultaneously:

  • A valid Anthropic Agent Skill (just remove tau.toml to ship to claude-code or another Anthropic consumer).
  • A tau package with capabilities, semver, dependencies, lockfile participation.

What each layer owns

flowchart LR
    subgraph A["Anthropic Agent Skills format"]
        SK["SKILL.md<br/><i>prompt content</i><br/>+ YAML frontmatter (name, description)"]
    end
    subgraph T["tau-specific layer"]
        TT["tau.toml<br/><i>typed package metadata</i><br/>kind = &quot;skill&quot;<br/>[[capabilities]]<br/>[skill.requires_skills]<br/>version, source, authors"]
    end
    SK -.->|name<br/>must match| TT
    A -->|<code>tau install</code>| INSTALLED[("installed skill<br/>SKILL.md + tau.toml<br/>+ lockfile entry")]
    T -->|<code>tau install</code>| INSTALLED
    INSTALLED -->|"<code>tau skill export</code>"| OUT["SKILL.md only<br/>(capabilities dropped<br/>with warning)"]
    OUT -.->|byte-identical iff<br/>capabilities = [] and<br/>no requires_skills| SK

SKILL.md owns: the prompt content.

  • The YAML frontmatter declares name and description (both required, both validated).
  • The Markdown body is the system prompt. It becomes the spawned child agent's system_prompt at runtime (per ADR-0028).
  • Format is fixed by the Anthropic Agent Skills spec; tau doesn't extend it.

tau.toml owns: everything else.

  • Package identity: name, version, source, authors.
  • Capability declarations ([[capabilities]] blocks).
  • Sub-skill dependencies ([skill.requires_skills]).
  • Package kind (kind = "skill" — disambiguates from kind = "tool" / kind = "llm-backend").

The two layers must agree on name (validated on install). Everything else is independent: tau can add [skill.requires_tools], requires_skills, future fields, without touching SKILL.md.

The roundtrip claim

For any tau skill with capabilities = [] and no requires_skills:

tau install <source> → tau skill export <name> → re-install

produces an identical SKILL.md byte-for-byte (and the same name + description). Skills-5 ships this as tests/skill_format_roundtrip.rs.

For capability-bearing skills, the export is one-way (Anthropic format doesn't preserve capabilities). tau skill export --strict makes the metadata-drop a hard error if round-trippability matters.

The roundtrip claim is what makes the two-layer architecture worth it: tau can extend the Anthropic format without forking it.

What this rules out

Two consequences worth being explicit about:

1. We can't bake tau-specific behavior into SKILL.md. No tau- specific YAML frontmatter extensions (e.g., x-tau-capabilities), no tau-flavored Markdown syntax. Why: any such extension would break the byte-identical roundtrip claim for pure-prompt skills, and the Anthropic ecosystem ignores unknown YAML keys anyway so there's no benefit.

Skills-5 explicitly rejected an x-tau-capabilities YAML extension for this reason.

2. We can't combine tau.toml and SKILL.md into a single file. A skill is fundamentally a directory of files. The ${SKILL_DIR}/... substitution + multi-file payloads (e.g., references/ subdirs) depend on the directory being the unit of distribution. Embedding everything in tau.toml would lose that.

Comparison with neighboring systems

SystemPrompt encodingPackaging
Anthropic Agent Skills (vanilla)SKILL.md (YAML + Markdown)none (just the directory)
tauSKILL.md (same)tau.toml (additive)
Single-file agents (e.g., .prompt files)one TOML / YAML / JSON filenone
Plugin-style (Python decorators, MCP servers)code-embeddedlanguage-native imports

tau differs from each:

  • vs Anthropic vanilla: gains semver, capabilities, lockfile.
  • vs single-file: gains multi-file payloads, structured packaging.
  • vs plugin-style: gains LLM-readable prompts (skills aren't code).

Sub-skill composition (currently advisory)

The [skill.requires_skills] block lets a skill declare that it's meant to be used with another skill:

[[skill.requires_skills]]
name = "fact-checker"
version_req = "^0.1"

In tau v1, this is advisory. The runtime doesn't:

  • Auto-install dependencies on tau install.
  • Auto-spawn sub-skills when the parent is invoked.
  • Enforce that the dependency is present at spawn time.

It documents the relationship for users authoring agents (so they can install the dependencies + grant the parent skill skill.spawn authorization for them).

A future Skills sub-project may tighten this if a concrete use case emerges.

When NOT to write a skill

A skill is the right shape when:

  • The work is purely prompt-driven (LLM reads input → emits output).
  • The skill has clear boundaries (one purpose, one entry point).
  • The capability set is small (one or two fs / process / net access).

A skill is the WRONG shape when:

  • The work requires real code (compute, parsing, custom logic). Use a tool plugin instead (kind = "tool").
  • The work requires many capabilities or long chains of tool calls. Compose smaller skills + tools instead.
  • The work doesn't generalize beyond a single project. Just inline the prompt in your agent definition.

The skill abstraction earns its keep when it's installable, named, versioned, and reusable across agents.

Further reading

  • ADR-0025: foundation
  • ADR-0028: runtime invocation
  • ADR-0029: Anthropic interop
  • Tutorial: Build your first skill
  • Reference: Skill manifest schema

Trigger ingress

tau compiles a declarative [trigger] table into the workflow artifact as portable, capability-safe metadata. A host adapter reads that metadata and wires the real trigger. tau emits the binding; the host owns the substrate — the scheduler, the socket, the durable queue. This is the same delegation tau applies to inference and credentials.

Slice 1 (this page) ships cron and manual triggers plus a retry policy. webhook and queue are slice 2 and are not yet available.

The two halves of a trigger

HalfExample (cron)Who owns it
Substratethe timer that fires at 03:00the host (systemd, k8s, Lambda, …)
Binding"fire summarizer on 0 3 * * *"tau (declared once, compiled, portable)

tau adds only the binding — as compiled, content-hashed metadata — and leaves the substrate where it already lives.

Declaring triggers in tau.toml

# A named cron binding.
[trigger.nightly]
kind     = "cron"
agent    = "summarizer"        # entrypoint — must be an existing agent id
schedule = "0 3 * * *"         # 5-field cron
timezone = "UTC"               # optional; default UTC

[trigger.nightly.retry]
max_attempts = 3               # total attempts including the first
backoff      = { strategy = "exponential", base = "30s", max = "10m" }
dead_letter  = "dlq-sink"      # sink reference (an MCP contract or granted target)

# The default, made explicit: tau is invoked by an external driver.
[trigger.manual]
kind  = "manual"
agent = "summarizer"

cron requires a 5-field schedule; manual takes no schedule. tau build validates the entrypoint agent exists, the cron field count, plain-integer field ranges, and the retry durations.

How a trigger compiles

A trigger lowers as metadata — it adds no executable node:

  • It rides inside the canonical IR (IrModule.triggers), so it is content-hashed and reproducible. A trigger-less project hashes identically to before triggers existed.
  • It is mirrored in the bundle manifest as a [[trigger]] section, which bumps the bundle schema_version to 3 so an older tau rejects a trigger-bearing bundle rather than silently dropping the binding.

Emitting host-adapter descriptors

tau build --emit-trigger=<adapter> writes scheduler wiring next to the bundle:

tau build --emit-trigger=systemd   # writes tau-<name>.timer + tau-<name>.service
tau build --emit-trigger=k8s       # writes tau-<name>.cronjob.yaml

k8s CronJob consumes the 5-field cron verbatim. systemd OnCalendar is generated for schedules whose fields are * or plain integers; schedules using ranges, lists, or steps are skipped for systemd (use k8s for those). manual triggers emit nothing — the host invokes tau directly.

Why retry is host-honoured

Retry is a trigger-level re-invocation policy, not a per-node interpreter retry. The host re-invokes the artifact; tau's interpreter stays deterministic and stateless across invocations. dead_letter names a sink (an MCP contract or an already-granted capability target) — never a tau-owned queue. This keeps durable state out of tau's core.

See ADR-0044 for the design rationale.

Workflows

A workflow is a deterministic, step-by-step pipeline of agent runs and tool calls, persisted to disk, resumable, and authored as a single TOML file. Workflows are the external-script-driven counterpart to in-run multi-agent orchestration: orchestration composes agents from inside one root agent's tool loop; a workflow composes agents (and direct tool calls) from outside, with no LLM in the glue between steps.

This page explains the model, when to reach for it vs in-run orchestration, and what v1 deliberately doesn't ship.

What problem this solves

Inside an agent's tool loop, the LLM decides what comes next. That's exactly what you want for open-ended work, and exactly what you don't want for "always run X, then Y, then Z" pipelines — where every LLM round-trip adds latency, cost, and a slim chance of the model deciding to skip step Y. Workflows give you the same sandboxed plugin host (tau run's machinery), the same capability checks, the same JSONL persistence — but the transitions between steps are written in TOML, not delegated to a model.

The shape of a workflow

A workflow lives under workflows/<name>.toml at the project root. Minimal example:

[workflow]
name        = "summarize-and-critique"
description = "Summarize a doc, then critique the summary."

[[steps]]
id    = "summarize"
kind  = "agent.run"
agent = "summarizer"
input = "${input}"

[[steps]]
id    = "critique"
kind  = "agent.run"
agent = "critic"
input = "${steps.summarize.output}"

Two kind values v1 supports:

  • agent.run — spawn one of the project's declared agents (from tau.toml's [agents.<id>]), feed it the rendered input, capture its final completion as the step's output.
  • tool.call — invoke a single tool method directly without an LLM round-trip. Uses Runtime::invoke_tool under the hood — same capability checks, same sandbox, no model latency.

Templates use ${input} (the workflow's top-level input) and ${steps.<id>.output} (any prior step's captured output) as flat string substitutions. No conditionals, no loops, no expression language. ADR-0022 §"Decision" pins this scope.

How a workflow runs

flowchart LR
    U[user] -->|<code>tau workflow run &lt;name&gt; --input ...</code>| W[workflow runner]
    W -->|step 1| A1[agent.run summarizer]
    A1 -->|completion| W
    W -->|step 2| A2[agent.run critic]
    A2 -->|completion| W
    W -->|step k<br/><code>tool.call</code>| T[(tool method<br/>via invoke_tool)]
    T -->|result| W
    W --> J["JSONL log<br/><code>.tau/workflows/runs/&lt;run-id&gt;.jsonl</code>"]
    J -.->|<code>tau workflow resume</code>| W

Verbs the user sees:

CommandPurpose
tau workflow listenumerate workflows/*.toml
tau workflow run <name> --input <text>execute end-to-end
tau workflow log <run-id>read a previous run's JSONL trace
tau workflow resume <run-id>continue an interrupted run from the last completed step

The runner is a tau-workflow crate; the CLI is a thin dispatcher. Both consume the same tau-runtime kernel as tau run / tau chat, which means workflows inherit the full sandbox + capability stack for free.

Workflows vs in-run orchestration

When to reach for which:

TraitWorkflowIn-run orchestration
Who decides the next stepTOML authorthe parent agent's LLM
LLM hops between stepszero (glue is deterministic)one per agent.<kind>.spawn
Persistenceone JSONL per runtrace inside the run
Resumabilitytau workflow resumewithin a session via REPL persistence
Topologylinear list of stepstree (five named patterns)
Tool calls without an agentyes — tool.call stepyes — but inside an agent's loop
Typical lifetimeminutes to hoursseconds to minutes
Right-tool-for-the-job"always run A then B then C""the agent decides what to do next"

Both compose: a single workflow step can be an agent.run that itself spawns sub-agents via orchestration. The wire to Runtime::run_with_history is the same.

The persistence promise

Every step's input, output, started/ended timestamps, and capture of any error are appended to <scope>/.tau/workflows/runs/<run-id>.jsonl. The format is committed to as a public surface — schema changes will be additive with a once-per-process warn on read, same model as the lockfile v3→v4 transition (ADR-0026).

Consequences:

  • Inspectable post-mortem. tau workflow log <run-id> is a plain file dump; no special tooling. The trace is grep-able by agent id, step id, or status.
  • Resumable on demand. tau workflow resume <run-id> reads the JSONL, replays its declared state, picks up at the first step without a completion record.
  • Deterministic, not idempotent. A resumed run will not re-execute steps that already completed. If a step had a side-effect that the user wants re-attempted, deleting that step's JSONL record is the supported escape hatch.

v1 deliberate limits

Per ADR-0022 §"v1 limitations":

  • Single Runtime per workflow. The runtime is built from the first referenced agent's plugin config. Workflows whose agents use different LLM-backend packages will work but share one backend instance.
  • No DAG. Steps execute in declaration order. Parallel fan-out / fan-in / conditional branches are deferred (sub-project "workflow-DAG").
  • No conditionals or expressions. Templates are flat string substitution. No if, no loops, no variable assignment beyond ${steps.<id>.output}.
  • No per-step capability override. A step inherits the capabilities of the referenced agent verbatim.
  • No scheduling. Cron-style "run this nightly" is not in scope; that's an at / cron / launchd problem and tau is not a workflow engine (NG5).

What this is not

Two clarifications, drawn from the constitution non-goals:

  • Not a general-purpose workflow engine (NG5). "Pipeline" in tau means "coordinates agents," not "coordinates arbitrary tasks." tool.call exists to avoid forcing an LLM round-trip on the trivial cases; it does not turn tau into a substitute for Airflow / Temporal / n8n.
  • Not an alternative to in-run orchestration (G9). The same composition primitives sit under both surfaces. Pick the one whose authoring model fits the problem; mix freely.

See also

  • Multi-agent orchestration — the in-run companion. Use that when the LLM decides what's next.
  • Packages — workflows reference agents; agents reference packages.
  • Capabilities and consent — each step inherits its referenced agent's grant.
  • Sandboxing — every step's plugin spawn flows through the same adapter resolution.
  • ADR-0022 — full design rationale + v1 limits + considered alternatives.
  • Runtime::invoke_tool (in tau-runtime) — the API tool.call steps go through.

Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)

This directory holds tau's ADRs. Each ADR is a numbered Markdown file (NNNN-title.md) recording one decision in MADR style.

When an ADR is required

Per QG18, ADRs are required for:

  • Changes to project guidelines (anything in CONSTITUTION.md).
  • Additions to or breaking changes in public APIs (tau-runtime exports, serve-mode IPC schema).
  • Changes to the serve-mode protocol.
  • Changes to the package manifest format.
  • Changes to plugin trait boundaries.

Other changes (bugfixes, refactors within a crate, docs updates) do not require ADRs and are recorded in commit messages and PR discussion (PG3).

Filing an ADR

  1. Copy template.md to NNNN-<short-title>.md where NNNN is one greater than the highest existing ADR number.
  2. Fill in Context, Decision, Consequences, and Alternatives.
  3. Open a PR. The ADR's status starts as Proposed.
  4. The maintainer reviews. On acceptance, status changes to Accepted and the PR is merged.
  5. Per the Constitution §4 amendment process, guideline-changing ADRs wait at least 24 hours between draft and merge.

This ADR records the v0.1 manifest field set, the rules under which the <code>Capability</code> typed enum evolves, and the policy governing all escape-hatch variants in tau core.</p> <h2 id="decision-2"><a class="header" href="#decision-2">Decision</a></h2> <h3 id="1-manifest-field-set-v01"><a class="header" href="#1-manifest-field-set-v01">1. Manifest field set (v0.1)</a></h3> <p>The v0.1 <code>UncheckedManifest</code> / <code>PackageManifest</code> carries:</p> <ul> <li><code>name: PackageName</code></li> <li><code>version: semver::Version</code></li> <li><code>description: String</code> (non-empty; enforced by <code>validate()</code>)</li> <li><code>authors: Vec<String></code></li> <li><code>license: Option<String></code> (SPDX expression as opaque text)</li> <li><code>source: PackageSource</code></li> <li><code>kind: PackageKind</code></li> <li><code>dependencies: Vec<PackageDep></code></li> <li><code>capabilities: Vec<Capability></code></li> </ul> <p>Adding fields is a non-breaking minor (the struct is <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code>). Removing or renaming is a breaking minor pre-1.0 per QG11.</p> <h3 id="2-hierarchical-capability-shape"><a class="header" href="#2-hierarchical-capability-shape">2. Hierarchical Capability shape</a></h3> <p><code>Capability</code> is a top-level <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> enum with five variants: <code>Filesystem(FsCapability)</code>, <code>Network(NetCapability)</code>, <code>Process(ProcessCapability)</code>, <code>Agent(AgentCapability)</code>, and <code>Custom { name, params }</code>. Each per-namespace sub-enum is also <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code>, and each variant within (e.g. <code>FsCapability::Read</code>) is <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> so additive field evolution is non-breaking.</p> <h3 id="3-canonicalization-at-deserialization"><a class="header" href="#3-canonicalization-at-deserialization">3. Canonicalization at deserialization</a></h3> <p>Manifest TOML uses the flat dot-namespaced form:</p> <pre><code class="language-toml">[[capabilities]] kind = "fs.read" paths = ["${PROJECT}/**"] </code></pre> <p>A custom <code>Deserialize</code> impl on <code>Capability</code> maps recognized <code>kind</code> strings (<code>"fs.read"</code>, <code>"fs.write"</code>, <code>"net.http"</code>, <code>"process.spawn"</code>, <code>"agent.spawn"</code>, etc.) onto the variant tree. Unknown <code>kind</code> values fall through to <code>Capability::Custom { name, params }</code>. New typed variants in v0.X auto-promote existing manifests via the same canonicalization — plugin authors do not need to update manifests when typed variants land.</p> <p>A consequence of canonicalization-at-deserialization is that the shadowed-name case round-trips into the typed variant: a <code>Capability::Custom { name: "fs.read", params: ... }</code> constructed in Rust serializes to <code>kind = "fs.read"</code> and re-deserializes as the typed <code>Capability::Filesystem(FsCapability::Read { ... })</code>. This is intentional and supports the v0.X auto-promotion path above. Reserved typed param names (<code>paths</code>, <code>max_bytes</code>, <code>hosts</code>, <code>methods</code>, <code>commands</code>, <code>allowed_kinds</code>) should therefore not be reused inside <code>Capability::Custom.params</code> for unrelated meanings.</p> <h3 id="4-naming-convention"><a class="header" href="#4-naming-convention">4. Naming convention</a></h3> <p>The dot-namespaced <code><domain>.<verb></code> convention (e.g. <code>fs.read</code>, <code>net.http</code>) is <strong>recommended, not mandated</strong>. tau-domain validates only "non-empty" on <code>Capability::Custom.name</code>. Plugin authors who want a non-conforming name (e.g. <code>myorg/special-cap</code>) may use it via <code>Custom</code>.</p> <h3 id="5-escape-hatch-policy"><a class="header" href="#5-escape-hatch-policy">5. Escape-hatch policy</a></h3> <p>Prefer typed variants for known shapes; allow <code>Custom</code> / <code>InternalError</code> escape hatches with documented rationale. <strong>Every escape hatch in tau core is tracked in <code>docs/explanation/escape-hatches.md</code></strong> with location, reason, promotion trigger, and status. PRs that introduce, promote, or remove an escape hatch update the registry in the same commit. Each escape-hatch variant's rustdoc carries a link to its registry anchor.</p> <p>This applies uniformly to:</p> <ul> <li><code>Capability::Custom</code></li> <li><code>MessagePayload::Custom</code></li> <li><code>PackageKind::Custom</code></li> <li><code>FailureKind::InternalError</code></li> <li>any future escape hatches added in tau core.</li> </ul> <h3 id="6-required-llm_backend"><a class="header" href="#6-required-llm_backend">6. Required <code>llm_backend</code></a></h3> <p><code>AgentDefinition.llm_backend</code> is <code>PackageName</code> (non-optional) at v0.1. Rationale: Constitution Appendix C explicitly defines an agent as a process with an LLM backend; G4 reinforces. If a non-LLM agent use case materializes (sub-project 4+), <code>llm_backend</code> becomes <code>Option<PackageName></code> via a pre-1.0 minor breaking change.</p> <h3 id="7-mechanical-enforcement-of-the-registry"><a class="header" href="#7-mechanical-enforcement-of-the-registry">7. Mechanical enforcement of the registry</a></h3> <p>A CI-blocking integration test (<code>crates/tau-domain/tests/escape_hatch_registry.rs</code>) scans every <code>.rs</code> file in the workspace for variants named <code>Custom</code> or <code>InternalError</code>, parses their rustdoc for a link to the registry, and verifies each anchor exists in <code>docs/explanation/escape-hatches.md</code>. Stale registry entries also fail the test. Combined with the PR template checkbox and the rustdoc convention, this enforces decision 5 in three layers: documentation (CONTRIBUTING.md + rustdoc), PR-time prompt (template), and CI gate (test).</p> <h3 id="8-valuebytes-wire-format"><a class="header" href="#8-valuebytes-wire-format">8. <code>Value::Bytes</code> wire format</a></h3> <p><code>Value::Bytes(Vec<u8>)</code> (the message-payload byte-vector variant) is serialized in human-readable formats (TOML, JSON) as a base64 string prefixed with the reserved sentinel <code>@bytes:</code>. The prefix lets the custom <code>Deserialize</code> distinguish a byte-payload string from an ordinary <code>Value::String</code>. Consequently, <code>@bytes:</code> is a reserved prefix on <code>Value::String</code> — strings starting with <code>@bytes:</code> are not representable as <code>Value::String</code> and must use <code>Value::Bytes</code>. Binary formats (e.g. bincode) carry bytes natively and ignore this convention.</p> <h2 id="consequences-2"><a class="header" href="#consequences-2">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>The wire format for <code>Capability</code> is committed at v0.1: flat <code>kind = "<dot.namespaced>"</code> form with sibling field-shaped params. Deviating from this form is a breaking change.</li> <li>Plugin authors need to know the canonical names (<code>fs.read</code>, etc.) to produce manifests that map to typed variants; they don't <em>have</em> to use them — <code>Custom</code> always works.</li> <li>The escape-hatch registry is a living document; every PR that introduces or modifies an escape hatch touches it.</li> <li>The CI registry test depends on the rustdoc convention of linking to <code>escape-hatches.md#<anchor></code>. Variants that violate this fail CI.</li> <li>Adding new typed <code>FailureKind</code> variants is non-breaking (the enum is <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code>); demoting <code>InternalError</code> to a typed kind is similarly additive.</li> <li>Required <code>llm_backend</code> rules out non-LLM agents at v0.1; we accept the migration cost if and when that case appears.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-2"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-2">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>String-only capability dispatch</strong> (rejected at brainstorm). Forces every consumer to write <code>match name.as_str()</code> boilerplate; gives up type safety for no v0.1 benefit.</li> <li><strong>Flat <code>Capability</code> enum without namespace structure</strong> (α; rejected in favor of β). Would have been more compact at v0.1 but β anticipates per-namespace enforcement layers in tau-runtime.</li> <li><strong>No escape-hatch registry</strong>, just rustdoc warnings (rejected). Aspirational rules without mechanical enforcement decay quickly.</li> <li><strong>Top-level <code>DomainError</code> umbrella</strong> (rejected at brainstorm Q5). Per-concern enums forever; consumers wanting "any tau-domain error" wrap their own.</li> <li><strong><code>Option<PackageName></code> for <code>llm_backend</code> from day one</strong> (rejected). Adds permanent ceremony at every reader for a case that may not materialize; pre-1.0 SemVer makes the loosen-later path cheap.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0003-tau-ports-trait-surface"><a class="header" href="#adr-0003-tau-ports-trait-surface">ADR-0003: tau-ports trait surface</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-04-26 <strong>Supersedes:</strong> —</p> <h2 id="context-3"><a class="header" href="#context-3">Context</a></h2> <p>tau-ports (sub-project 2) defines the four plugin trait boundaries that every tau plugin author programs against: <code>LlmBackend</code>, <code>Tool</code>, <code>Storage</code>, and <code>Sandbox</code>. These traits, together with their request/response data shapes, are the most permanent surface in the workspace — once a plugin ecosystem starts, breaking them invalidates every out-of-tree plugin.</p> <p>Per QG18, plugin trait boundaries require an ADR. Per Constitution §1 crate scope, tau-ports is <code>no_std</code>-leaning (currently <code>std</code>-only but runtime-agnostic) and depends only on <code>tau-domain</code> plus <code>thiserror</code>. This ADR records the decisions taken across spec §3 (the type-by-type design) and locks them at v0.1: async story, trait shapes, error policy, serde stance, escape-hatch registration, sandbox provisionality, and where mocks live.</p> <h2 id="decision-3"><a class="header" href="#decision-3">Decision</a></h2> <h3 id="1-native-async-fn-in-trait"><a class="header" href="#1-native-async-fn-in-trait">1. Native <code>async fn in trait</code></a></h3> <p>tau-ports uses native <code>async fn in trait</code> (stabilized in Rust 1.75, covered by MSRV 1.91 from ADR-0001) for every async trait method. The <code>async-trait</code> macro is not used; a sync-only API is rejected. Each public trait carries <code>#[allow(async_fn_in_trait)]</code> to suppress the "may have undesirable side-effects" clippy warning, since tau-ports does not require <code>Send</code> futures at the trait level — runtimes that need <code>Send</code> impose it at the bound site.</p> <p>The crate stays runtime-agnostic: no <code>tokio</code>, <code>async-std</code>, or <code>futures-executor</code> dependency. Returned futures are <code>impl Future</code> in trait position, bound by the trait's lifetime parameters.</p> <h3 id="2-four-trait-shapes"><a class="header" href="#2-four-trait-shapes">2. Four trait shapes</a></h3> <h4 id="llmbackend"><a class="header" href="#llmbackend"><code>LlmBackend</code></a></h4> <ul> <li>Two methods: <code>complete(&self, req: CompletionRequest) -> Result<CompletionResponse, LlmError></code> and <code>stream(&self, req: CompletionRequest) -> Result<CompletionStream, LlmError></code>.</li> <li>A blanket helper provides "implement one, get the other" via the <code>BackendCompletionExt</code> extension trait (drains a stream into a response; or upgrades a <code>complete</code> to a one-shot stream).</li> <li>Messages are multi-block: <code>LlmProviderMessage</code> carries <code>Vec<LlmContentBlock></code> so a single assistant turn can mix text, tool-use, and tool-result blocks.</li> <li>Streaming chunks for <code>tool_use</code> are plugin-buffered: the backend accumulates the JSON until the block closes, then emits one <code>StreamEvent::ToolUse</code> rather than partial-JSON chunks. Consumers do not see incomplete tool calls.</li> </ul> <h4 id="tool"><a class="header" href="#tool"><code>Tool</code></a></h4> <ul> <li>Stateful: associated type <code>Session: Send + 'static</code>, with <code>init(&self) -> Result<Session, ToolError></code>, <code>invoke(&self, session: &mut Session, args: Value) -> Result<ToolResult, ToolError></code>, and <code>teardown(&self, session: Session) -> Result<(), ToolError></code>.</li> <li>Stateless tools use a <code>StatelessAdapter<F></code> newtype that implements <code>Tool</code> with <code>Session = ()</code>; authors write a single async closure.</li> <li>Dual error model: <code>Result<ToolResult, ToolError></code>, where <code>ToolResult</code> itself carries an <code>is_error: bool</code> flag. Hard errors (the tool itself failed to execute) return <code>Err(ToolError)</code>; soft errors (the tool ran but the model should see a failure message) return <code>Ok(ToolResult { is_error: true, .. })</code>.</li> </ul> <h4 id="storage"><a class="header" href="#storage"><code>Storage</code></a></h4> <ul> <li>KV-only at v0.1: <code>get</code>, <code>put</code>, <code>delete</code>, <code>list_prefix</code>. No transactions, no TTL, no watch/subscribe.</li> <li>Typed newtypes <code>Namespace(String)</code> and <code>Key(String)</code> prevent string-typing collisions and namespace forgery; both validate non-empty and reject <code>\0</code> on construction.</li> <li>Values are <code>Vec<u8></code>. Serialization is the caller's responsibility.</li> </ul> <h4 id="sandbox"><a class="header" href="#sandbox"><code>Sandbox</code></a></h4> <ul> <li>Provisional stub at v0.1 (see decision 6).</li> <li>Opaque <code>Handle</code> newtype: implementations may park a PID, container id, or VM handle behind it; consumers may only <code>wait</code>, <code>kill</code>, or query status.</li> <li><code>ResourceLimits</code> is four-axis: <code>cpu_seconds</code>, <code>memory_bytes</code>, <code>file_descriptors</code>, <code>wall_clock</code>. The wall-clock axis is belt-and-suspenders against runaway sandboxed work.</li> <li><code>WorkingContext</code> (cwd, env, stdin handle) is optional on <code>spawn</code> — some sandbox kinds (e.g. WASI) do not honor a host cwd.</li> </ul> <h3 id="3-error-policy"><a class="header" href="#3-error-policy">3. Error policy</a></h3> <p>Each trait has its own concrete error enum: <code>LlmError</code>, <code>ToolError</code>, <code>StorageError</code>, <code>SandboxError</code>. There is no top-level <code>PortsError</code> umbrella.</p> <p><code>ToolError</code> composes the others via <code>#[from]</code> conversions: <code>ToolError::Llm(LlmError)</code> and <code>ToolError::Storage(StorageError)</code>. Tools that delegate to a backend or read from storage propagate errors with <code>?</code> without manual mapping.</p> <p>Every error enum exposes <code>is_retryable(&self) -> bool</code> — a <em>heuristic</em> predicate for transient-vs-permanent classification (rate limits, transient network, broken pipe → true; bad request, schema error, missing key → false). Consumers may build retry loops on it but should not treat the answer as authoritative.</p> <p>Each enum carries an <code>Internal { source: anyhow::Error }</code> (or <code>InternalError</code>) variant as a typed escape hatch. Per ADR-0002 decision 5, every <code>Internal*</code> variant is registered in <code>docs/explanation/escape-hatches.md</code> with reason and promotion trigger; the CI registry test enforces this.</p> <h3 id="4-no-serde-feature-at-v01"><a class="header" href="#4-no-serde-feature-at-v01">4. No serde feature at v0.1</a></h3> <p>tau-ports does not expose a <code>serde</code> feature on any of its types. Plugin trait shapes are in-process Rust values; (de)serialization is unnecessary for v0.1 dispatch.</p> <p>The trigger for adding a <code>serde</code> feature is the first cross-process consumer: either a Phase-1 RPC sandbox kind (where requests/responses cross a process boundary) or the eventual out-of-process plugin model. Adding the feature is non-breaking (gated behind <code>#[cfg(feature = "serde")]</code>).</p> <h3 id="5-provider_specific-escape-hatch-on-completionrequest"><a class="header" href="#5-provider_specific-escape-hatch-on-completionrequest">5. <code>provider_specific</code> escape hatch on <code>CompletionRequest</code></a></h3> <p><code>CompletionRequest</code> carries a <code>provider_specific: BTreeMap<String, Value></code> field for vendor-specific parameters that have no typed equivalent (e.g. Anthropic-only <code>extended_thinking_budget_tokens</code>, OpenAI-only <code>seed</code>). The <code>BTreeMap</code> deterministic ordering matters for snapshot tests and idempotent retry signatures.</p> <p>This is a registered escape hatch: it lives in <code>docs/explanation/escape-hatches.md</code> with the <strong>promotion rule</strong> that any key appearing in two or more independent plugins is promoted to a typed field on <code>CompletionRequest</code> (or a typed sub-struct under it) in the next minor.</p> <h3 id="6-sandbox-provisional-caveat"><a class="header" href="#6-sandbox-provisional-caveat">6. Sandbox provisional caveat</a></h3> <p>The v0.1 <code>Sandbox</code> trait is a <strong>provisional sketch</strong>. Real sandboxing work (Linux namespaces, seccomp, WASI capabilities, Firecracker VM, or the eventual choice) lives in Phase 1+ and will likely require shape changes — additional methods, different <code>Handle</code> semantics, or splitting <code>Sandbox</code> into multiple traits per kind.</p> <p>SemVer is <strong>disclaimed</strong> for the <code>Sandbox</code> trait beyond the major-version bump that introduces production sandboxing. The trait's rustdoc carries a "Stability: provisional" notice. Plugin authors targeting v0.1 sandbox may need to rewrite at the major bump.</p> <p>The other three traits (<code>LlmBackend</code>, <code>Tool</code>, <code>Storage</code>) are not provisional; they follow normal pre-1.0 SemVer (QG11).</p> <h3 id="7-mocks-live-in-tau-ports-under-test-fixtures"><a class="header" href="#7-mocks-live-in-tau-ports-under-test-fixtures">7. Mocks live in tau-ports under <code>test-fixtures</code></a></h3> <p>Test fixtures (<code>MockLlmBackend</code>, <code>MockTool</code>, <code>MockStorage</code>, <code>MockSandbox</code>) live in tau-ports itself, gated behind a <code>test-fixtures</code> cargo feature. Consumer crates depend on tau-ports with <code>features = ["test-fixtures"]</code> in their <code>[dev-dependencies]</code>.</p> <p>Alternatives — per-consumer mocks or a separate <code>tau-ports-test</code> crate — were rejected. Per-consumer duplicates the same mock five times across the workspace and drifts. A separate crate adds a publish target and a SemVer surface for what is conceptually one trait surface; the cargo-feature pattern colocates the mock with the trait it mocks, so a trait change updates the mock in the same diff.</p> <h2 id="consequences-3"><a class="header" href="#consequences-3">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>The trait shapes and request/response types are the v0.1 public surface for plugin authors. Adding methods is a breaking minor pre-1.0 (QG11); adding fields to <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> request/response types is non-breaking.</li> <li><code>async fn in trait</code> without <code>Send</code> bounds means runtimes that need <code>Send</code> futures (most multi-threaded executors) impose <code>Send</code> at the bound site. tau-runtime does this; standalone consumers may not need to.</li> <li><code>is_retryable()</code> is heuristic — consumers building retry loops should expect occasional misclassification and complement with retry budgets / circuit breakers in their own layer.</li> <li>The <code>provider_specific</code> escape hatch puts pressure on the registry: every entry there is a candidate for promotion; the registry needs periodic review (no automated mechanism at v0.1).</li> <li>The <code>Sandbox</code> provisional caveat means downstream plugins targeting v0.1 sandbox accept rewrite cost at the next major. Acceptable because no real sandbox plugins exist at v0.1.</li> <li>The <code>test-fixtures</code> feature means tau-ports has two compile configurations CI must exercise (default + <code>test-fixtures</code>); the CI matrix already runs <code>--all-features</code>.</li> <li><code>ToolError::Llm</code> / <code>ToolError::Storage</code> composition means tool authors get one error type to thread, not three. The <code>From</code> impls keep <code>?</code> propagation ergonomic.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-3"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-3">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong><code>async-trait</code> macro</strong> for trait methods. Rejected: adds a proc-macro dependency, boxes every future (<code>Pin<Box<dyn Future>></code>), and was the workaround for the missing language feature that 1.91 now provides natively. No reason to take the dependency.</li> <li><strong>Sync trait methods, with consumers spawning their own tasks.</strong> Rejected: most LLM and storage backends are inherently async (HTTP, file I/O); forcing a sync façade pessimizes the common path.</li> <li><strong>Top-level <code>PortsError</code> umbrella.</strong> Rejected (same reasoning as ADR-0002 decision on <code>DomainError</code>): per-trait enums forever; consumers wanting "any tau-ports error" wrap their own.</li> <li><strong>Stateless <code>Tool</code> only</strong> (no <code>Session</code> associated type). Rejected: long-running stateful tools (database connection, MCP session, subprocess pool) are real; forcing them to thread state through <code>Storage</code> is awkward and pays a serialization cost per call.</li> <li><strong>Single-block <code>LlmProviderMessage</code></strong> (one content per message). Rejected: Anthropic and OpenAI both emit multi-block assistant turns (text + tool_use); a single-block shape would lose fidelity at the wire.</li> <li><strong>Streaming <code>tool_use</code> JSON to consumers as it arrives.</strong> Rejected: consumers (agents, UIs) cannot safely act on partial JSON; every consumer would have to buffer. Buffering at the plugin removes the duplication.</li> <li><strong><code>Storage</code> with TTL / transactions / watch at v0.1.</strong> Rejected: no v0.1 consumer needs them; adding now commits an API surface that may not match real backends. Additive in a later minor.</li> <li><strong>Production sandbox at v0.1.</strong> Rejected: a real sandbox is its own multi-week sub-project (Linux capabilities, seccomp, WASI research). Provisional stub keeps the trait slot reserved.</li> <li><strong>Serde-derive everything from day one.</strong> Rejected: no in-process consumer needs it; gated additive feature is the cheap path when cross-process arrives.</li> <li><strong>Mocks in a separate <code>tau-ports-test</code> crate.</strong> Rejected: extra publish target, extra SemVer surface, drift between mock and trait. The <code>test-fixtures</code> cargo feature colocates them.</li> <li><strong>No <code>provider_specific</code> escape hatch; force every param to be typed.</strong> Rejected: every new vendor would block on a tau-ports PR before plugin authors could wire up the param. The escape hatch + promotion rule keeps tau-ports out of the critical path while still curating the typed surface.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0004-tau-pkg-package-manager--public-api-storage-layout-lockfile"><a class="header" href="#adr-0004-tau-pkg-package-manager--public-api-storage-layout-lockfile">ADR-0004: tau-pkg package manager — public API, storage layout, lockfile</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-04-27 <strong>Supersedes:</strong> —</p> <h2 id="context-4"><a class="header" href="#context-4">Context</a></h2> <p>tau-pkg (sub-project 3) is the package manager that implements <code>tau install</code> from git URLs, as specified by ROADMAP row 3 and Constitution G7, G8, G14. It is the first sub-project that performs real I/O: git clone, file-system mutation, TOML parse-and-write. The earlier sub-projects (tau-domain, tau-ports) were pure data structures and trait boundaries.</p> <p>Per QG18, public API additions require an ADR. This ADR records the decisions made during the sub-project 3 implementation and locks them at v0.1.</p> <p>Relevant Constitution constraints: G7 (package manager is the only way to add extensions), G8 (global + project scopes), G14 (capabilities declared at install), NG9 (no credential management), NG11 (developer tool, not an end-user consumer product), NG12 (runtime not framework).</p> <p>Note that ADR-0005 (custom serde for <code>PackageSource</code> and <code>PackageKind</code>) was filed mid-implementation as a focused fix. ADR-0004 records the broader tau-pkg decisions and cross-references ADR-0005 where relevant.</p> <h2 id="decision-4"><a class="header" href="#decision-4">Decision</a></h2> <h3 id="1-sync-public-api"><a class="header" href="#1-sync-public-api">1. Sync public API</a></h3> <p>The <code>tau_pkg</code> public surface (<code>install</code>, <code>uninstall</code>, <code>list</code>, <code>get</code>, <code>read_manifest</code>, <code>Scope::resolve</code>) is fully synchronous — no <code>async fn</code>, no <code>tokio</code> runtime dependency. The only v0.1 caller is <code>tau-cli</code>, a CLI tool where blocking on git clone is acceptable and concurrency adds no value.</p> <p>Trigger to revisit: a concrete async-server use case where multiple packages must be installed concurrently, or a long-running daemon that must remain responsive during installs.</p> <h3 id="2-shell-out-to-the-git-binary"><a class="header" href="#2-shell-out-to-the-git-binary">2. Shell out to the <code>git</code> binary</a></h3> <p>All git operations (clone, rev-parse) invoke the system <code>git</code> binary via <code>std::process::Command</code>. tau is a developer tool (NG11); users have git on PATH. This eliminates a C dependency (<code>libgit2</code> via <code>git2-rs</code>) and reduces binary size.</p> <p>Trigger to revisit: shipping pre-built binaries to non-developer environments where <code>git</code> is not guaranteed on PATH (NG11 guard).</p> <h3 id="3-storage-layout"><a class="header" href="#3-storage-layout">3. Storage layout</a></h3> <p>Packages are stored at <code><scope>/.tau/packages/<name>/<version>/</code>, where <code><scope></code> is either the project root or the global home directory. This layout supports multi-version cohabitation: two packages at different versions live under different paths and do not conflict. The <code>.tau/</code> directory is considered local state and is not committed (see decision 6).</p> <h3 id="4-scope-resolution"><a class="header" href="#4-scope-resolution">4. Scope resolution</a></h3> <p>tau-pkg walks up the directory tree looking for a <code>.tau/</code> directory (or the project root marker). If no project scope is found, it falls back to the global scope at <code>~/.tau</code>. The global directory respects <code>$TAU_HOME</code> if set, and <code>$XDG_DATA_HOME/tau</code> if <code>$TAU_HOME</code> is absent and <code>$XDG_DATA_HOME</code> is set.</p> <p>This walk-up matches developer intuitions from tools like <code>git</code> and <code>npm</code>. The two-level fallback (env vars → XDG → <code>~/.tau</code>) follows the XDG Base Directory specification.</p> <h3 id="5-lockfile-location"><a class="header" href="#5-lockfile-location">5. Lockfile location</a></h3> <p>Project lockfile: <code><project-root>/tau-lock.toml</code> — at the project root, alongside <code>tau.toml</code> and <code>Cargo.toml</code>. It is intended to be committed to version control (reproducible installs).</p> <p>Global lockfile: <code>~/.tau/tau-lock.toml</code> — inside the global tau home directory, treated as local state and not committed anywhere.</p> <p>The project lockfile lives outside <code>.tau/</code> deliberately: it must be committed while <code>.tau/</code> must not. Placing them in the same directory would require selective <code>.gitignore</code> entries that are fragile and easy to mis-configure.</p> <h3 id="6-tau-is-gitignored-local-state"><a class="header" href="#6-tau-is-gitignored-local-state">6. <code>.tau/</code> is gitignored local state</a></h3> <p>The <code>.tau/</code> directory holds installed package trees and the advisory lock file. It is local, machine-specific state and must not be committed. <code>tau init</code> (Phase 1, in <code>tau-cli</code>) will print a hint recommending that the user add <code>.tau/</code> to <code>.gitignore</code>, but does NOT modify <code>.gitignore</code> automatically. The hint is pure information; the user owns their gitignore.</p> <h3 id="7-lockfile-schema"><a class="header" href="#7-lockfile-schema">7. Lockfile schema</a></h3> <p>The lockfile is versioned (<code>schema_version = 1</code>). Each <code>[[package]]</code> entry records <code>name</code>, <code>active_version</code>, <code>source</code>, and a list of installed versions (<code>[[package.versions]]</code>). Each version entry records <code>version</code>, <code>rev</code>, <code>resolved_commit</code>, <code>sha256</code>, and <code>installed_at</code>. At v0.1 the <code>sha256</code> slot is written as an empty string. Phase 1+ <code>tau verify</code> will populate it by hashing the installed package tree. The schema version field allows future readers to detect and reject or migrate incompatible formats.</p> <h3 id="8-public-api-verbs"><a class="header" href="#8-public-api-verbs">8. Public API verbs</a></h3> <p>The v0.1 public API exports six operations: <code>install</code>, <code>uninstall</code>, <code>list</code>, <code>get</code>, <code>read_manifest</code>, and <code>Scope::resolve</code>. <code>update</code> and <code>verify</code> are deferred to Phase 1+; no stubs are included in the v0.1 crate surface to avoid committing a signature before the implementation exists.</p> <h3 id="9-manifest-location-convention"><a class="header" href="#9-manifest-location-convention">9. Manifest location convention</a></h3> <p><code>tau-pkg</code> expects the package manifest at <code>tau.toml</code> in the root of the cloned repository. This is a convention, not enforced by a config field. ADR-0002 established the manifest schema; ADR-0005 established its serde representation. tau-pkg reads the manifest using <code>read_manifest</code>, which parses to <code>UncheckedManifest</code>, validates it, and returns a <code>PackageManifest</code>.</p> <h3 id="10-no-transitive-dependency-resolution-at-v01"><a class="header" href="#10-no-transitive-dependency-resolution-at-v01">10. No transitive dependency resolution at v0.1</a></h3> <p>The <code>dependencies</code> field in <code>tau.toml</code> is parsed and stored but is informational only. <code>tau install A</code> does not automatically install A's declared dependencies. Users must <code>tau install B</code> separately. This keeps the v0.1 resolver trivially correct (no resolution graph, no version conflict analysis) and avoids committing a resolution algorithm before real use cases are known.</p> <p>Trigger to revisit: the first concrete multi-package workflow where manual chaining becomes a user pain point.</p> <h3 id="11-concurrent-install-protection"><a class="header" href="#11-concurrent-install-protection">11. Concurrent install protection</a></h3> <p>tau-pkg acquires an advisory exclusive file lock at <code>Scope::install_lock_path()</code> (project: <code><project>/.tau/locks/install.lock</code>; global: <code>~/.tau/locks/install.lock</code>) at the start of every mutating operation (<code>install</code>, <code>uninstall</code>) via <code>fs4::FileExt::lock_exclusive</code>. If <code>block_on_lock</code> is <code>false</code>, it uses <code>try_lock_exclusive</code> and returns an error immediately instead of blocking. The lock prevents two concurrent <code>tau install</code> invocations from corrupting the package tree (a real risk in CI pipelines that run multiple install scripts in parallel).</p> <p>The lock is advisory: it does not protect against callers that skip tau-pkg and write to <code>.tau/packages/</code> directly. This is acceptable; such callers are outside the defined API.</p> <h3 id="12-error-taxonomy"><a class="header" href="#12-error-taxonomy">12. Error taxonomy</a></h3> <p>Six typed error enums cover the public surface: <code>ScopeError</code>, <code>GitError</code>, <code>ManifestReadError</code>, <code>RegistryError</code> (shared by <code>list</code>, <code>get</code>, and lockfile load/save), <code>InstallError</code>, <code>UninstallError</code>. There is no top-level <code>PkgError</code> umbrella. The composing errors (<code>InstallError</code>, <code>UninstallError</code>) use <code>#[from]</code> over the leaf errors so <code>?</code> propagation works without manual mapping. This mirrors the tau-domain and tau-ports error policy (see ADR-0003 §3).</p> <h3 id="13-file-scheme-support-in-packagesource"><a class="header" href="#13-file-scheme-support-in-packagesource">13. <code>file://</code> scheme support in <code>PackageSource</code></a></h3> <p><code>PackageSource::Git</code> accepts <code>file://</code> URLs in addition to <code>https</code>, <code>http</code>, <code>ssh</code>, and <code>git</code> schemes (an extension to tau-domain made during the tau-pkg integration test phase). This enables hermetic local test fixtures (no network required in CI) and supports air-gapped installs from a local mirror.</p> <p>The <code>file://</code> scheme is a first-class extension point: <code>GitLocation::from_str</code> in tau-domain accepts <code>file</code> alongside the other schemes, and the serde round-trip (ADR-0005) preserves it as the canonical string form.</p> <h3 id="14-protocolfileallowalways-override-in-gitclone"><a class="header" href="#14-protocolfileallowalways-override-in-gitclone">14. <code>protocol.file.allow=always</code> override in <code>Git::clone</code></a></h3> <p>git 2.38+ sets <code>protocol.file.allow=user</code> by default as a mitigation for <a href="https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-39253">CVE-2022-39253</a>. With that default, cloning a <code>file://</code> URL on a stock git 2.38+ installation "succeeds" with exit code 0 but writes nothing — the protocol layer silently blocks the transfer.</p> <p>tau-pkg passes <code>-c protocol.file.allow=always</code> when invoking <code>git clone</code> with a <code>file://</code> source. The CVE-2022-39253 attack vector requires <code>--recurse-submodules</code>; tau-pkg does not use submodules. The override is therefore safe for the current implementation. This analysis must be re-checked if tau-pkg ever adds submodule support.</p> <h2 id="consequences-4"><a class="header" href="#consequences-4">Consequences</a></h2> <h3 id="positive"><a class="header" href="#positive">Positive</a></h3> <ul> <li>v0.1 ships a working <code>install</code> / <code>uninstall</code> / <code>list</code> / <code>get</code> path against real git repositories, with no async runtime dependency for callers.</li> <li>73 unit tests + 24 integration tests cover the public API surface.</li> <li>Per-operation typed errors enable <code>?</code>-propagation throughout the codebase and give callers precise match arms.</li> <li><code>file://</code> support lets integration tests run hermetically in CI with no network access.</li> </ul> <h3 id="negative"><a class="header" href="#negative">Negative</a></h3> <ul> <li>The sync API blocks the calling thread during git clone. This is fine for a CLI, but embeds in an async server would require <code>spawn_blocking</code>. Trigger to revisit: a concrete async-server use case.</li> <li><code>file://</code> support requires the <code>protocol.file.allow=always</code> env override. The security analysis (CVE-2022-39253 not applicable because we do not use <code>--recurse-submodules</code>) is documented here, but must be re-checked if submodule support is ever added.</li> <li>No transitive dependency resolution: <code>tau install A</code> does not install A's declared dependencies. Users must install each dependency manually.</li> <li>v0.1 lockfile has an empty <code>sha256</code> field — Phase 1+ <code>tau verify</code> will populate it, but until then <code>tau-lock.toml</code> cannot be used to detect tampered installs.</li> </ul> <h3 id="neutral--new-obligations"><a class="header" href="#neutral--new-obligations">Neutral / new obligations</a></h3> <ul> <li>Future PRs that change tau-pkg's public API surface require their own ADRs (QG18).</li> <li>ADR-0005 governs the manifest TOML serde format for <code>PackageSource</code> and <code>PackageKind</code>; this ADR governs the broader tau-pkg API and storage decisions.</li> <li>The walk-up scope resolution algorithm is now the v0.1 standard; changing it (e.g., to never fall back to global scope) requires a new ADR.</li> <li>Adding submodule support in the future requires revisiting the <code>protocol.file.allow=always</code> security analysis in decision 14.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-4"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-4">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <h3 id="a-async-first-public-api"><a class="header" href="#a-async-first-public-api">A. Async-first public API</a></h3> <p>Rejected for v0.1. The only caller is <code>tau-cli</code> (a CLI, not a server), there is no concurrency value at the call site, and adding a <code>tokio</code> dependency would impose a runtime on every future crate that links tau-pkg. Cost vs. benefit is poor; see decision 1.</p> <h3 id="b-pure-rust-git-client-gitoxide-or-git2-rs"><a class="header" href="#b-pure-rust-git-client-gitoxide-or-git2-rs">B. Pure-Rust git client (gitoxide or git2-rs)</a></h3> <p>Rejected for v0.1. tau is a developer tool (NG11); developers have git on PATH. Shelling out avoids a complex C dependency (<code>libgit2</code> via <code>git2-rs</code>) and keeps binary size small. <code>gitoxide</code> is promising but not yet stable across all needed operations. Reconsider when shipping pre-built binaries to environments where git may not be present.</p> <h3 id="c-centralized-package-registry"><a class="header" href="#c-centralized-package-registry">C. Centralized package registry</a></h3> <p>Rejected permanently (NG4). Git URLs are the canonical source of truth for tau packages. A centralized registry introduces availability, trust, and governance dependencies that tau explicitly avoids.</p> <h3 id="d-top-level-pkgerror-umbrella-with-all-variants"><a class="header" href="#d-top-level-pkgerror-umbrella-with-all-variants">D. Top-level <code>PkgError</code> umbrella with all variants</a></h3> <p>Rejected. Per-operation error enums give callers more precision and allow <code>?</code>-propagation through <code>#[from]</code> without pattern-matching over a large umbrella that mixes unrelated variants. Mirrors the error policy established in tau-domain and tau-ports (ADR-0003 §3).</p> <h3 id="e-project-lockfile-under-tautau-locktoml"><a class="header" href="#e-project-lockfile-under-tautau-locktoml">E. Project lockfile under <code>.tau/tau-lock.toml</code></a></h3> <p>Rejected. Project lockfiles must be committed to enable reproducible installs; <code>.tau/</code> must not be committed (it is machine-local state). Placing the lockfile at the project root alongside <code>tau.toml</code> makes the commit vs. non-commit distinction visible and does not require complex <code>.gitignore</code> exceptions.</p> <h3 id="f-tau-init-modifies-gitignore-automatically"><a class="header" href="#f-tau-init-modifies-gitignore-automatically">F. <code>tau init</code> modifies <code>.gitignore</code> automatically</a></h3> <p>Rejected. Automatically mutating a user-owned configuration file is too magical and surprising. <code>tau-cli</code>'s <code>tau init</code> will print a hint; the user decides whether and how to update their <code>.gitignore</code>. Pure information, no mutation.</p> <h3 id="g-no-advisory-file-lock--rely-on-users-not-running-concurrent-installs"><a class="header" href="#g-no-advisory-file-lock--rely-on-users-not-running-concurrent-installs">G. No advisory file lock — rely on users not running concurrent installs</a></h3> <p>Rejected. CI pipelines routinely run multiple install scripts in parallel; a TUI tool may run an install concurrently with a background script. The <code>fs4</code> file lock costs nothing in the non-contended path and prevents silent corruption. Relying on user discipline to avoid concurrency is a footgun.</p> <h3 id="h-protocolfileallowuser-git-238-default-for-file-clones"><a class="header" href="#h-protocolfileallowuser-git-238-default-for-file-clones">H. <code>protocol.file.allow=user</code> (git 2.38+ default) for <code>file://</code> clones</a></h3> <p>Initially considered. Rejected because CI runners with stock git 2.38+ config would produce silently empty clones from <code>file://</code> test fixtures — <code>git clone</code> exits 0 but writes nothing, since the protocol layer blocks the transfer. The override to <code>always</code> is safe because tau-pkg does not use <code>--recurse-submodules</code> (the CVE-2022-39253 attack vector). See decision 14.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0005-custom-serde-for-packagesource-and-packagekind"><a class="header" href="#adr-0005-custom-serde-for-packagesource-and-packagekind">ADR-0005: Custom serde for <code>PackageSource</code> and <code>PackageKind</code></a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-04-27 <strong>Supersedes:</strong> —</p> <h2 id="context-5"><a class="header" href="#context-5">Context</a></h2> <p><code>PackageSource</code> and <code>PackageKind</code> are two of the most user-facing types in tau-domain: every hand-written <code>tau.toml</code> carries them. ADR-0002 ("Manifest format, capability evolution, escape-hatch policy") established the manifest format but left the per-field serde shape implicit — the v0.1 implementation derived <code>Serialize</code>/<code>Deserialize</code> for both types via <code>#[derive]</code>.</p> <p>The derived shape produces awkward TOML for two reasons:</p> <ol> <li> <p><strong><code>PackageSource::Git { location: GitLocation::Url(url::Url), rev }</code></strong> with derived serde produces nested tables because <code>url::Url</code>'s serde is itself nested. A user-written manifest needed:</p> <pre><code class="language-toml">[source] [source.Git] rev = "v0.3.0" [source.Git.location] [source.Git.location.Url] "https" = "_" # ... </code></pre> <p>This is so verbose that the existing <code>tests/manifest_roundtrip.rs</code> integration test side-stepped TOML entirely and exercised the round-trip via <code>serde_json</code>, with a comment calling the format "finicky" and the SAMPLE TOML constant marked as documentary-only.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong><code>PackageKind::Custom { kind: String }</code></strong> is a single-variant <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> enum at v0.1. Derived serde produces <code>[kind.Custom] kind = "tool"</code> for a value that semantically reduces to the string <code>"tool"</code>.</p> </li> </ol> <p>Per QG18, "Changes to the package manifest format" require an ADR. The format users write is a function of the serde representation, so changing the representation is a manifest format change.</p> <p>The natural form a user would write is:</p> <pre><code class="language-toml">source = "https://github.com/x/y.git#main" kind = "tool" </code></pre> <p>Both types already have the necessary infrastructure for this:</p> <ul> <li><code>PackageSource: FromStr + Display</code> round-trips through <code><location>#<rev></code> (proved by <code>proptest_package_source.rs</code>).</li> <li><code>PackageKind</code> carries an inner <code>kind: String</code> that is the canonical text.</li> </ul> <h2 id="decision-5"><a class="header" href="#decision-5">Decision</a></h2> <p>We replace the derived <code>Serialize</code>/<code>Deserialize</code> on <code>PackageSource</code> and <code>PackageKind</code> with custom impls that round-trip through the string form. The change applies whenever the <code>serde</code> feature is enabled.</p> <h3 id="1-packagesource--string-form-via-displayfromstr"><a class="header" href="#1-packagesource--string-form-via-displayfromstr">1. <code>PackageSource</code> — string form via <code>Display</code>/<code>FromStr</code></a></h3> <p><code>Serialize</code> uses <code>serializer.collect_str(self)</code> (formats via <code>Display</code>, no allocation). <code>Deserialize</code> uses a <code>Visitor</code> that delegates to <code>PackageSource::from_str</code>, converting parse failures via <code>serde::de::Error::custom</code>. The visitor implements <code>visit_str</code> and <code>visit_string</code>.</p> <p>Wire form (TOML):</p> <pre><code class="language-toml">source = "https://github.com/x/y.git#main" </code></pre> <p>Wire form (JSON):</p> <pre><code class="language-json">"https://github.com/x/y.git#main" </code></pre> <p><code>GitLocation</code>'s derived serde is removed at the same time. <code>GitLocation</code> is <code>pub</code> but no longer reachable through the manifest's serde path; if a future caller needs to serialize a <code>GitLocation</code> directly, the derive can be added back at that time.</p> <h3 id="2-packagekind--inner-kind-string-form"><a class="header" href="#2-packagekind--inner-kind-string-form">2. <code>PackageKind</code> — inner-kind string form</a></h3> <p><code>Serialize</code> matches the variants exhaustively (legal inside the defining crate even on <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> enums) and emits the inner <code>kind</code> field as a plain string. At v0.1 the only variant is <code>Custom { kind }</code>. <code>Deserialize</code> uses a <code>Visitor</code> that rejects empty strings with a useful serde error and constructs <code>Custom { kind: <input> }</code>.</p> <p>Wire form (TOML):</p> <pre><code class="language-toml">kind = "tool" </code></pre> <p>Wire form (JSON):</p> <pre><code class="language-json">"tool" </code></pre> <p>When typed <code>PackageKind</code> variants land later (e.g., <code>Tool { entrypoint: String }</code>), the custom serde will need to distinguish between a plain-string input (current path → <code>Custom { kind: <s> }</code>) and a richer table input (new typed variant). The chosen mechanism at that point will be a custom string-or-table deserializer with a tagged-discriminator inside the table form. This decision is deferred until a typed variant is concretely needed; the current single-variant case does not require pre-emptive complexity.</p> <h3 id="3-adr-0002-amendment"><a class="header" href="#3-adr-0002-amendment">3. ADR-0002 amendment</a></h3> <p>ADR-0002 referred to "the manifest format" without specifying serde representations. This ADR refines that: the manifest format is canonically what users write in <code>tau.toml</code>, and ADR-0005 documents the serde shapes for two of its fields. Future per-field shape changes follow the same pattern (an ADR per field-or-type whose representation changes).</p> <h2 id="consequences-5"><a class="header" href="#consequences-5">Consequences</a></h2> <h3 id="positive-1"><a class="header" href="#positive-1">Positive</a></h3> <ul> <li>Hand-written <code>tau.toml</code> files are dramatically simpler — the <code>source</code> and <code>kind</code> fields each fit on one line.</li> <li>The <code>tests/manifest_roundtrip.rs</code> integration test now exercises an actual TOML round-trip via the <code>SAMPLE</code> constant (rather than treating it as documentary). The "finicky TOML" caveat is gone.</li> <li>The wire form is symmetric with <code>PackageSource::FromStr</code>/<code>Display</code> — there is one canonical text representation, used consistently in CLI input, manifests, lockfiles, and error messages.</li> <li>Lockfile diffs become readable: a <code>tau-lock.toml</code> records <code>source = "https://github.com/x/y.git#main"</code> instead of nested tables.</li> </ul> <h3 id="negative-1"><a class="header" href="#negative-1">Negative</a></h3> <ul> <li>A small forward-compatibility burden when typed <code>PackageKind</code> variants land later. The mitigation is documented in §2: a string-or-table custom deserializer at that time. The burden is local to one type and one impl.</li> <li>The derived <code>Serialize</code>/<code>Deserialize</code> on <code>GitLocation</code> is removed. If a future caller needs to serialize a <code>GitLocation</code> directly (without going through <code>PackageSource</code>), the derive must be re-added. This is YAGNI for v0.1 — the only known consumer is the manifest format, and that path now goes through <code>PackageSource</code>'s custom impl.</li> </ul> <h3 id="neutral--new-obligations-1"><a class="header" href="#neutral--new-obligations-1">Neutral / new obligations</a></h3> <ul> <li>Any future ADR proposing a new variant on <code>PackageSource</code> or <code>PackageKind</code> must specify how the variant interacts with the string-form serde. The natural extension for <code>PackageKind</code> is a string-or-table form (described in §2). For <code>PackageSource</code>, future variants would extend the <code>Display</code>/<code>FromStr</code> grammar — e.g. a <code>Path</code> variant could serialize as <code>"file:///abs/path"</code> or similar — preserving the single-string property.</li> <li>Proptest coverage (added in <code>tests/proptest_package_source_serde.rs</code>) becomes a regression gate: any future change to the custom impls must keep the proptest passing.</li> <li>Lockfile schema unaffected at the field-list level: <code>LockedPackage.source: PackageSource</code> stays the same type, only the serialization differs. Existing <code>schema_version = 1</code> covers both before and after this ADR (no on-disk lockfile shipped in the wild yet).</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-5"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-5">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <h3 id="a-keep-derived-serde-document-the-verbose-form-in-user-facing-docs"><a class="header" href="#a-keep-derived-serde-document-the-verbose-form-in-user-facing-docs">A. Keep derived serde, document the verbose form in user-facing docs</a></h3> <p>Rejected. The derived <code>[source.Git.location.Url] "https" = "_"</code> form is unworkable as a user-facing format — it leaks <code>url::Url</code>'s internal representation, requires users to know the Rust enum variant tags, and makes hand-written manifests impractical. The cost of writing custom serde impls (one per type, ~30 lines each) is far smaller than the cost imposed on every plugin author writing a manifest.</p> <h3 id="b-custom-serde-for-packagesource-only-leave-packagekind-derived"><a class="header" href="#b-custom-serde-for-packagesource-only-leave-packagekind-derived">B. Custom serde for <code>PackageSource</code> only, leave <code>PackageKind</code> derived</a></h3> <p>Rejected. <code>PackageKind</code>'s derived form (<code>[kind.Custom] kind = "tool"</code>) is also user-facing and equally awkward. The fix is symmetric — both types have a canonical inner-string form. Doing one but not the other would leave users writing a mix of natural and verbose forms in the same <code>tau.toml</code>, which is worse than either uniform alternative.</p> <h3 id="c-use-serde_withs-displayfromstr-attribute"><a class="header" href="#c-use-serde_withs-displayfromstr-attribute">C. Use <code>serde_with</code>'s <code>DisplayFromStr</code> attribute</a></h3> <p>Rejected for v0.1. Adding a <code>serde_with</code> workspace dependency for two impls is over-tooling. The explicit <code>Visitor</code> impls are ~30 lines each, easy to read, and make the validation behavior (empty-string rejection on <code>PackageKind</code>, <code>PackageSourceError</code> propagation on <code>PackageSource</code>) explicit. Reconsider if a third or fourth type needs the same treatment.</p> <h3 id="d-field-level-serdewith---on-uncheckedmanifestsource--kind"><a class="header" href="#d-field-level-serdewith---on-uncheckedmanifestsource--kind">D. Field-level <code>#[serde(with = "...")]</code> on <code>UncheckedManifest.source</code> / <code>.kind</code></a></h3> <p>Rejected. The custom (de)serialization belongs to the type, not to a particular field that uses it. Putting it on the field would force every consumer of <code>PackageSource</code> (the lockfile, future serialization paths) to repeat the attribute — and would diverge if any consumer forgot.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0006-tau-runtime-kernel--tool-capabilities-amendment"><a class="header" href="#adr-0006-tau-runtime-kernel--tool-capabilities-amendment">ADR-0006: tau-runtime kernel + Tool capabilities amendment</a></h1> <blockquote> <p><strong>Updated 2026-05-31 (β.1.4):</strong> kernel now lives in <code>tau-runtime-core</code> (no_std + alloc, executor-agnostic); the tokio host shell is <code>tau-runtime-tokio</code>. References below to <code>tau-runtime</code> should be read as the union of the two crates unless otherwise noted.</p> </blockquote> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-04-28 <strong>Supersedes:</strong> — <strong>Amends:</strong> ADR-0003 §2 "Four trait shapes" (the <code>Tool</code> trait gains an additive <code>capabilities()</code> default method).</p> <h2 id="context-6"><a class="header" href="#context-6">Context</a></h2> <p>tau-runtime (sub-project 4, ROADMAP row 4) is the kernel that runs agents: it loads pre-constructed plugin instances, dispatches the multi-turn agent loop against an <code>LlmBackend</code> and the registered <code>Tool</code>s, enforces capability declarations at runtime, and emits structured logs. It is the first sub-project that orchestrates plugin instances rather than just defining their data shapes (tau-domain), trait boundaries (tau-ports), or installation (tau-pkg). Per ROADMAP row 4 the v0.1 scope is the <strong>solo path</strong> only; multi-agent orchestration (G10) is sub-project 5+.</p> <p>Per QG18, public API additions and plugin-trait amendments require ADRs. This ADR records BOTH the kernel design AND the additive <code>Tool::capabilities() -> &[Capability]</code> amendment to ADR-0003. The two are tightly coupled: typed enforcement at runtime (G14) requires the trait-level declaration, and the amendment exists solely because tau-runtime needs it. Bundling avoids splitting one motivated change across two ADRs; future tau-ports amendments motivated by their own sub-projects will get their own ADRs (no promiscuous bundling).</p> <p>Relevant Constitution constraints: G6 (tau is a runtime, not a framework), G7 (package manager is the only way to add extensions), G9 (observable by default), G10 (solo + orchestration paths; sub-project 4 is solo only), G11 (typed addressed messages), G14 (capabilities declared at install AND enforced at runtime), G16 (overhead bounds), NG6 (no persistent agent memory), NG9 (tau does not redact for the caller), NG12 (runtime not framework), QG2 (<code>thiserror</code> everywhere), QG3 (panics are bugs), QG5 (parsers earn proptests), QG18 (ADRs for public API + trait changes).</p> <p>ADR-0006 also notes a small set of mid-implementation <strong>additive constructors</strong> added during the run-loop work: <code>Message::new</code>, <code>AgentStatus::failed</code>, <code>CompletionRequest::new</code>, <code>LlmProviderMessage::{user, assistant, tool_result}</code>, <code>ToolUse::new</code>, <code>TokenUsage::new</code>, <code>SessionContext::new</code>, <code>PackageId::new</code>. They were forced by <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> on those types blocking struct-literal construction across crates and were registered in the same commit as Task 10 (the run loop). All are additive (no existing API broken). The kernel decisions in this ADR depend on those constructors existing.</p> <h2 id="decision-6"><a class="header" href="#decision-6">Decision</a></h2> <h3 id="1-pure-kernel-skeleton-scope"><a class="header" href="#1-pure-kernel-skeleton-scope">1. Pure kernel skeleton scope</a></h3> <p>Sub-project 4 ships a kernel testable in isolation against tau-ports' mock plugins (<code>MockLlmBackend</code>, <code>MockTool</code>, <code>MockStorage</code> under the <code>test-fixtures</code> cargo feature). Real plugin packages — concrete Anthropic / OpenAI backends, real filesystem / shell / HTTP tools — land in sub-project 5 (tau-cli) and beyond. tau-runtime accepts pre-constructed plugin instances via the builder; it does not load packages from disk at v0.1 (no cdylib, no dlopen). The integration tests at <code>crates/tau-runtime/tests/run_*.rs</code> exercise the loop end-to-end against mocks; sub-project 5 wires the same kernel to real plugins.</p> <p>Trigger to revisit: when sub-project 5+ lands real plugins and the kernel needs to surface a serve-mode protocol on top of the embeddable Rust API.</p> <h3 id="2-async-public-api"><a class="header" href="#2-async-public-api">2. Async public API</a></h3> <p><code>Runtime::run</code> and <code>Runtime::run_default</code> are <code>async fn</code>. tau-ports' <code>LlmBackend::complete</code>, <code>Tool::invoke</code>, <code>Storage::*</code> etc. are native <code>async fn in trait</code> (per ADR-0003 §1). Wrapping them in a sync facade would require <code>tokio::runtime::Handle::current().block_on(...)</code> at every call site, which fails outside a running runtime and pushes complexity onto the kernel for no value. The kernel's library code is async-runtime agnostic — bare <code>async fn</code> and <code>.await</code> only, no <code>tokio::sync</code>, <code>tokio::spawn</code>, or <code>tokio::select!</code>. <code>tokio</code> is a dev-dependency only; callers (typically tau-cli) bring the runtime at the binary level.</p> <p>Trigger to revisit: a concrete use case where async forces unwanted complexity on a small embedding.</p> <h3 id="3-builder-pattern-construction-with-name-keyed-registries"><a class="header" href="#3-builder-pattern-construction-with-name-keyed-registries">3. Builder pattern construction with name-keyed registries</a></h3> <p><code>Runtime::builder().with_*(...)*.build()</code> is the public construction path. The builder accumulates plugin instances under their <code>name()</code>; this enables dispatch by name in messages (<code>Address::Tool(String)</code>) and allows build-time detection of name collisions within a kind. The builder methods are <code>with_llm_backend(impl LlmBackend + 'static)</code>, <code>with_tool(impl Tool<Session = ()> + 'static)</code>, and <code>with_storage(impl Storage + 'static)</code> — generics, NOT <code>Box<dyn Trait></code> — because the underlying plugin traits are not dyn-compatible (native <code>async fn in trait</code> is not object-safe in Rust 1.93).</p> <p>The builder boxes through internal wrapper traits (<code>DynLlmBackend</code>, <code>DynTool</code>, <code>DynStorage</code>) with blanket impls for <code>T: Trait + 'static</code>. This is the standard "box once at the dyn-cast boundary" pattern. The wrapper types are <code>pub</code> so future tau-runtime helpers can refer to them, but they are <strong>not part of the public API contract</strong> — they are an implementation detail and will be removed when tau-ports gains a <code>trait_variant</code>-generated dyn-compatible variant.</p> <p>Build-time validations: at least one LLM backend must be registered; no name collisions within a kind (two LLM backends, two tools, or two storages with the same <code>name()</code>). Both produce typed <code>BuildError</code> variants (<code>NoLlmBackend</code>, <code>NameCollision { kind, name }</code>).</p> <p>Trigger to revisit: when tau-ports gains native dyn-compatibility (the dyn-shim becomes deletable boilerplate).</p> <h3 id="4-session---v01-tool-limitation"><a class="header" href="#4-session---v01-tool-limitation">4. <code>Session = ()</code> v0.1 tool limitation</a></h3> <p>The kernel's tool registry stores <code>Arc<DynTool></code> where the underlying trait is <code>Tool<Session = ()></code>. Stateless tools (the common case) work directly; stateful tools must wrap themselves in <code>tau_ports::StatelessAdapter</code> or wait for a future <code>DynTool</code> extension once erased associated types stabilize on stable Rust. Accepting arbitrary <code>Session</code> types from external plugins would require erased-associated-type machinery beyond v0.1's scope.</p> <p>Trigger to revisit: the first stateful tool that genuinely cannot be expressed via <code>StatelessAdapter</code> — e.g., a long-lived database connection that must persist across <code>invoke</code> calls within one agent run.</p> <h3 id="5-multi-turn-batch-loop-not-streaming"><a class="header" href="#5-multi-turn-batch-loop-not-streaming">5. Multi-turn batch loop, not streaming</a></h3> <p><code>LlmBackend::complete</code> (batch) is the v0.1 surface used by the agent loop. <code>LlmBackend::stream</code> exists in tau-ports (per ADR-0003 §2) but tau-runtime does not invoke it at v0.1. Streaming integration is purely additive (a new <code>Runtime::run_streaming</code> method) and does not break the batch surface when it lands.</p> <p>Trigger to revisit: a streaming-UX-driven use case (TUI rendering tokens as they arrive, latency-sensitive interactive flows).</p> <h3 id="6-caller-supplied-manifest"><a class="header" href="#6-caller-supplied-manifest">6. Caller-supplied manifest</a></h3> <p><code>Runtime::run(agent_def, package_manifest, initial_message, options)</code> takes the package manifest as a parameter rather than fetching it itself. tau-runtime has no <code>tau-pkg</code> dependency. Callers (tau-cli, in-process embedders) call <code>tau_pkg::read_manifest</code> and feed the result in. The dependency direction stays crisp: tau-runtime → tau-domain, tau-ports; tau-cli → tau-runtime, tau-pkg.
