The user never writes a list of toolchains in priority order.</li> <li><strong>Probe results are runtime data; chain authoring is upfront.</strong> A chain in <code>tau.toml</code> can't react to "Docker isn't installed on this host" as cleanly as a resolver invoked at runtime against a registry of "what does each adapter advertise?".</li> <li><strong>Plugin-side requirements are first-class.</strong> A plugin that genuinely requires Strict tier (e.g. one that handles untrusted user input) needs to express that, and the project + plugin requirements need to <em>unify</em> before the resolver picks an adapter. A chain has no place for this.</li> <li><strong>Activation default needs a defensible failure mode.</strong> macOS without Docker has no Linux-native landlock, no container runtime — should tau refuse to start, fall back to no isolation with a warn, or something else? The chain model didn't have a clean answer.</li> </ul> <p>The design space (full options table in <a href="decisions/../superpowers/specs/2026-05-04-sandbox-activation-design.html">the design doc</a>) was explored fresh. The chain was rejected in favor of declarative requirements + a static adapter registry + a runtime resolver. Six discrete decisions follow.</p> <h2 id="decision-1--sandboxing-is-on-by-default-opt-out-is-explicit-and-visible"><a class="header" href="#decision-1--sandboxing-is-on-by-default-opt-out-is-explicit-and-visible">Decision 1 — Sandboxing is ON by default; opt-out is explicit and visible</a></h2> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> every <code>Runtime::run</code> builds a <code>SandboxPlan</code> per plugin, calls <code>resolve_adapter</code> to obtain a concrete <code>SandboxAdapter</code>, and passes both into <code>wrap_spawn</code> at the plugin host layer. The escape hatch is the explicit <code>--no-sandbox</code> global flag (or <code>[sandbox] required_tier = "none"</code> in scope config), which selects the <code>passthrough</code> adapter — never silent fall-through.</p> <p><strong>Context:</strong> the alternative was opt-in (a flag like <code>--enable-sandbox</code>). Defense in depth means the secure default must be the path of least resistance; if the user opts out, they declare it. Constitution G12 and ADR-0014 §6 already established "OS-level enforcement is the backstop"; not activating it by default would leave that promise unredeemed.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Existing tau projects with no <code>[sandbox]</code> block default to <code>required_tier = strict</code>. On Linux, the native adapter satisfies this. On macOS without Docker, resolution fails with a guided diagnostic (see Decision 3).</li> <li>The <code>passthrough</code> adapter (Decision 4) is a registered first-class adapter, not a "no sandbox" sentinel. <code>--no-sandbox</code> is honored by routing to passthrough; the user always knows which adapter is in play.</li> <li>Operators get a one-line CI rule: "no project ships without a <code>[sandbox]</code> block AND that block resolves on the target platform". <code>tau resolve --check-sandbox</code> is the gate.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Opt-in flag.</strong> Rejected: violates secure-by-default. Defense-in-depth is undermined when the kernel layer is dormant unless explicitly turned on.</li> <li><strong>Auto-fall-soft to passthrough on resolution failure.</strong> Rejected: silent demotion is the worst possible failure mode for a security feature. The user must learn that resolution failed, not discover via a post-mortem.</li> </ul> <h2 id="decision-2--pluginhostoptionssandbox_adapter-not-runtimebuilder-di"><a class="header" href="#decision-2--pluginhostoptionssandbox_adapter-not-runtimebuilder-di">Decision 2 — <code>PluginHostOptions.sandbox_adapter</code>, not Runtime::builder DI</a></h2> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> the resolved <code>Arc<SandboxAdapter></code> is carried on <code>PluginHostOptions</code> (along with <code>force_passthrough: bool</code> and <code>force_adapter_kind: Option<SandboxAdapterKind></code> for the CLI overrides), not injected through a builder method on <code>Runtime</code>. The CLI's <code>tau-cli/src/cmd/plugin_loader.rs::load_plugins</code> is the single integration point that reads scope config, calls <code>resolve_adapter</code>, and threads results through.</p> <p><strong>Context:</strong> the alternative was <code>Runtime::builder().with_sandbox(adapter)</code> — closer to the <code>with_*</code> methods already on the builder. But the builder is constructed in <code>Runtime::run</code>, before scope config is loaded. Pushing sandbox resolution into the builder would have required the builder to depend on <code>tau_pkg::scope</code>, which inverts the existing dependency graph (<code>tau-pkg</code> depends on <code>tau-runtime</code> for <code>RuntimeBuilder</code> reuse).</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li><code>Runtime</code> itself is unaware of sandboxing. The kernel still calls <code>plugin_host::spawn_and_handshake</code>; the sandbox enforcement happens during <code>wrap_spawn</code>, transparent to the agent loop.</li> <li>The CLI's <code>plugin_loader</code> becomes the natural home for resolver + adapter wiring — it already loads scope config, lockfile, and plugin manifests.</li> <li>Tests that don't go through the CLI (the runtime's own integration tests) can construct <code>PluginHostOptions { sandbox_adapter: None, .. }</code> to skip sandboxing entirely. The mock adapter is still injectable via the <code>TAU_TESTING_ALLOW_MOCK_SANDBOX=1</code> env-var override (preserved from priority 12).</li> <li>A future "library mode" caller (Phase 2 work) sets the field directly without going through the CLI surface.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong><code>Runtime::builder().with_sandbox(adapter)</code>.</strong> Rejected: inverts dep graph; adds a builder method that's only called from one place.</li> <li><strong>Static config / lazy_static.</strong> Rejected: testing is harder; resolution becomes implicit.</li> </ul> <h2 id="decision-3--hard-refuse-on-resolution-failure-no-silent-fall-through"><a class="header" href="#decision-3--hard-refuse-on-resolution-failure-no-silent-fall-through">Decision 3 — Hard refuse on resolution failure (no silent fall-through)</a></h2> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> when <code>resolve_adapter</code> returns <code>Err(ResolutionError)</code>, the runtime exits with code 2 and a guided multi-option diagnostic. There is no fall-back to passthrough, no warning-and-continue, no degraded mode. The user must either (a) install a satisfying adapter (e.g. Docker), (b) lower <code>required_tier</code> in scope config, or (c) pass <code>--no-sandbox</code> explicitly.</p> <p><strong>Context:</strong> the failure mode of a security feature is what defines it. Silent demotion gives users a sandbox icon in their config and zero enforcement at runtime. Three-bucket exit codes (ADR-0007 §7) give us "configuration error" = exit 2; this is the canonical case.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>macOS users without Docker who don't have a <code>[sandbox]</code> block and don't pass <code>--no-sandbox</code> get exit 2 on first run. The diagnostic shows: which adapters were tried, why each was rejected (platform / probe / tier / shape / plugin tier), and three remediations they can pick from. <code>tau sandbox setup</code> (Decision 5 corollary) walks them through option (b) interactively.</li> <li>The <code>tau resolve --check-sandbox</code> subcommand exits 2 on the same conditions, giving CI a pre-flight gate without needing to spawn plugins.</li> <li>The error rendering surface (<code>crates/tau-cli/src/cmd/error_render.rs</code>) gets formal multi-option output with insta snapshot tests.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Fall-soft to passthrough with a warn.</strong> Rejected: see Decision 1's discussion. The whole point of activation is that the kernel layer is real, not optional.</li> <li><strong>Refuse only if no <code>[sandbox]</code> block exists; permit fall-soft if the block lists alternatives.</strong> Rejected: the chain model in disguise; we already rejected chains.</li> </ul> <h2 id="decision-4--passthrough-is-a-registered-first-class-adapter-not-none"><a class="header" href="#decision-4--passthrough-is-a-registered-first-class-adapter-not-none">Decision 4 — <code>passthrough</code> is a registered first-class adapter, not "None"</a></h2> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> add a <code>passthrough</code> adapter (<code>crates/tau-runtime/src/sandbox/passthrough.rs</code>, ~30 LOC) that implements <code>tau_ports::Sandbox</code> directly. It probes <code>Available</code> everywhere, advertises every shape as supported, validates every plan as Ok, and <code>wrap_spawn</code> returns the command unchanged. It's registered in the adapter registry with <code>tier = None</code> and <code>priority = 0</code> (lowest). <code>SandboxAdapter</code> gains a <code>Passthrough</code> variant.</p> <p><strong>Context:</strong> the priority-12 design represented "no sandbox" as <code>Option<SandboxAdapter>::None</code>. That was always going to age badly: every consumer of <code>Option<&SandboxAdapter></code> gets a special case for <code>None</code>, the overrides logic (<code>--no-sandbox</code>) has to short-circuit before reaching the adapter layer, and the registry has to model "the always-available fall-back" as a separate concept from "the available adapters".</p> <p><strong>Decision</strong> treats "no isolation" as a real adapter with its own behavior: it satisfies <code>required_tier = none</code>, fails <code>required_tier = light</code> and stronger via the tier filter, and fails plugin tier requirements via the plugin-tier filter. The user-facing name is "passthrough", consistent across <code>tau sandbox status</code>, error messages, and <code>--sandbox passthrough</code>.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li><code>--no-sandbox</code> is sugar for <code>--sandbox passthrough</code> (forces the adapter regardless of registry filtering).</li> <li><code>tau sandbox status</code> always shows passthrough as Available, with an explicit "delivers no isolation" note. Users see what they'd be getting.</li> <li>The registry's lowest-priority entry catches all <code>required_tier = none</code> requests when no other adapter probed Available.</li> <li>Plugin-tier filtering: a plugin declaring <code>required_tier = strict</code> rejects passthrough even when the project says <code>required_tier = none</code> (see Decision 6).</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Keep <code>Option<SandboxAdapter>::None</code>.</strong> Rejected: special cases ripple through every caller; the override logic gets increasingly fragile.</li> <li><strong>Name it <code>bare</code>, <code>host</code>, or <code>none</code>.</strong> Rejected: <code>none</code> collides with the tier name; <code>bare</code> is jargon; <code>host</code> is ambiguous (host vs guest namespace). <code>passthrough</code> is the established term in the network/security space for "let the bytes through unchanged".</li> </ul> <h2 id="decision-5--declarative-requirements--adapter-registry--resolver-bazel-style"><a class="header" href="#decision-5--declarative-requirements--adapter-registry--resolver-bazel-style">Decision 5 — Declarative requirements + adapter registry + resolver (Bazel-style)</a></h2> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> the scope config schema migrates from v2 chain (<code>[sandbox] chain = [{ kind = "native" }, { kind = "container" }, { kind = "passthrough" }]</code>) to v3 declarative (<code>[sandbox] required_tier = "strict"</code>, optional <code>required_shapes = [...]</code>). A static <code>AdapterRegistration</code> slice in <code>tau-runtime::sandbox::registry</code> enumerates the four adapters with their <code>(platforms, tiers_supported, shapes_supported, priority)</code> metadata. <code>resolve_adapter</code> filters the registry through a 5-stage pipeline (platform → probe → tier → shape → plugin tier) and picks the highest-priority remaining candidate.</p> <p><strong>Context:</strong> Bazel's platforms/toolchains is the closest analogue. The BUILD file declares the <em>target platform</em> (<code>cpu="arm64", os="linux"</code>); each toolchain declares which <code>target_compatible_with</code> constraints it satisfies; Bazel's resolver picks. The user writes intent ("I need to build for arm64-linux"), the toolchain author writes capability ("I support arm64-linux", with priority), and the resolver produces a concrete pick at build time.</p> <p>The same shape applies to sandboxing:</p> <ul> <li>The project author writes intent: <code>required_tier = "strict"</code>, optionally <code>required_shapes = ["FilesystemRead", "ProcessExec"]</code>.</li> <li>The adapter author registers capability: native says <code>(linux, [light, strict], [Filesystem*, Process*, Network*], priority=100)</code>; container says <code>(any, [light, strict], [Filesystem*, Process*, Network*], priority=50)</code>; remote says <code>(any, [light, strict], [Filesystem*, Process*], priority=25, probe=Unavailable)</code>; passthrough says <code>(any, [none], [all], priority=0)</code>.</li> <li>The resolver — invoked at every <code>Runtime::run</code> — computes the intersection and picks.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>New adapters land additively. Adding a <code>tau-sandbox-macos</code> adapter (sub-project J) becomes one new <code>AdapterRegistration</code> entry plus the adapter crate. No changes to consumers.</li> <li>The error message for "nothing matches" can list every adapter that was tried and why — the resolver has all the data; it just renders it via <code>ResolutionError::NoAdapterMatches { tried: Vec<(name, ResolutionRejection)> }</code>.</li> <li>Tests can probe the resolver directly (<code>resolve_adapter(&requirements, &plugins).await</code>) without spawning a runtime. The 5-stage pipeline is unit-testable in isolation.</li> <li>Schema migration from v2 to v3 is best-effort: v2 lockfiles auto-load with a <code>tracing::warn!</code> (consistent with the lockfile v3→v4 precedent from priority 7) and the resolver picks a sensible v3 equivalent. v3 is the canonical form going forward.</li> <li>A new family of CLI subcommands grows naturally: <code>tau sandbox status</code> (read-only diagnostic), <code>tau sandbox setup</code> (interactive + non-interactive scope config writer). The resolver is the single source of truth that <code>status</code> queries.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Keep the chain model.</strong> Rejected for the reasons in Context: conflates intent with mechanism, doesn't model plugin-side requirements cleanly, can't react to runtime probe data.</li> <li><strong>Custom scoring function instead of priority + filter pipeline.</strong> Rejected: more flexible than needed; harder to reason about; the priority sort suffices for the four adapters we have, and adding new ones doesn't require rebalancing scores.</li> <li><strong>Dynamic adapter loading (plugins as adapters).</strong> Rejected: out of scope; the registry is intentionally compile-time so adapters can be type-checked. Future work could add a registration ABI.</li> </ul> <h2 id="decision-6--plugin-side-tier-declarations-symmetric-to-project-requirements"><a class="header" href="#decision-6--plugin-side-tier-declarations-symmetric-to-project-requirements">Decision 6 — Plugin-side tier declarations (symmetric to project requirements)</a></h2> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> add <code>[sandbox]</code> to the plugin manifest (<code>PluginSandboxRequirements { required_tier: Option<PluginRequiredTier>, required_shapes: Vec<CapabilityShape> }</code>). The resolver's 5th filter stage rejects any adapter whose tier is below the maximum tier required across all plugins in the load set. <code>ResolutionError::PluginTierMismatch</code> is a separate error variant from <code>NoAdapterMatches</code> so the diagnostic can identify which plugin is asking for what.</p> <p><strong>Context:</strong> a plugin that processes untrusted input (e.g. a parser, a code formatter, an HTTP client) has a defensible reason to insist on Strict tier even if the project author would have been content with Light. Without a plugin-side declaration, the project's <code>[sandbox]</code> block is the only signal — and the project author may not know which plugins need stronger isolation.</p> <p>The symmetry mirrors <code>dependencies</code> resolution: the project declares "I want package X"; the plugin declares "I require package Y at version Z". The dep resolver intersects. The sandbox resolver does the same with tiers.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Existing plugin manifests with no <code>[sandbox]</code> block default to <code>required_tier = None</code> (no extra requirement beyond the project's). This is <code>#[serde(default)]</code> on <code>PluginSandboxRequirements</code>, so unmodified plugin manifests remain valid.</li> <li>The five existing plugins (anthropic, ollama, openai, fs-read, shell) ship with no <code>[sandbox]</code> block in this sub-project. Sub-project B adds explicit declarations as part of the per-plugin compatibility verification pass.</li> <li><code>tau resolve --check-sandbox</code> is extended to surface plugin-tier mismatches even when the project's <code>required_tier = none</code> would otherwise have skipped tier checks. (Without this, a project with <code>required_tier = none</code> would silently let a plugin's <code>required_tier = strict</code> slip through.)</li> <li>The diagnostic for plugin-tier mismatch names the offending plugin: "plugin <code>foo</code> requires Strict but resolved adapter <code>passthrough</code> provides None — please install Docker or run on Linux".</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Plugin-side declarations only (no project-side).</strong> Rejected: the project author needs to declare "I want this whole agent to run Strict" for the case where a plugin's manifest is silent.</li> <li><strong>Project-side only (no plugin-side).</strong> Rejected: makes the project author responsible for knowing each plugin's needs. Doesn't scale to a real plugin ecosystem.</li> <li><strong><code>required_shapes</code> on plugins, no <code>required_tier</code>.</strong> Rejected: shapes are a finer-grained vocabulary that plugins use to express <em>what they need to do</em> (FilesystemRead, ProcessExec, ...). Tier is a coarser vocabulary expressing <em>how strong an isolation regime they require</em>. They're not interchangeable; both exist on the plugin side, with <code>required_shapes</code> already present from priority 12.</li> </ul> <h2 id="implementation-summary"><a class="header" href="#implementation-summary">Implementation summary</a></h2> <p>The 12 commits on <code>feat/sandbox-activation-spec</code> (PR #23) realize these decisions via:</p> <div class="table-wrapper"><table><thead><tr><th>Layer</th><th>Crate</th><th>Files</th></tr></thead><tbody> <tr><td>Schema migration v2 → v3</td><td><code>tau-pkg</code></td><td><code>src/scope.rs</code></td></tr> <tr><td>Plugin manifest schema</td><td><code>tau-domain</code></td><td><code>src/package/sandbox.rs</code></td></tr> <tr><td>Adapter registry</td><td><code>tau-runtime</code></td><td><code>src/sandbox/registry.rs</code></td></tr> <tr><td>Passthrough adapter</td><td><code>tau-runtime</code></td><td><code>src/sandbox/passthrough.rs</code></td></tr> <tr><td>Resolution error taxonomy</td><td><code>tau-runtime</code></td><td><code>src/sandbox/resolution_error.rs</code></td></tr> <tr><td>Resolver (5-stage pipeline)</td><td><code>tau-runtime</code></td><td><code>src/sandbox/resolver.rs</code></td></tr> <tr><td>Plugin host integration</td><td><code>tau-runtime</code></td><td><code>src/plugin_host/mod.rs</code></td></tr> <tr><td>CLI integration</td><td><code>tau-cli</code></td><td><code>src/cmd/plugin_loader.rs</code></td></tr> <tr><td>Global CLI flags</td><td><code>tau-cli</code></td><td><code>src/cli.rs</code></td></tr> <tr><td>Error renderer</td><td><code>tau-cli</code></td><td><code>src/cmd/error_render.rs</code></td></tr> <tr><td>Sandbox subcommands</td><td><code>tau-cli</code></td><td><code>src/cmd/sandbox.rs</code></td></tr> <tr><td><code>--check-sandbox</code> extension</td><td><code>tau-cli</code></td><td><code>src/cmd/resolve.rs</code></td></tr> </tbody></table> </div> <p>Test coverage: ~250 unit tests across the workspace pass on the 25-job CI matrix (Linux/macOS/Windows × stable/1.91); 24 doc tests pass. No new CI jobs were added (branch protection stays at 25 required checks, unchanged from the priority-12 baseline).</p> <p>The mock adapter is unchanged in <code>tau-ports/src/fixtures.rs</code>; the <code>TAU_TESTING_ALLOW_MOCK_SANDBOX=1</code> env-var injection path bypasses the registry directly. Sub-project H from the followups doc handles the eventual cleanup.</p> <h2 id="forward-links"><a class="header" href="#forward-links">Forward links</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>Sub-project B</strong> (plugin compatibility verification) builds directly on this work: per-plugin <code>tau resolve --check-sandbox</code> runs, plugin manifest <code>[sandbox]</code> blocks added where appropriate, Layer 2 install-time cross-check.</li> <li><strong>Sub-project D</strong> (e2e CI) gains a clean activation point: e2e tests can rely on resolved adapters rather than mocking the chain.</li> <li><strong>Phase 2 sub-project A</strong> (<code>tau check</code> standalone) reuses <code>resolve_adapter</code> + <code>validate_plan_against_adapter</code> as the pre-flight validation surface.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0016-plugin-compatibility-verification--layer-2-install-time-cross-check--per-plugin-harness"><a class="header" href="#adr-0016-plugin-compatibility-verification--layer-2-install-time-cross-check--per-plugin-harness">ADR-0016: Plugin compatibility verification — Layer 2 install-time cross-check + per-plugin harness</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-05-04 <strong>Deciders:</strong> Titouan Lebocq <strong>Supersedes:</strong> — <strong>Closes:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Sub-project B from <a href="decisions/../superpowers/specs/2026-05-03-sandboxing-followups.html">the sandboxing follow-ups</a> — the 5 real shipped plugins now declare <code>[sandbox] required_tier = "strict"</code>, install carries Layer 2 cross-check at step 8.7, and a verification harness exists in <code>tau-plugin-compat</code>.</li> <li>The foundation portion of sub-project D (controlled-environment test binary + landlock-symlink fix in <code>tau-sandbox-native::light::resolve_symlinks_for_landlock</code>) — D's remainder (re-introducing 5 e2e test files) stays as a separate sub-project. <strong>Amends:</strong></li> <li><a href="decisions/0015-sandbox-activation.html">ADR-0015</a> Decision 6 — plugin manifests can now declare <code>[sandbox] required_tier</code>. The 5 real plugins (<code>anthropic</code>, <code>ollama</code>, <code>openai</code>, <code>fs-read</code>, <code>shell</code>) declare <code>Strict</code>. Toy plugins (<code>echo-llm</code>, <code>echo-tool</code>) omit the block. <strong>Refines:</strong></li> <li><a href="decisions/0008-plugin-loading.html">ADR-0008</a> — install lifecycle gains step 8.7 between source SHA-256 (8.6) and lockfile write (9). On cross-check failure, install aborts with <code>InstallError::CrossCheck { message }</code>; user retries via <code>tau install --force</code> after fixing the manifest.</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-16"><a class="header" href="#context-16">Context</a></h2> <p>Sub-project A (<a href="decisions/0015-sandbox-activation.html">ADR-0015</a>) shipped sandboxing on by default at commit <code>7fe6cfb</code> on 2026-05-04. Every plugin spawn now flows through <code>resolve_adapter</code> against the static adapter registry. That work proved 250+ unit tests pass; the workspace compiles cleanly across Linux/macOS/Windows × stable/1.91.</p> <p>What sub-project A's CI did <strong>not</strong> prove: that the 5 real shipped plugins actually work end-to-end when sandbox enforcement is engaged. Activation is theoretical until verified against the real plugin surface.</p> <p>Two further gaps:</p> <ol> <li> <p><strong>Layer 2 install-time cross-check is unimplemented.</strong> The kernel host already issues <code>tool.describe_capabilities</code> calls per tool method (priority 12 work) — but the responses are advisory, not validated against the manifest. A buggy or compromised plugin binary can claim capabilities its manifest doesn't declare; the kernel's capability check uses the manifest, so the binary's claims silently expand the attack surface.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>No automated end-to-end plugin verification.</strong> Nothing today exercises "install plugin → resolve adapter → spawn under enforcement → run golden path → assert success" for any of the 5 real plugins. Regressions go undetected until a human runs <code>tau chat</code>.</p> </li> </ol> <p>Sub-project D's "end-to-end landlock CI integration" is the third gap (re-introducing 5 e2e test files removed at priority-12 ship). Sub-project B absorbs D's <em>foundation</em> (the symlink-resolution fix + a controlled-environment test binary), leaving D's remaining work focused on actually re-introducing those tests using B's foundation.</p> <p>Seven discrete decisions follow.</p> <h2 id="decision-1--layer-2-cross-check-is-tool-port-dynamic-cross-port-universal-mechanism-deferred"><a class="header" href="#decision-1--layer-2-cross-check-is-tool-port-dynamic-cross-port-universal-mechanism-deferred">Decision 1 — Layer 2 cross-check is tool-port dynamic; cross-port universal mechanism deferred</a></h2> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> the Layer 2 install-time cross-check spawns the plugin binary, performs <code>meta.handshake</code>, and for tool-port plugins enumerates <code>tool.describe_capabilities</code> per method. The aggregated capability set is compared bidirectionally against the manifest's <code>[[capabilities]]</code> block (binary-claims-extra and manifest-declares-unused both hard-fail). For LLM-backend / storage plugins the cross-check returns the manifest's capabilities verbatim with a <code>tracing::debug!</code> noting the manifest-only path.</p> <p><strong>Context:</strong> alternatives were (A) manifest-only static check (no wire mechanism — defeats the cross-check's purpose) and (C) universal wire-level extension to <code>HandshakeResponse</code> (full coverage but adds protocol-level scope across all 7 plugins and the SDK). Option B catches the security-critical case (tool plugins, where capability drift is the prototypical attack vector) without forcing a protocol bump in this sub-project.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Tool plugins' install path now validates: binary's actually-claimed capabilities match the manifest exactly. Drift in either direction aborts install.</li> <li>LLM-backend and storage plugins fall through to manifest-only Layer 2; the cross-check still runs (the binary must spawn + handshake successfully) but per-method enumeration doesn't apply because those ports lack the wire mechanism.</li> <li>A future hardening pass can add <code>meta.describe_capabilities</code> (or extend <code>HandshakeResponse</code> with a <code>capabilities: Vec<Capability></code> field) to enable universal cross-port checking. Tracked as a Phase 2 hardening item.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Manifest-only static check.</strong> Rejected: doesn't catch the actual attack vector (binary diverges from manifest claims).</li> <li><strong>Universal wire-level cross-port mechanism.</strong> Deferred: scope creep into protocol design when the security-critical surface is already covered by the tool-port path.</li> </ul> <h2 id="decision-2--cross-check-timing-is-install-time-only-spawn-time-skipped"><a class="header" href="#decision-2--cross-check-timing-is-install-time-only-spawn-time-skipped">Decision 2 — Cross-check timing is install-time only; spawn-time skipped</a></h2> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> the cross-check runs once during <code>tau install</code> (and <code>tau update</code>, which re-installs) at the moment the binary has just finished building. Spawn-time cross-check is not added.</p> <p><strong>Context:</strong> alternatives were (B) first-spawn-after-install lazy check (adds state-machine complexity to <code>LockedPlugin</code>; doesn't catch drift any earlier than spawn) and (C) install-time + every-spawn (overlaps with <code>tau verify</code>'s tree-hash check from priority 7, which is strictly stronger than re-running a capability handshake).</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li><code>LockedPlugin.required_shapes</code> becomes the source of truth for runtime resolution. The runtime trusts the lockfile; the lockfile was verified at install time.</li> <li>A binary swap on disk after install is detected by <code>tau verify</code>, not by the sandbox layer. This separates concerns cleanly.</li> <li>An <code>InstallOptions::skip_cross_check: bool</code> field (default <code>false</code>) provides an escape hatch for tests that build stub plugin binaries that don't implement the handshake. Production code never sets it, so cross-check always fires there.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>First-spawn-after-install lazy.</strong> Rejected: doesn't catch drift earlier; adds state-machine complexity.</li> <li><strong>Install-time + every-spawn.</strong> Rejected: overlaps with <code>tau verify</code>'s tree-hash check, which is strictly stronger than re-running a handshake.</li> </ul> <h2 id="decision-3--live-spawn-depth--layer-3--container--native-absorb-sub-project-ds-foundation"><a class="header" href="#decision-3--live-spawn-depth--layer-3--container--native-absorb-sub-project-ds-foundation">Decision 3 — Live spawn depth = Layer 3 + container + native; absorb sub-project D's foundation</a></h2> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> verification depth covers all three layers: Layer 3 (<code>tau resolve --check-sandbox</code>, no real spawn), Layer 4 container (live spawn under Docker on Linux CI), and Layer 4 native (live spawn under landlock + seccomp + namespaces on Linux CI). The controlled-environment test binary and the landlock-symlink fix from sub-project D's foundation are absorbed into B; D's remaining scope (re-introducing 5 e2e test files using the controlled-env binary) stays as a separate sub-project.</p> <p><strong>Context:</strong> the alternatives were (A) Layer 3 only (theoretical validation; no kernel verification) and (B) Layer 3 + container only (skips native; punts native verification to a future sub-project). Container coverage alone leaves the native adapter — the only adapter that exercises landlock + seccomp directly — unvalidated end-to-end. Decoupling B from D would create an artificial boundary where the harness exists in one place and the thing it's supposed to verify exists somewhere else.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>The plugin compat tests <em>are</em> the symlink fix's reproducer.</li> <li>B's PR is larger (~16 commits over the implementation tasks) but ships a complete, verified milestone in one merge.</li> <li>The native adapter touchup (<code>tau-sandbox-native/src/light.rs::resolve_symlinks_for_landlock</code>) lands in B; sub-project D's later PR doesn't have to re-modify the adapter.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Honest scope notes:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Layer 4 container Tier-A tests (shell + fs-read via <code>tau plugin run --script</code>) verify build + handshake but do NOT route through the sandbox adapter. Marked <code>#[ignore]</code> with rationale because <code>tau plugin run --script</code> hardcodes the handshake port to <code>llm_backend</code>, incompatible with tool-port plugins. Sub-project D will provide a port-aware driver.</li> <li>Layer 4 container Tier-B tests (anthropic, ollama, openai cassette-replay) marked <code>#[ignore]</code> pending sub-project D's cassette-replay-through-sandboxed-process infrastructure.</li> <li>All 5 Layer 4 native tests marked <code>#[ignore]</code> and gated <code>cfg(target_os = "linux")</code> for the same reason.</li> <li>Layer 3 tests (<code>tau resolve --check-sandbox</code>) all pass: 5/5 plugins on Linux CI.</li> </ul> <h2 id="decision-4--tau-install---rehash-dropped-from-scope"><a class="header" href="#decision-4--tau-install---rehash-dropped-from-scope">Decision 4 — <code>tau install --rehash</code> dropped from scope</a></h2> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> the <code>--rehash</code> flag from the original sub-project B scope is removed. Not deferred; dropped.</p> <p><strong>Context:</strong> the existing command surface already covers every realistic use case:</p> <ul> <li><code>tau update <pkg></code> covers refetch + rebuild + lockfile rewrite.</li> <li><code>tau install --force <pkg></code> covers local-source rebuild without netfetch.</li> <li><code>tau verify</code> covers read-only drift detection.</li> <li>Auto-upgrade-with-<code>tracing::warn!</code> (priority 7 / priority 12 / sub-project A pattern) covers schema migration silently on next read.</li> <li><code>--rehash</code> would only uniquely fill the niche "refresh lockfile metadata without rebuilding and without going to the network" — a developer convenience saving ~5 seconds per refresh, with no security-critical use case. YAGNI applies.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong> if a real need surfaces post-ship, <code>--rehash</code> can be added in a later sub-project with concrete user motivation. Adding flags is a one-way ratchet; surgically removing them after they're documented is harder.</p> <h2 id="decision-5--all-5-real-plugins-declare-sandbox-required_tier--strict"><a class="header" href="#decision-5--all-5-real-plugins-declare-sandbox-required_tier--strict">Decision 5 — All 5 real plugins declare <code>[sandbox] required_tier = "strict"</code></a></h2> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> each of <code>anthropic</code>, <code>ollama</code>, <code>openai</code>, <code>fs-read</code>, <code>shell</code> gets <code>[sandbox] required_tier = "strict"</code> in its <code>tau.toml</code>. Toy plugins (<code>echo-llm</code>, <code>echo-tool</code>) omit the block (default is None tier).</p> <p><strong>Context:</strong> alternatives were (B) all real plugins declare Light (strictly weaker enforcement with identical host coverage) and (C) plugins declare nothing, project drives entirely (defeats ADR-0015 Decision 6's purpose; trusts every project author to know which plugins handle untrusted data).</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>macOS / Windows users without Docker get exit 2 on first run with the guided diagnostic from sub-project A: "your project requires Strict; install Docker, switch to Linux, or pass <code>--no-sandbox</code> for an explicit opt-out". This is the correct friction.</li> <li>Per-run opt-out via <code>--no-sandbox</code> keeps dev workflow viable.</li> <li>Toy plugins remain useful as tier-None test fixtures.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Light tier.</strong> Rejected: same host availability as Strict but strictly weaker enforcement (compromised HTTP plugins can still exfiltrate via the network under Light).</li> <li><strong>No declaration; project drives.</strong> Rejected: makes the plugin author transparent to the project, defeating ADR-0015 Decision 6's purpose.</li> </ul> <h2 id="decision-6--new-crate-tau-plugin-compat-for-the-test-harness"><a class="header" href="#decision-6--new-crate-tau-plugin-compat-for-the-test-harness">Decision 6 — New crate <code>tau-plugin-compat/</code> for the test harness</a></h2> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> create a new workspace crate <code>crates/tau-plugin-compat/</code> (<code>publish = false</code>) holding the per-plugin verification harness, fixtures, and the controlled-environment test binary.</p> <p><strong>Context:</strong> alternatives were (A) centralized in <code>tau-runtime/tests/</code> (pollutes runtime crate's test surface; rule-of-three not yet justified at one sub-project's worth of need) and (B) per-plugin alongside existing test surface (duplicates fixture boilerplate 5×).</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Branch protection rises from 25 to 27 required checks (2 new CI jobs: <code>build (tau-plugin-compat)</code> + <code>test (tau-plugin-compat / linux)</code>).</li> <li>One GitHub-settings configuration change after first push to add the new checks to branch protection.</li> <li>The crate becomes the natural home for cross-plugin compatibility testing across sub-projects D, E, F, J, K.</li> <li><code>tau-cli</code> is a dev-dependency on <code>tau-plugin-compat</code> so cargo builds the <code>tau</code> binary into target/debug for the harness's <code>tau_bin()</code> helper to discover. CI explicitly builds <code>tau-cli</code> first to ensure the binary exists in the test job's environment.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Centralize in <code>tau-runtime/tests/</code>.</strong> Rejected: pollutes runtime crate's test surface.</li> <li><strong>Per-plugin under <code>tau-plugins/<name>/tests/</code>.</strong> Rejected: duplicates fixture boilerplate 5×.</li> </ul> <h2 id="decision-7--cross-check-function-lives-in-tau-pkgsandbox_check-public-module"><a class="header" href="#decision-7--cross-check-function-lives-in-tau-pkgsandbox_check-public-module">Decision 7 — Cross-check function lives in <code>tau-pkg::sandbox_check</code> (public module)</a></h2> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> the <code>cross_check_plugin_capabilities(binary_path, manifest) -> Result<Vec<CapabilityShape>, CrossCheckError></code> function is public on <code>tau-pkg::sandbox_check</code>. Both production code (the install path in <code>tau-pkg</code>) and test code (the harness in <code>tau-plugin-compat</code>) call it directly.</p> <p><strong>Context:</strong> alternatives were (A) private to <code>tau-pkg::install</code> (makes Layer 2 untestable except through <code>install_with_options</code>'s side effects, which is bad for a security feature) and (C) new shared crate <code>tau-sandbox-check</code> (premature; one module, one function, one error type doesn't justify a workspace crate).</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li><code>tau-plugin-compat</code> adds a <code>tau-pkg = { path = "../tau-pkg" }</code> dev-dependency.</li> <li>The public surface is small: one function, one <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> error enum (4 variants).</li> <li><code>InstallError::CrossCheck { message: String }</code> (not <code>#[from] CrossCheckError</code>) because <code>tau-domain::Capability</code> derives <code>PartialEq</code> but not <code>Eq</code>, and <code>InstallError</code> requires <code>Eq</code>. The <code>Display</code> string preserves all necessary information.</li> <li>The cross-check IPC bridge: <code>tokio::process::Command</code> + <code>tau_plugin_protocol::Frame</code> + <code>FramedReader</code>/<code>FramedWriter</code>. <code>cross_check_plugin_capabilities</code> is async; <code>install_with_options</code> is sync. Bridge via a current-thread tokio runtime spun up just for this step.</li> <li><code>kill_on_drop(true)</code> on the spawned <code>Command</code> ensures the child is reaped on every error-return path. IPC reads / writes are wrapped in <code>tokio::time::timeout</code> (10s for handshake response, 5s per per-method <code>tool.describe_capabilities</code> response).</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Private to <code>install_with_options</code>.</strong> Rejected: makes Layer 2 untestable except via install side effects.</li> <li><strong>New shared crate <code>tau-sandbox-check</code>.</strong> Rejected: premature for one module / one function.</li> </ul> <h2 id="implementation-summary-1"><a class="header" href="#implementation-summary-1">Implementation summary</a></h2> <p>The 16 commits on <code>feat/plugin-compat-spec</code> (PR #24) realize these decisions via:</p> <div Of those, the Layer 4 tests (10) are <code>#[ignore]</code>'d pending sub-project D's e2e infrastructure.</p> <p>CI matrix: 27 jobs across Linux + macOS + Windows × stable + 1.91. All green on the final commit.</p> <h2 id="forward-links-1"><a class="header" href="#forward-links-1">Forward links</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>Sub-project D</strong> (end-to-end landlock CI integration) is unblocked by B's foundation: the symlink-resolution fix and controlled-environment binary now exist; D's remaining scope is re-introducing the 5 e2e test files removed at priority-12 ship plus building the port-aware driver that flips the 10 <code>#[ignore]</code>'d tests in <code>tau-plugin-compat/tests/layer4_*.rs</code>.</li> <li><strong>Sub-project E</strong> (per-command exec gating, landlock V2) gains a verified compat baseline.</li> <li><strong>Sub-project F</strong> (per-host network filtering via nftables-in-netns) gains the same.</li> <li><strong>Sub-projects J, K</strong> (macOS sandbox-exec, Windows AppContainer) extend <code>tau-plugin-compat</code> with platform-specific compat suites.</li> <li><strong>Phase 2 sub-project A</strong> (<code>tau check</code> standalone command) gains a verified production surface to re-expose; <code>cross_check_plugin_capabilities</code> could become callable from <code>tau check</code> directly in addition to the install path.</li> <li><strong>Phase 2 hardening</strong> (deferred): universal cross-port <code>meta.describe_capabilities</code> wire mechanism extending Decision 1's tool-port-only check to LLM-backend and storage plugins.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0017-end-to-end-landlock-ci-integration--port-aware-layer-4-driver"><a class="header" href="#adr-0017-end-to-end-landlock-ci-integration--port-aware-layer-4-driver">ADR-0017: End-to-end landlock CI integration + port-aware Layer 4 driver</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-05-05 <strong>Deciders:</strong> Titouan Lebocq <strong>Supersedes:</strong> — <strong>Closes:</strong></p> <ul> <li>The kernel-enforcement test debt from priority-12 ship (5 e2e test files removed because Ubuntu's <code>/bin → /usr/bin</code> symlinks tripped landlock V1 path resolution). Re-introduced + passing on Linux CI.</li> <li>Sub-project D foundation work absorbed by sub-project B (controlled-env binary, landlock-symlink fix). D's remainder shipped here. <strong>Refines:</strong></li> <li><a href="decisions/0014-sandboxing.html">ADR-0014</a> — native adapter gains real-kernel e2e verification + two correctness fixes (Execute access flag + binary-parent auto-add).</li> <li><a href="decisions/0016-plugin-compat-verification.html">ADR-0016</a> — sub-project B's <code>#[ignore]</code>'d Layer 4 plugin-compat tests stay deferred; the port-aware driver foundation is in place but plugin startup-IO cataloging is its own work. <strong>Amends:</strong> —</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-17"><a class="header" href="#context-17">Context</a></h2> <p>Two debts entered this sub-project:</p> <ol> <li> <p><strong>5 kernel-enforcement e2e tests</strong> (<code>light_landlock.rs</code>, <code>strict_seccomp.rs</code>, <code>strict_net_filter.rs</code>, <code>strict_exec_gating.rs</code>, <code>sandbox_native.rs</code>) were drafted at priority-12 ship but removed because Ubuntu's <code>/bin → /usr/bin</code> symlinks combined with landlock V1's path resolution returned EACCES on real binary spawns. Sub-project B's <code>resolve_symlinks_for_landlock</code> helper resolved that issue; the tests needed to be re-introduced.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>10 <code>#[ignore]</code>'d Layer 4 plugin-compat tests</strong> in <code>tau-plugin-compat/tests/layer4_*.rs</code> (5 container + 5 native, scaffolded by sub-project B) needed flipping. The blocker was a port-aware test driver — sub-project B's <code>tau plugin run --script</code> hardcoded the handshake port to <code>LlmBackend</code>, breaking tool-port plugin tests.</p> </li> </ol> <p>The sub-project's intent was to retire both debts. The actual ship retired only the first.</p> <h2 id="five-design-decisions"><a class="header" href="#five-design-decisions">Five design decisions</a></h2> <h3 id="decision-1--single-sub-project-d-both-halves-shipped-together"><a class="header" href="#decision-1--single-sub-project-d-both-halves-shipped-together">Decision 1 — Single sub-project D, both halves shipped together</a></h3> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> ship the 5 e2e files AND the port-aware driver as one sub-project; one PR; one verification milestone.</p> <p><strong>Rationale:</strong> the 5 e2e files use the controlled-env binary that sub-project B's foundation absorbed; the port-aware driver builds on the same foundation. Splitting would create artificial boundaries between work that shares infrastructure.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>One PR with ~20 commits including 7 reactive fix commits for CI failures (see "Honest scope notes" below).</li> <li>One verification milestone with all 29 CI checks green.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Split into D1 (e2e files) + D2 (driver). Rejected as discussed in the spec's brainstorming — the work shares enough infrastructure that splitting was overhead.</li> </ul> <h3 id="decision-2--driver--thin-wrapper-in-tau-plugin-compatdriver-reusing-tau_runtimeplugin_hostload_"><a class="header" href="#decision-2--driver--thin-wrapper-in-tau-plugin-compatdriver-reusing-tau_runtimeplugin_hostload_">Decision 2 — Driver = thin wrapper in <code>tau-plugin-compat::driver</code> reusing <code>tau_runtime::plugin_host::load_*</code></a></h3> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> the port-aware driver is a public module <code>crates/tau-plugin-compat/src/driver.rs</code> exposing <code>spawn_tool_under_sandbox</code>, <code>spawn_llm_under_sandbox</code>, <code>spawn_storage_under_sandbox</code>. Each is a thin wrapper around the corresponding public <code>tau_runtime::plugin_host::load_*</code> function.</p> <p><strong>Rationale:</strong> alternatives were (A) extending <code>tau plugin run</code> with <code>--port=<kind></code> (adds public CLI surface to a debug verb) and (B) duplicating spawn-and-handshake logic outside <code>plugin_host</code> (sub-project B's <code>tau-pkg::sandbox_check</code> pattern, but inappropriate here because <code>tau-plugin-compat</code> already depends on <code>tau-runtime</code>). Reusing the public production-path functions gave the cleanest test surface.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>~150 LOC of new code in the driver module + 5 unit tests.</li> <li>Returns <code>Arc<dyn DynTool></code> / <code>Arc<dyn DynLlmBackend></code> / <code>Arc<dyn DynStorage></code> for direct trait-method invocation in tests; no manual <code>Frame::Request</code> construction needed.</li> <li><code>DriveError</code> is <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> with 5 variants (LoadFailed, PortMismatch, ToolFailed, LlmFailed, StorageFailed).</li> <li>The driver is invoked by the (currently <code>#[ignore]</code>'d) Layer 4 plugin-compat tests; when those are flipped in a follow-up, the same driver wires them up.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Public CLI verb extension: rejected (test-only concern shouldn't add public CLI surface).</li> <li>Custom IPC outside <code>plugin_host</code>: rejected (duplicates production code; <code>tau-plugin-compat</code> can depend on <code>tau-runtime</code>, no circular concern).</li> </ul> <h3 id="decision-3--honest-deferral-0-of-10-layer-4-tests-flipped-revised-from-specs-7-of-10"><a class="header" href="#decision-3--honest-deferral-0-of-10-layer-4-tests-flipped-revised-from-specs-7-of-10">Decision 3 — Honest deferral: 0 of 10 Layer 4 tests flipped (revised from spec's 7 of 10)</a></h3> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> all 10 Layer 4 plugin-compat tests stay <code>#[ignore]</code>'d, despite the spec's plan to flip 7 of them. The driver infrastructure is in place; the blocker is per-plugin startup-IO cataloging.</p> <p><strong>What we discovered during implementation:</strong></p> <p>After fixing two genuine native-adapter bugs (see Decision 4 below), plugins under strict-tier sandboxing now successfully <strong>spawn</strong> but <strong>EOF before sending the meta.handshake response</strong>. Each plugin's startup touches filesystem state (config dirs, tmpfile creation, /proc reads, etc.) that's outside the test's narrow plan. The plans we constructed cover only the plugin's <em>application data</em> (e.g. <code>process.spawn { commands: ["echo"] }</code> for shell, <code>fs.read { paths: [data_dir] }</code> for fs-read) — they don't cover the plugin's <em>runtime state</em> surface.</p> <p>Cataloging that startup-IO surface per plugin and deriving correct plans is itself non-trivial work. It's the natural sequel to D and arguably belongs in a sub-project D-followup or rolls into sub-project F's per-host network filter work.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>The 10 Layer 4 plugin-compat <code>#[ignore]</code>'s from sub-project B persist. The IOU stays open.</li> <li>The driver foundation is ready for a future sub-project to flip them.</li> <li>ADR-0016's "we'll flip 7 of 10" expectation is amended honestly here.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Add overly broad <code>fs.read</code> (e.g., <code>[/]</code>) to test plans to make them pass without cataloging. Rejected — defeats the verification goal; if the plan grants everything, the test isn't testing isolation.</li> <li>Investigate per-plugin startup-IO in this sub-project. Rejected — that work would double D's scope and the most economical analysis happens when paired with sub-project F's per-host network filter.</li> </ul> <h3 id="decision-4--native-adapter-bug-fixes-real-wins-not-in-original-scope"><a class="header" href="#decision-4--native-adapter-bug-fixes-real-wins-not-in-original-scope">Decision 4 — Native adapter bug fixes (real wins, not in original scope)</a></h3> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> ship two fixes to the priority-12 native adapter that were uncovered during D's e2e testing:</p> <ol> <li> <p><strong><code>AccessFs::Execute</code> granted alongside <code>ReadFile | ReadDir</code></strong> in <code>tau-sandbox-native::light::install_landlock</code>. Without this, exec of any binary inside a path in the ruleset returns EACCES — even though <code>Ruleset::handle_access(AccessFs::from_all(abi))</code> declared the ruleset would handle Execute. The priority-12 unit tests didn't catch this because they never spawned a binary; D's e2e tests caught it on the first CI run.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Auto-add the spawned binary's parent directory to <code>read_paths</code></strong> in <code>tau-sandbox-native::light::collect_landlock_paths</code>. Plugins built into a workspace's <code>target/release/</code> (or any non-system path) need their containing directory in the ruleset so the kernel can both read the binary file (to load it) and exec it. The priority-12 design assumed only system paths (<code>/bin</code>, <code>/usr/bin</code>, <code>/lib</code>, etc.), which doesn't cover real-world plugin layouts. Both Light and Strict tiers benefit since they share the same <code>collect_landlock_paths</code> helper.</p> </li> </ol> <p>Together these fixes mean: every real plugin under the native adapter can now load itself end-to-end. Without them, the adapter shipped at priority-12 would have failed in production the first time a plugin was actually spawned with a strict requirement.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Two real bug fixes in <code>tau-sandbox-native::light</code> shipped via D.</li> <li><code>collect_landlock_paths</code> now always returns at least one entry (the spawned binary's parent), which required updating one priority-12 unit test that asserted <code>read.is_empty()</code>.</li> <li>Future native sandbox spawns "just work" regardless of where the binary lives.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Punt fixes to a separate ADR amending ADR-0014. Rejected — the bugs only surface via the e2e tests this sub-project added, so the fix and the test that proves the fix belong together.</li> <li>Document the v0.1 limitation instead of fixing. Rejected — the priority-12 native adapter would be unusable for any real plugin without these fixes.</li> </ul> <h3 id="decision-5--2-new-linux-ci-jobs-revised-from-specs-3"><a class="header" href="#decision-5--2-new-linux-ci-jobs-revised-from-specs-3">Decision 5 — 2 new Linux CI jobs (revised from spec's 3)</a></h3> <p><strong>Decision:</strong> add two new Linux-only CI jobs:</p> <ul> <li><code>test (tau-sandbox-native e2e / linux)</code> — runs the 4 adapter-level e2e tests</li> <li><code>test (tau-runtime e2e / linux)</code> — runs the 1 runtime-level e2e test</li> </ul> <p>The existing <code>test (tau-plugin-compat / linux)</code> job continues to run the Layer 3 + Layer 4 plugin-compat tests (no shape change).</p> <p><strong>Rationale:</strong> the spec said "3 separate Linux jobs" but the third job was always going to be the existing <code>test (tau-plugin-compat / linux)</code>. Branding it as a fresh "third job" is misleading; documenting honestly here.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Branch protection rises 27 → 29 required checks.</li> <li>One GitHub-settings configuration change after the first PR push to add the new check names.</li> <li>Each test job names the responsible crate; failures point cleanly.</li> <li>Per-job parallelism on GH Actions runners.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Alternatives considered:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Single combined Linux job. Rejected — misleading job names when failures surface.</li> <li>Bundle sandbox-native and runtime e2e under one job. Rejected — same misleading-name concern; the marginal cost of separate jobs is low.</li> </ul> <h2 id="honest-scope-notes"><a class="header" href="#honest-scope-notes">Honest scope notes</a></h2> <p>This sub-project required 7 reactive fix commits after the initial PR push surfaced real CI failures. Each fix was a real bug discovered by the e2e tests:</p> <div class="table-wrapper"><table><thead><tr><th>Commit</th><th>What broke</th><th>Root cause</th></tr></thead><tbody> <tr><td><code>61ebadc</code></td><td>Layer 4 e2e EACCES + non-exhaustive types + import path</td><td>landlock blocks exec without Execute flag (caught by Ubuntu CI); compile-time issues only Linux catches</td></tr> <tr><td><code>8971e23</code></td><td>(improvement, not a bug) GitHub Actions caching via composite action + <code>Swatinem/rust-cache@v2</code></td><td></td></tr> <tr><td><code>38b942b</code></td><td>Layer 4 e2e still EACCES on exec</td><td><code>install_landlock</code> granted <code>Read*</code> only; Execute access needed too</td></tr> <tr><td><code>574d634</code></td><td>tau-runtime test compile error</td><td>Missing <code>..</code> for <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> destructure + unused import</td></tr> <tr><td><code>ef2addd</code></td><td>Layer 4 container tool tests fail with handshake EOF</td><td><code>tau plugin run --script</code> plumbing not container-adapter-aware</td></tr> <tr><td><code>6e47402</code></td><td>Layer 4 native tool tests STILL EACCES on exec</td><td><code>apply_landlock</code> got binary-parent auto-add; needed it in <code>apply_strict</code> too</td></tr> <tr><td><code>175eb8f</code></td><td>Same fix moved into shared <code>collect_landlock_paths</code> helper</td><td>Single point of truth instead of duplicated fix</td></tr> <tr><td><code>b193013</code></td><td>Existing unit test broke after <code>collect_landlock_paths</code> change</td><td>Test expected <code>read.is_empty()</code>; auto-add now adds the binary parent</td></tr> <tr><td><code>bdb7675</code></td><td>Layer 4 native tool/HTTP tests EOF before handshake</td><td>Plugins exec but exit during init under strict-tier landlock; per-plugin startup-IO not cataloged</td></tr> <tr><td><code>61f14f6</code></td><td>macOS test_trace_context_unique_across_calls flaked</td><td>macOS clock resolution made identical nanosecond timestamps from back-to-back calls; fixed with atomic counter</td></tr> </tbody></table> </div> <p>This pattern — push to CI, see real failures the local macOS dev box couldn't catch, fix, repeat — is exactly the value Linux CI provides. Two of these commits surfaced REAL native-adapter bugs that the priority-12 unit tests missed.</p> <h2 id="implementation-summary-2"><a class="header" href="#implementation-summary-2">Implementation summary</a></h2> <div class="table-wrapper"><table><thead><tr><th>Layer</th><th>Crate</th><th>Files changed</th></tr></thead><tbody> <tr><td>Adapter e2e (kernel-enforcement)</td><td><code>tau-sandbox-native</code></td><td><code>Cargo.toml</code> (integration-tests feature) + 4 new test files</td></tr> <tr><td>Runtime e2e</td><td><code>tau-runtime</code></td><td><code>Cargo.toml</code> + new <code>tests/sandbox_native.rs</code></td></tr> <tr><td>Test driver</td><td><code>tau-plugin-compat</code></td><td>new <code>src/driver.rs</code> (~150 LOC, 5 unit tests)</td></tr> <tr><td>Native adapter fixes</td><td><code>tau-sandbox-native</code></td><td><code>src/light.rs</code> — Execute access flag + binary-parent auto-add</td></tr> <tr><td>Existing unit test fix</td><td><code>tau-sandbox-native</code></td><td><code>src/light.rs::tests::collect_landlock_paths_ignores_non_filesystem_capabilities</code></td></tr> <tr><td>Layer 4 plugin compat</td><td><code>tau-plugin-compat</code></td><td>tests/layer4_*.rs <code>#[ignore]</code> rationale updated</td></tr> <tr><td>Controlled-env binary</td><td><code>tau-plugin-compat</code></td><td>mode dispatch (4 modes) for e2e fixture coverage</td></tr> <tr><td>Documentation</td><td>(root)</td><td><code>docs/reference/sandbox-platform-support.md</code></td></tr> <tr><td>CI infrastructure</td><td>(root)</td><td>new <code>.github/actions/setup-rust</code> composite action; <code>Swatinem/rust-cache@v2</code>; 2 new Linux jobs</td></tr> </tbody></table> </div> <p>Total LOC delta: ~700. Test count delta: 9 e2e adapter tests passing + 2 runtime e2e tests passing + 5 driver unit tests passing on every run. 10 Layer 4 plugin-compat tests still <code>#[ignore]</code>'d.</p> <h2 id="forward-links-2"><a class="header" href="#forward-links-2">Forward links</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>Sub-project D-followup or sub-project F:</strong> flip the 10 Layer 4 plugin-compat <code>#[ignore]</code>'s by cataloging per-plugin startup-IO and deriving correct plans. The driver is ready; the work is per-plugin investigation.</li> <li><strong>Sub-project E:</strong> <code>strict_exec_gating.rs</code> is <code>#[ignore]</code>'d pending landlock V2; once E lands, the test body fills in.</li> <li><strong>Sub-project F:</strong> the 3 container × HTTP plugin tests' rationale points here; per-host network filter via nftables-in-netns unblocks them.</li> <li><strong>Sub-projects J / K (macOS / Windows native adapters):</strong> can extend <code>tau-plugin-compat::driver</code> for platform-specific compat suites.</li> <li><strong>CI caching infrastructure</strong> is now in place for all future sub-projects. Initial cache populates on first main-branch push after this merge.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0018-ci-optimization--five-phase-migration-sub-project-e"><a class="header" href="#adr-0018-ci-optimization--five-phase-migration-sub-project-e">ADR-0018: CI optimization — five-phase migration (sub-project E)</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted (Decision 3 partially superseded — see "Subsequent revisions" below) <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-05-06 <strong>Deciders:</strong> Titouan Lebocq <strong>Supersedes:</strong> — <strong>Closes:</strong></p> <ul> <li>The 23-required-check / ~33-min PR critical-path CI baseline that had accumulated since priority-12 shipped.</li> </ul> <h2 id="subsequent-revisions"><a class="header" href="#subsequent-revisions">Subsequent revisions</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>2026-05-17 (PR #122, "ci: round 1 upgrades"):</strong> The <code>msrv-check</code> job was collapsed from a 3-OS matrix (<code>linux</code>, <code>macos</code>, <code>windows</code>) to Linux-only. Decision 3 below still holds — MSRV remains a <code>cargo check</code> job, not <code>cargo test</code> — but the cross-OS dimension is gone, on the basis that MSRV is a rustc-version property and the OS-gated code paths are already exercised by <code>test-stable</code> on stable toolchain. Section "14 required checks across 3 jobs types" in Decision 6 below is therefore now overstated by 2 checks. See <code>docs/superpowers/specs/2026-05-17-ci-upgrades-round-1-design.md</code> for full rationale.</li> </ul> <h2 id="context-18"><a class="header" href="#context-18">Context</a></h2> <p>At the start of sub-project E (CI optimization), the CI configuration was the product of incremental organic growth: each sub-project added jobs as needed without ever cleaning up redundancy. The pre-Phase-A state was:</p> <ul> <li><strong>23 required checks</strong> gating <code>main</code>.</li> <li><strong>~33-minute PR critical path</strong> dominated by redundant compilation: the 5 real plugin binaries were built independently in every Linux job that needed them.</li> <li><strong>One undifferentiated <code>test:</code> job</strong> per OS that ran everything — doctests, <code>cargo test --ignored</code> integration tests, and unit tests — in a single step, blocking on the slowest test in the set.</li> <li><strong>No cross-job compilation cache</strong>: each runner compiled from scratch; <code>Swatinem/rust-cache</code> was not wired in.</li> <li><strong>No sccache</strong> (though <code>RUSTC_WRAPPER=sccache</code> was in the dev env, it was absent from CI runners).</li> <li><strong>Windows running as <code>continue-on-error: true</code></strong> — failures were advisory, not gating.</li> <li><strong>7 <code>--no-default-features</code> jobs</strong> for individual crates, running as separate workflow jobs with full compiler invocations each.</li> <li><strong>6 redundant plugin release-build jobs</strong> that duplicated what <code>build-fixtures-linux</code> (Phase C) would centralize.</li> <li><strong>MSRV verification</strong> done via <code>cargo test</code> on the full test suite, slower than necessary since MSRV is a compile-time contract.</li> </ul> <p>The spec estimated baseline at 29 required checks; the actual baseline from branch protection was 23 (the delta is because several running-but-not-gating advisory checks were counted in the spec's analysis but were never in the required list).</p> <p>The spec estimated final count at 18 required checks; actual final is 14 (the spec's floor assumed all 6 advisory checks-in-use would remain; they were not required and were cleanly dropped).</p> <h2 id="decisions"><a class="header" href="#decisions">Decisions</a></h2> <h3 id="decision-1--conservative-within-constraint-optimization-path"><a class="header" href="#decision-1--conservative-within-constraint-optimization-path">Decision 1 — Conservative within-constraint optimization path</a></h3> <p>Full e2e coverage on every OS × toolchain combination is preserved. The optimization goal was to eliminate redundant <em>compilation</em> and redundant <em>advisory</em> checks, not to thin the test matrix or relax coverage guarantees. Every test that ran before sub-project E still runs after; it just runs cheaper.</p> <p><strong>Rationale:</strong> the spec's brainstorming explicitly rejected test-matrix slimming and smoke-test substitution as coverage regressions.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>No tests were removed from any OS or toolchain.</li> <li>The 14-check floor is structurally sound: each check covers a real test surface.</li> <li>Regression risk of the optimization work itself is bounded; any phase can be reverted independently.</li> </ul> <h3 id="decision-2--windows-promoted-from-advisory-to-hard-gate-w2"><a class="header" href="#decision-2--windows-promoted-from-advisory-to-hard-gate-w2">Decision 2 — Windows promoted from advisory to hard gate (W2)</a></h3> <p>As part of Phase B, <code>continue-on-error: true</code> was removed from all Windows jobs. Windows became a hard gate on the same footing as Linux and macOS.</p> <p><strong>Rationale:</strong> a 4-of-4 Windows audit during Phase B confirmed no Windows-specific failures; the advisory flag was historical caution that had outlived its purpose. Keeping it advisory meant Windows failures were silent to the merge gate.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Any Windows-specific breakage now blocks <code>main</code> merges.</li> <li>CI noise risk from Windows flakes is real but acceptable given the clean audit.</li> </ul> <h3 id="decision-3--msrv-is-a-compile-time-contract-use-cargo-check-not-cargo-test"><a class="header" href="#decision-3--msrv-is-a-compile-time-contract-use-cargo-check-not-cargo-test">Decision 3 — MSRV is a compile-time contract; use <code>cargo check</code>, not <code>cargo test</code></a></h3> <p>The <code>msrv-check / {linux, macos, windows}</code> jobs run <code>cargo check</code> under the MSRV toolchain rather than <code>cargo test</code>. The <code>test-stable</code> jobs run the full test suite.</p> <p><strong>Rationale:</strong> MSRV is about API and syntax availability — a compile-time question. Running the full test suite under MSRV burns runner minutes on tests that already run under stable and adds nothing to the MSRV guarantee.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li><code>msrv-check</code> jobs are fast (check-only, no test binary linking or execution).</li> <li>MSRV violations surface as compile errors, which is the correct signal.</li> <li>Behavioral regressions on the MSRV compiler are not caught, but that risk is accepted: the MSRV toolchain is not used in production; the stable toolchain is.</li> </ul> <h3 id="decision-4--upload-specific-compiled-binaries-rely-on-rust-cache--sccache-for-the-rest"><a class="header" href="#decision-4--upload-specific-compiled-binaries-rely-on-rust-cache--sccache-for-the-rest">Decision 4 — Upload specific compiled binaries; rely on rust-cache + sccache for the rest</a></h3> <p><code>target/</code> directories are never uploaded as artifacts. The <code>build-fixtures-linux</code> job (Phase C) builds 9 specific binaries (5 real plugins + 2 toy plugins + tau-cli + controlled-env) into an <code>_artifacts/</code> staging directory, uploads that as <code>linux-fixture-binaries</code>, and downstream jobs download it. Per-job <code>Swatinem/rust-cache</code> with a shared <code>shared-key</code> handles incremental reuse within a job type; <code>mozilla-actions/sccache-action@v0.0.10</code> provides cross-job rustc caching.</p> <p><strong>Rationale:</strong> uploading the full <code>target/</code> (multi-GB per crate configuration) was considered and rejected (see Alternatives). Uploading only the final binaries is cheap, deterministic, and eliminates the ~9-minute per-PR redundant plugin compilation.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li><code>build-fixtures-linux</code> is the single point of failure for the binary artifact. If it fails, all downstream jobs fail. This is acceptable: the build job is fast and its failures are informative.</li> <li>Executable bits are stripped by <code>actions/upload-artifact</code> — downstream jobs must <code>chmod +x</code> the binaries after download (a real fix shipped during Phase C).</li> <li><code>actions/upload-artifact</code> preserves directory tree relative to the upload root — the <code>_artifacts/</code> staging step was added to give a clean download target (another real fix shipped during Phase C).</li> </ul> <h3 id="decision-5--no-reusable-workflow-files-at-this-ci-scale"><a class="header" href="#decision-5--no-reusable-workflow-files-at-this-ci-scale">Decision 5 — No reusable workflow files at this CI scale</a></h3> <p>The composite action <code>.github/actions/setup-rust</code> absorbs duplication (toolchain + cache wiring). Reusable workflow files (<code>.github/workflows/reusable-*.yml</code> via <code>workflow_call</code>) were considered and rejected.</p> <p><strong>Rationale:</strong> at 14 required checks across 3 jobs types (test-stable, msrv-check, e2e), the duplication remaining after the composite action is limited. Reusable workflows add indirection that makes CI debugging harder without proportionate reduction in maintenance burden at this scale.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Future job additions copy-paste from the existing job blocks. This is acceptable at the current scale.</li> <li>If the workflow grows significantly (10+ job types), reusable workflows should be reconsidered.</li> </ul> <h3 id="decision-6--phased-migration-over-big-bang"><a class="header" href="#decision-6--phased-migration-over-big-bang">Decision 6 — Phased migration over big-bang</a></h3> <p>The optimization was delivered in five independently revertable phases (A–E), each landing as a separate PR.</p> <p><strong>Rationale:</strong> big-bang CI rewrites are high-risk: a mistake that breaks the merge gate on <code>main</code> is a production incident. Phased delivery means each phase can be verified green before the next starts, and any phase can be reverted if it causes problems.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>5 PRs instead of 1; each requires a branch-protection config update after merge to add/remove required check names.</li> <li>The phase boundaries (A: tooling; B: matrix split; C: artifact passing; D: job drop; E: feature-flag consolidation) were chosen to be maximally independent.</li> </ul> <h3 id="decision-7--phase-a-and-phase-b-are-valid-resting-points"><a class="header" href="#decision-7--phase-a-and-phase-b-are-valid-resting-points">Decision 7 — Phase A and Phase B are valid resting points</a></h3> <p>The design was explicitly structured so that, if phases C–E proved problematic, the repo could remain at Phase A or Phase B indefinitely.</p> <p><strong>Phase A</strong> (shared cache + nextest + sccache + mold) is a pure win: it reduces wall time and cache misses with zero structural change to the job graph.</p> <p><strong>Phase B</strong> (matrix split + MSRV as check-only + Windows hard gate) is a structural improvement with minor risk (Windows flakes, MSRV-only check). It is a stable long-term configuration even without phases C–E.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Phases C–E can each be reverted without rolling back A or B.</li> <li>The spec and plan document this explicitly; if follow-up phases prove too fragile, rolling back to Phase B leaves CI in a better state than pre-optimization.</li> </ul> <h3 id="decision-8--required-check-count-drops-23--14"><a class="header" href="#decision-8--required-check-count-drops-23--14">Decision 8 — Required check count drops 23 → 14</a></h3> <p>The spec estimated 29 → 18; actual is 23 → 14.</p> <p>The 6-check spec-vs-actual baseline delta: the spec's analysis counted all running checks in the CI configuration as required; in practice, several checks were running-but-not-gating (no entry in the branch protection required-checks list). The optimization correctly identified and dropped those.</p> <p>The 4-check spec-vs-actual final delta: the spec assumed 6 advisory checks would remain; they were not in the required list and were cleanly eliminated.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>14 required checks is a lean, well-justified set.</li> <li>Any re-introduction of required checks should be deliberate (a new test surface, not a redundant rebuild).</li> </ul> <h3 id="decision-9--doctests-stay-on-cargo-test---doc"><a class="header" href="#decision-9--doctests-stay-on-cargo-test---doc">Decision 9 — Doctests stay on <code>cargo test --doc</code></a></h3> <p><code>cargo nextest</code> does not support doctests. The <code>test-stable</code> jobs run <code>cargo nextest run</code> for all non-doctest tests AND <code>cargo test --doc</code> for doctests in the same job step.</p> <p><strong>Rationale:</strong> nextest's doctest support is incomplete upstream. Skipping doctests would regress coverage on a class of tests that verifies API documentation is accurate. Running doctests under legacy <code>cargo test</code> for only the doctest invocation is the lowest-friction compatibility path.</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Two test invocations per <code>test-stable</code> job (nextest for unit/integration, cargo test --doc for doctests).</li> <li>If nextest gains complete doctest support in a future release, the <code>--doc</code> invocation can be dropped.</li> </ul> <h3 id="decision-10--matrix------ignored-integration-test-block-removed-in-phase-b"><a class="header" href="#decision-10--matrix------ignored-integration-test-block-removed-in-phase-b">Decision 10 — Matrix <code>-- --ignored</code> integration test block removed in Phase B</a></h3> <p>The <code>test:</code> matrix had a <code>features: ["-- --ignored"]</code> entry that ran <code>cargo test -- --ignored</code> to exercise <code>#[ignore]</code>'d integration tests. This was removed in Phase B.</p> <p><strong>Rationale:</strong> the <code>-- --ignored</code> block was a legacy holdover from before the dedicated e2e jobs existed. The sub-project D e2e jobs (<code>test (tau-sandbox-native e2e / linux)</code>, <code>test (tau-runtime e2e / linux)</code>, <code>test (tau-plugin-compat / linux)</code>) cover the integration test scope properly, with correct Linux-only gating and <code>integration-tests</code> feature flags. Running them again inside the matrix was redundant and caused <code>cargo nextest</code> to exit 4 on empty filter sets (see Errata).</p> <p><strong>Consequences:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Integration tests run exactly once (in the dedicated e2e jobs), not twice.</li> <li>The <code>--no-tests=pass</code> flag was added to the nextest invocations to guard against the exit-4 edge case on other empty filter sets.</li> </ul> <h2 id="what-diverged-from-the-specplan-errata"><a class="header" href="#what-diverged-from-the-specplan-errata">What diverged from the spec/plan (errata)</a></h2> <p>These are honest departures from the original spec and plan, documented for future reference:</p> <ol> <li> <p><strong>sccache-action version:</strong> spec said <code>v0.0.6</code>; actual install was <code>v0.0.10</code>. The legacy GitHub Actions cache v1 API was sunset in February 2025; v0.0.6 stopped working on GHA runners. Bumped to v0.0.10 which uses the v2 cache API.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong><code>cargo nextest --run-ignored only</code> exits 4 on empty filter sets:</strong> nextest returns exit code 4 when <code>--run-ignored only</code> finds no tests to run (the filter matches nothing). Fixed by adding <code>--no-tests=pass</code> to nextest invocations. This was not anticipated in the spec.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>macOS test flake exposed by nextest parallelism:</strong> <code>tau-cli::session::store::tests::list_sessions_returns_descending_by_created_at</code> flaked under nextest's parallel execution because nextest runs test binaries in parallel (unlike cargo test's serial execution within a binary). The test relied on monotonic ordering from <code>std::time::SystemTime</code>, which macOS's clock resolution made non-monotonic under tight loops. Fixed by adding <code>.config/nextest.toml</code> with <code>retries = 2</code>. The underlying test was also fixed.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong><code>actions/upload-artifact</code> preserves directory tree:</strong> when uploading files, the artifact contains the full directory tree relative to the repository root. Added an <code>_artifacts/</code> staging directory in the <code>build-fixtures-linux</code> job to give a clean, predictable download root. The spec did not anticipate this behavior.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong><code>actions/upload-artifact</code> strips executable bits:</strong> downloaded binaries lack the executable bit. Added <code>chmod +x</code> after every artifact download step. The spec did not anticipate this behavior.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Layer 3 tests hardcode <code>target/debug/tau</code>:</strong> the plugin-compat Layer 3 tests resolve the tau binary as <code>target/debug/tau</code> (not a configurable path). Restored <code>cargo build -p tau-cli --bin tau</code> (debug, not release) in the <code>test-tau-plugin-compat</code> job to satisfy this constraint. The spec assumed only release builds would be needed.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Plugin binary names have <code>-plugin</code> suffix:</strong> the spec and plan referred to plugin binary names as <code>anthropic</code>, <code>ollama</code>, <code>openai</code>, <code>fs-read</code>, <code>shell</code>. The actual <code>[[bin]] name</code> values in the Cargo manifests are <code>anthropic-plugin</code>, <code>ollama-plugin</code>, <code>openai-plugin</code>, <code>fs-read-plugin</code>, <code>shell-plugin</code>. All <code>build-fixtures-linux</code> invocations and artifact copy steps use the correct suffixed names.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Spec baseline / final check counts:</strong> spec estimated 29 → 18; actual is 23 → 14. Explained fully in Decision 8.</p> </li> </ol> <h2 id="consequences-14"><a class="header" href="#consequences-14">Consequences</a></h2> <p><strong>Positive:</strong></p> <ul> <li>PR critical path reduced from ~33 minutes to ≤25 minutes (estimated; actual varies by cache hit rate).</li> <li>Required check count reduced from 23 to 14 — branch protection is simpler and more meaningful.</li> <li>Windows is now a hard gate, surfacing cross-platform regressions immediately.</li> <li>MSRV verification is fast and unambiguous (compile-time check only).</li> <li><code>cargo nextest</code> runs in CI; local dev can match CI behavior with a one-time <code>cargo install cargo-nextest --locked</code>.</li> <li>sccache provides cross-job rustc caching; per-job rust-cache provides incremental reuse within a job type. Both layers are now active.</li> <li><code>mold</code> linker on Linux reduces link time for large Rust binaries.</li> <li>Plugin binaries are compiled once per PR (in <code>build-fixtures-linux</code>) and reused by all downstream jobs.</li> <li>Each phase was independently verified green; no extended CI outage during migration.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Negative:</strong></p> <ul> <li><code>build-fixtures-linux</code> is a new single point of failure for all Linux e2e jobs. A flake or build failure in that job blocks the entire downstream pipeline.</li> <li>Two test invocations per <code>test-stable</code> job (nextest + <code>--doc</code>) adds minor complexity vs. a single <code>cargo test</code>.</li> <li>The <code>_artifacts/</code> staging step and <code>chmod +x</code> post-download are non-obvious CI idioms that future contributors must maintain.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Neutral:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Branch protection required-check names must be manually updated after any job rename.
