Rejected: torn-line fragility and no storage benefit under full-history rehydration (see D3).</li> <li><strong>Carry β.4 <code>context_state</code> in the checkpoint</strong> (per the original handoff). Rejected as unnecessary: the context pipeline is stateless, so there is nothing to serialize beyond the message history (D4).</li> <li><strong>Event-sourced replay now</strong> (A-full). Rejected/deferred: it imposes a permanent replay-determinism tax on every future engine change; gated until a concrete exactly-once need exists and β.6 is green on both profiles.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0054-in-wasm-mcp-facilitator"><a class="header" href="#adr-0054-in-wasm-mcp-facilitator">ADR-0054: in-wasm MCP facilitator</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-06-20 <strong>Deciders:</strong> Titouan (architect), implementing session <strong>Supersedes:</strong> none <strong>Renumbered from:</strong> the β.7.5 design's "ADR-0050" (0050/0051/0052 were taken by output-schema, the tau-ir crate split, and per-agent model resolution).</p> <h2 id="context-57"><a class="header" href="#context-57">Context</a></h2> <p>The β.7.5 wasm guest runs the workflow IR with no host imports beyond inference, clock, and randomness (ADR-0046). The canonical β.6 fan-monitor includes an MCP <code>weather</code> tool. To run that scenario in-guest the facilitator must execute inside the wasm component — a host MCP import would re-introduce a transport the determinism + parity story (ADR-0049) does not account for.</p> <p><code>tau-mcp</code> is <code>#![no_std]</code> and already contains the pure cassette <code>Replayer</code> (<code>crates/tau-mcp/src/cassette/replayer.rs</code>); the std pieces (<code>CassetteTransport</code>, <code>McpClient</code>) live behind <code>with-std-adapters</code> / <code>tau-mcp-tokio</code>.</p> <h2 id="decision-46"><a class="header" href="#decision-46">Decision</a></h2> <ol> <li>The MCP facilitator runs <strong>in-guest</strong> on the no_std <code>tau-mcp</code> types. The conformance <code>weather</code> tool replays a <strong>cassette baked into the component</strong> via <code>tau_mcp::cassette::Replayer</code> — zero host import.</li> <li>A no_std MCP client path over <code>Replayer</code> is built for the guest; the std <code>tau-mcp-tokio</code> <code>McpClient</code> stays the host/dev path. Both consume the same cassette bytes, so dev and wasm replay identically.</li> <li><strong>Real (non-cassette) MCP transport from inside wasm is reserved for γ.1</strong> via a future <code>tau:mcp</code> WIT import slot. β.7.5 ships cassette-only.</li> </ol> <h2 id="consequences-51"><a class="header" href="#consequences-51">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>The simplified fan-monitor (PR-F) needs no MCP and ships first; the full fan-monitor with in-guest <code>weather</code> + conformance fixture <code>07</code> lands in <strong>PR-G</strong> alongside <code>WasmMode</code>.</li> <li>Parity holds: the same cassette bytes drive both profiles.</li> <li>Risk: untested no_std corners of <code>tau-mcp</code> when linked into wasm — PR-G smoke-compiles <code>tau-mcp</code> for <code>wasm32-wasip2</code> before wiring the tool.</li> </ul> <h2 id="references-28"><a class="header" href="#references-28">References</a></h2> <ul> <li>ADR-0046 — wasm AOT artifact + WIT world.</li> <li>ADR-0049 — single-channel typed conformance observable.</li> <li><code>docs/superpowers/specs/2026-06-14-beta-7-5-wasm-aot-design.md</code> §10–§11.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0055-tau-identity--a-compilerengine-between-two-contracts-the-cli-is-the-reference-host"><a class="header" href="#adr-0055-tau-identity--a-compilerengine-between-two-contracts-the-cli-is-the-reference-host">ADR-0055: tau identity — a compiler+engine between two contracts; the CLI is the reference host</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-06-22 <strong>Deciders:</strong> tau core</p> <h2 id="context-58"><a class="header" href="#context-58">Context</a></h2> <p>The 2026-06-20 roadmap-challenge / vision-reframe session (verified deep research) concluded that tau is a <strong>combination play</strong>: every individual axis (IR/durability, edge-wasm, MCP-hosting, wasm-sandboxing, prompt-compilation, per-tool sandboxing, on-MCU agents) already has a more-focused rival ahead. The only unoccupied square is the <strong>intersection + conformance + vendor-independence + root-governed capability safety</strong>.</p> <p>To defend that square, the project must be precise about <em>what tau's product is</em>. Historically the docs lead with "the <code>tau</code> CLI" and frame edge / browser / embedded as downstream build targets of a CLI-centric application. That framing privileges one host, makes the other hosts look like afterthoughts, and — most damagingly — risks tying tau's public stability surface to CLI verbs that should be free to churn. Parallel work is in flight (durability #373, β.7.5 #369/#372); without a locked identity it will drift.</p> <p><a href="decisions/../explanation/tau-philosophy.html"><code>docs/explanation/tau-philosophy.md</code></a> already establishes Conviction 1 ("tau is a <em>compiler</em>, not a framework"). This ADR locks the precise product boundary that conviction implies.</p> <h2 id="decision-47"><a class="header" href="#decision-47">Decision</a></h2> <p><strong>tau's product is <code>tau-runtime-core</code> (the engine) plus TWO versioned public contracts:</strong></p> <ol> <li><strong>The authoring / IR schema</strong> (JSON). This INCLUDES the root <code>[allow]</code> governance section — the capability ceiling and resource registry of the <code>tau.toml</code> constitution. <code>[allow]</code> is the <em>governance section of the authoring contract</em>, not a separate ABI (there are two contracts, not three).</li> <li><strong>The WIT host world</strong> (the embedding interface). The WIT world is <strong>generated from the no_std ports</strong> — it is never hand-maintained, so it cannot drift from the engine it describes.</li> </ol> <p><strong>The <code>tau</code> CLI is the REFERENCE HOST, not the product.</strong> The analogy is LLVM: the product is the LLVM core + the IR; <code>clang</code> is one reference frontend/driver built on it. For tau, the product is <code>tau-runtime-core</code> + the two contracts; the <code>tau</code> CLI is one reference host/embedder that exercises them.</p> <p><strong>The public stability / semver surface is the two contracts + the no_std ports API.</strong> CLI verbs get a separate, looser compatibility policy (documented with the CLI, not governed by the contract semver).</p> <p><strong>The CLI is held to the highest quality bar.</strong> It is the on-ramp and the example that edge / browser / embedded embedders copy. This decision demotes the CLI's <em>architectural privilege</em> (it is one host among peers), not its <em>importance</em> (it remains the reference standard).</p> <h2 id="consequences-52"><a class="header" href="#consequences-52">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>Docs lead with component + contracts.</strong> Features are framed engine-first; <code>philosophy.md</code> (Story 8.2) and <code>ROADMAP.md</code> (Story 8.3) are reframed to match. Future ADRs frame features as engine + contract changes, then note the CLI surface.</li> <li><strong>Edge / browser / embedded hosts are PEERS of the CLI</strong> — each is a host of one component, not a downstream target of a CLI-centric product.</li> <li><strong>Versioning + conformance attach to the two contracts</strong>; CLI verbs evolve under the looser policy. This is what lets the CLI stay the highest-quality, fastest-moving reference surface without destabilising embedders.</li> <li><strong>New obligation:</strong> the WIT host world must be <em>generated</em> from the ports (no hand-maintained drift). Locking and codegen of both contracts is EPIC 2 ("Lock the two contracts"); this ADR is the identity premise EPIC 2 implements.</li> <li><strong>Neutral:</strong> no code changes in this ADR. It is constitutional framing that constrains how subsequent engine, durability, and β.7.5 work is described and versioned.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-42"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-42">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>CLI-as-product (status-quo framing).</strong> Rejected: it privileges one host, makes edge / browser / embedded read as afterthoughts, and ties the public stability surface to CLI verbs that must be free to churn. The trade-off it imposes — a frozen CLI or unstable embedders — is exactly the failure this ADR prevents.</li> <li><strong>Three contracts (authoring schema, <code>[allow]</code> governance, WIT world).</strong> Rejected: <code>[allow]</code> is the governance <em>section</em> of the authoring contract, not an independent ABI with its own version line (reconciliation R1 of the vision audit). Counting it separately would create a third versioned surface that always moves in lockstep with the first — ceremony without value.</li> <li><strong>Engine-only product (contracts are implementation detail, not product).</strong> Rejected: an engine without versioned, conformance-checked contracts is not embeddable or provable-identical-across-targets. The contracts <em>are</em> the product surface; hiding them would forfeit the moat (conformance + vendor-independence).</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0056-the-two-contracts-are-the-semver-stability-surface"><a class="header" href="#adr-0056-the-two-contracts-are-the-semver-stability-surface">ADR-0056: the two contracts are the semver stability surface</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-06-22 <strong>Deciders:</strong> tau core</p> <h2 id="context-59"><a class="header" href="#context-59">Context</a></h2> <p><a href="decisions/0055-tau-identity-two-contracts.html">ADR-0055</a> fixed tau's <em>identity</em>: the product is <code>tau-runtime-core</code> (the engine) plus two versioned public contracts — the authoring / IR schema and the WIT host world — with the <code>tau</code> CLI as the reference host. But 0055 fixed the <em>identity</em>, not the <em>stability mechanics</em>, and its decision text carries a latent ambiguity. It says the public surface is "the two contracts <strong>+ the no_std ports API</strong>" (which reads like three surfaces), while two lines later it says "versioning + conformance attach to <strong>the two contracts</strong>" and its alternatives section explicitly rejects a three-contract model ("two contracts, not three").</p> <p>This ADR makes the versioning scheme <strong>normative and precise</strong> so that the rest of EPIC 2 (schema publish, WIT generation + drift test, operator policy) and the in-flight parallel work (durability #373, β.7.5) cannot diverge from one agreed contract shape. It is constitutional: it lands the <em>decision</em>; the operator <em>policy</em> (deprecation windows, migration how-tos, the <code>cargo-semver-checks</code> workflow) lands in Story 2.4.</p> <p>Three facts constrain the decision:</p> <ul> <li> <p>The IR already carries a version: <code>tau-ir::module</code> has an <code>ir_format</code> semver field (currently v2.2.0), separate from <code>tau_version</code>; both feed the IR content hash.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>tau-ports</code> is a broad no_std Rust trait surface; the WIT host world is only the minimal 3-function subset, <strong>generated from</strong> ports (Story 2.3) — never hand-maintained.</p> </li> <li> <p>The three surfaces have <strong>different consumers</strong> and a <strong>containment</strong> relationship — <code>WIT ⊊ ports</code>, WIT generated from ports — so every WIT-breaking change implies a ports-breaking change, but not vice-versa (ports-internal churn in <code>storage</code>/<code>orchestration</code> need not touch the 3 host functions):</p> <div class="table-wrapper"><table><thead><tr><th>surface</th><th>consumer</th><th>churn tolerance</th></tr></thead><tbody> <tr><td>IR JSON schema</td><td>frontend / SDK authors</td><td>track <code>ir_format</code></td></tr> <tr><td>WIT host world</td><td>wasm-guest embedders, any language</td><td>want zero false-alarm bumps</td></tr> <tr><td>ports API</td><td>no_std Rust embedders</td><td>see the full surface, correctly</td></tr> </tbody></table> </div></li> </ul> <h2 id="decision-48"><a class="header" href="#decision-48">Decision</a></h2> <p><strong>The public ABI is exactly two published, conformance-kitted contracts, each versioned by its own native mechanism</strong> — the "one source → no drift" principle applied to versioning itself. No bespoke version registry, no hand-maintained version constant:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Authoring contract</strong> — the IR JSON schema, including the root <code>[allow]</code> governance section — versioned by the existing <code>ir_format</code> field.</li> <li><strong>Embedding contract</strong> — versioned by the <strong>WIT package version</strong>, <code>package tau:host@x.y.z;</code>.</li> </ol> <p><strong>The no_std ports API is the Rust-native binding of the embedding contract</strong>, versioned by <code>tau-ports</code> <strong>crate semver</strong> and enforced by <code>cargo-semver-checks</code> in CI. It is <em>not</em> a third published contract. This is the precise meaning of 0055's "+ the no_std ports API": ports' stability is delivered by Rust's own semver mechanism, so it is covered without being a third language-neutral ABI.</p> <p><strong>Containment invariant:</strong> <code>WIT ⊊ ports</code>; WIT is generated from ports (Story 2.3), so every WIT-breaking change implies a ports-breaking change. The Story 2.3 drift test enforces this.</p> <p><strong>Breaking-change definition per surface</strong> (the normative semver semantics):</p> <ul> <li><strong>IR <code>ir_format</code></strong> — <em>major:</em> remove/rename/retype a field, or change the canonical encoding such that an older runtime cannot load the IR or a previously-valid IR becomes invalid; <em>minor:</em> additive (new optional field / forward-compatible variant); <em>patch:</em> non-semantic / doc only.</li> <li><strong>WIT <code>tau:host</code></strong> — <em>major:</em> remove, re-signature, or re-semantic any of the 3 host functions; <em>minor:</em> additive host function or additive optional parameter; <em>patch:</em> doc only.</li> <li><strong><code>tau-ports</code> crate</strong> — standard Rust semver, enforced by <code>cargo-semver-checks</code>.</li> </ul> <p><strong>CLI verbs are explicitly OUT of this surface.</strong> They evolve under a looser compatibility policy documented with the CLI, not governed by the contract semver (restates 0055).</p> <h3 id="relationship-to-adr-0055"><a class="header" href="#relationship-to-adr-0055">Relationship to ADR-0055</a></h3> <p>0055 is the <strong>premise</strong> of this ADR, not superseded. This ADR resolves 0055's "+ the no_std ports API" phrasing (the ports API is the Rust binding of the embedding contract, versioned by crate semver — point 2 above) and makes 0055's "versioning attaches to the two contracts" operational. 0055's status is unchanged.</p> <h2 id="consequences-53"><a class="header" href="#consequences-53">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>New CI obligation:</strong> a <code>cargo-semver-checks</code> lane for <code>tau-ports</code> (does not exist today). Named here; wired by Stories 2.3/2.4.</li> <li><strong>Wires the rest of EPIC 2:</strong> Story 2.2 surfaces the IR JSON Schema <code>$id</code> / version from <code>ir_format</code>; Story 2.3 emits WIT carrying <code>@x.y.z</code> plus the containment drift test; Story 2.4 owns the operator policy.</li> <li><strong><code>tau-ports</code> versioning wrinkle:</strong> <code>tau-ports</code> likely shares the workspace version today (<code>version.workspace = true</code>). To give it an independent semver signal it may need to break out of the workspace version, or we accept a coarse workspace version and rely on <code>cargo-semver-checks</code> to flag inadequate bumps. Story 2.4 resolves this; this ADR only names the constraint.</li> <li><strong>Neutral:</strong> no code in this ADR — the acceptance gate is "ADR merged" with a clean mdbook build + linkcheck.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-43"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-43">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>One bespoke <code>host-abi</code> version covering WIT ⊕ ports together.</strong> Rejected: a ports-internal break (e.g. in <code>storage</code>) that never touches the 3 host functions would still bump the exact number a wasm-guest author tracks — false-alarm major bumps land on tau's flagship "embed in any language" persona. A hand-maintained <code>HOST_ABI_VERSION</code> constant also violates one-source-no-drift.</li> <li><strong>Three independent published version lines</strong> (<code>ir_format</code> + a WIT-world version + a ports-crate version, each published). Rejected: reintroduces the three-surface ceremony 0055 explicitly killed, and creates WIT↔ports version drift risk — two hand-coordinated numbers for one generated relationship.</li> <li><strong>One unified <code>tau-abi</code> semver covering IR + WIT + ports together.</strong> Rejected: couples authoring and embedding — an IR-only additive change forces an embedding-version bump and churns embedders who depend on only one contract, and vice-versa.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0057-root-allow-governance--build-time-enforcement"><a class="header" href="#adr-0057-root-allow-governance--build-time-enforcement">ADR-0057: Root <code>[allow]</code> governance + build-time enforcement</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-06-22 (accepted 2026-07-19; EPIC 1 shipped via #445/#451/#453) <strong>Deciders:</strong> titouanlebocq</p> <h2 id="context-60"><a class="header" href="#context-60">Context</a></h2> <p>The tau philosophy's Conviction 3 (<a href="decisions/../explanation/tau-philosophy.html"><code>tau-philosophy.md</code></a>) states that every tool declares its capabilities <strong>once, in the root <code>tau.toml</code> constitution</strong>, and that <code>tau build</code> lowers that one declaration per target. ADR-0055 locks the precise product boundary that conviction implies: the root <code>[allow]</code> section is the <strong>governance section of the authoring contract</strong> — not a separate ABI, but the capability ceiling and resource registry of the <code>tau.toml</code> constitution.</p> <p>Today, no such root ceiling exists. The capability model is <strong>two layers</strong>:</p> <pre><code>package manifest caps ──(ceiling)──► agent [capabilities] override ──(narrows)──► effective ▲ ▲ "what the tool CAN do" "what THIS project lets it do" (ships with the package) (per-agent, narrows only) </code></pre> <p><code>tau_pkg::capability_override::compute_effective</code> already enforces <em>override ⊆ package</em> — the integrator may only <strong>narrow</strong> a package's grants, never widen them. But the package manifest is the de-facto top: there is no repo-root constitution above it, so a package author's declared grants are the ceiling. A project cannot express "no agent in this repo may ever touch the network, regardless of what a package requests."</p> <p>This is the gap EPIC 1 closes. tau's discipline (per the user's standing principle and Conviction 3) is <strong>Rust-like</strong>: any check that <em>can</em> run at build time <em>must</em> run at build time; deferring an enforceable constraint to runtime instantiation is a regression. The root constitution must therefore be proven at <code>tau check</code>, not merely honored at runtime.</p> <p>This ADR is <strong>constitutional framing</strong>: it locks the model that stories 1.2–1.6 implement. It writes no code.</p> <h3 id="existing-machinery-this-builds-on"><a class="header" href="#existing-machinery-this-builds-on">Existing machinery this builds on</a></h3> <ul> <li><code>Capability</code> / <code>FsCapability</code> / <code>NetCapability</code> / <code>ProcessCapability</code> (<code>tau-domain</code>) — the capability vocabulary, <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code>.</li> <li><code>compute_effective</code> + <code>glob_subset::is_glob_subset_set</code> (<code>tau-pkg</code>) — the subset relation (globs for filesystem paths, exact-set inclusion for hosts / commands, <code>≤</code> for <code>max_bytes</code>). ADR-0032 records its relocation to <code>tau-pkg</code>; ADR-0036 records its forward-compatibility stance.</li> <li><code>[models]</code> alias→<code>{backend, model}</code> map (ADR-0052).</li> <li><code>[tools]</code> definitions for IR lowering (β.2.2).</li> <li><code>[mcp.<name>]</code> server bindings (philosophy.md, β.3 MCP facilitator).</li> </ul> <h2 id="decision-49"><a class="header" href="#decision-49">Decision</a></h2> <h3 id="1-allow-is-an-additive-top-ceiling-above-packages"><a class="header" href="#1-allow-is-an-additive-top-ceiling-above-packages">1. <code>[allow]</code> is an additive top ceiling above packages</a></h3> <p>The root <code>tau.toml</code> gains an <code>[allow]</code> section that is a <strong>new top of the lattice</strong>, inserted <em>above</em> the existing package ceiling. Packages declare what a tool <em>needs</em> (a request); <code>[allow]</code> declares what the project <em>permits</em> (the ceiling). The existing <code>override ⊆ package</code> relation is unchanged; <code>[allow]</code> adds one link at the top:</p> <pre><code>[allow] ⊇ package ⊇ agent override ⊇ … ⊇ tool </code></pre> <p>A package may declare <code>fs.read = ["/**"]</code>, but if root <code>[allow]</code> caps <code>fs.read = ["/proj/**"]</code>, the package is bounded at build time. Packages become <em>requests</em>, not unconditional grants.</p> <h3 id="2-one-capability-vocabulary-one-subset-checker-for-every-link"><a class="header" href="#2-one-capability-vocabulary-one-subset-checker-for-every-link">2. One capability vocabulary, one subset checker, for every link</a></h3> <p><code>[allow]</code> is expressed in the <strong>same <code>Capability</code> kinds</strong> used everywhere else (<code>fs.read</code>, <code>fs.write</code>, <code>fs.exec</code>, <code>net.http</code>, <code>process.spawn</code>, <code>agent.spawn</code>), with the <strong>same field shapes</strong> (paths = globs, hosts / commands = exact sets, <code>max_bytes</code>). Consequently <strong>every lattice link is decided by the one reused subset function</strong> — there is exactly one comparison code path, already tested.</p> <pre><code class="language-toml">[allow] "fs.read" = { paths = ["/proj/**"] } "fs.write" = { paths = ["/proj/build/**"], max_bytes = 5_000_000 } "net.http" = { hosts = ["api.weather.com"] } "process.spawn" = { commands = ["git", "rg"] } </code></pre> <p><strong>Deny-by-default within a present <code>[allow]</code>:</strong> a capability <em>kind</em> that is absent from an <code>[allow]</code> block carries a ceiling of ∅ for that kind — nothing below it may use that capability. (Absence of the <em>entire</em> <code>[allow]</code> block is governed by §5.)</p> <h3 id="3-the-resource-registry-is-the-governance-ceiling--one-block-per-resource"><a class="header" href="#3-the-resource-registry-is-the-governance-ceiling--one-block-per-resource">3. The resource registry is the governance ceiling — one block per resource</a></h3> <p><code>[allow]</code> is <strong>pure governance</strong>: it carries the ceiling, never concrete configuration noise. The named-resource registries are:</p> <ul> <li><strong><code>[allow.models]</code></strong> — the <strong>sole home</strong> for the alias→<code>{backend, model}</code> map. This folds in today's top-level <code>[models]</code> table (ADR-0052): there is nothing to <em>narrow</em> about a model identity, so the permitted-alias map and the identity map are one and the same. Checked by set-membership.</li> <li><strong><code>[allow.mcp.<name>]</code></strong> — one block per MCP server. The <code>url</code> <strong>is</strong> the grant of network reach: the reachable-host ceiling is <strong>derived from the url's host</strong>. An explicit <code>hosts = [...]</code> is permitted only to widen (a multi-host contract) or narrow. There is <strong>no separate <code>[mcp.*]</code> instance table</strong> — the registry block is the binding.</li> <li><strong><code>[allow.tools.<name>]</code></strong> — one block per tool: its binding (<code>native = …</code> or <code>mcp = …</code>) plus an optional per-tool capability ceiling.</li> </ul> <pre><code class="language-toml">[allow.models] fast = { backend = "anthropic", model = "claude-haiku-4-5" } [allow.mcp.weather] url = "https://api.weather.com/mcp" # host ceiling derived from url [allow.tools.read_temp] native = "ReadTemp" "fs.read" = { paths = ["/proj/sensors/**"] } </code></pre> <p><strong>Closed-world (deny-by-default for references):</strong> an agent that references a model, MCP, or tool <strong>name</strong> not registered in the corresponding <code>[allow.*]</code> table fails <code>tau check</code>. Referencing an unregistered resource is an error, not a silent pass.</p> <h3 id="4-the-lattice-and-the-build--runtime-split"><a class="header" href="#4-the-lattice-and-the-build--runtime-split">4. The lattice and the build / runtime split</a></h3> <p>The complete capability lattice is <strong>five links</strong>, each the same <code>⊇</code> subset relation from §2:</p> <pre><code>[allow] ──┐ (new link) ▼ build: agent.effective ⊆ root agent ▼ build: declared region envelope ⊆ agent dyn-region ····· runtime: actual in-region caps ⊆ envelope ▼ build where static / runtime where spawned dynamically spawn (attenuation: child ⊆ parent) ▼ build: tool grant ⊆ spawn / agent tool (leaf — most narrow) </code></pre> <p>The governing principle — the Rust-like build-enforcement stance — is:</p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Every statically-decidable link is enforced at build time (<code>tau check</code>). Runtime enforcement exists only for the single genuinely runtime-determined input — the actual capabilities a dynamic region selects at runtime — and even that is bounded by a build-checked envelope. No capability is ever enforced <em>only</em> at runtime when it could have been proven at build.</strong></p> </blockquote> <p>This ADR declares <strong>all five links</strong> as the constitution so that EPIC 4 (dynamic regions, <code>StepRun::Dynamic</code>) slots into a pre-specified envelope contract without re-litigating the model. Enforcement scope is staged:</p> <div class="table-wrapper"><table><thead><tr><th>link</th><th>endpoints exist today</th><th>build / runtime</th><th>enforced by</th></tr></thead><tbody> <tr><td>root ⊇ agent</td><td>agents yes; root new</td><td><strong>build</strong></td><td><strong>EPIC 1</strong> (1.4 / 1.5)</td></tr> <tr><td>agent ⊇ tool</td><td>yes (<code>tool_refs</code>, <code>[allow.tools]</code>)</td><td><strong>build</strong></td><td><strong>EPIC 1</strong></td></tr> <tr><td>agent ⊇ spawn</td><td>yes (<code>agent.spawn</code>, ADR-0024)</td><td><strong>build</strong> (sub-agent kinds are static)</td><td><strong>EPIC 1</strong></td></tr> <tr><td>agent ⊇ dyn-region envelope</td><td><code>StepRun::Dynamic</code> not built</td><td><strong>build</strong> (envelope ⊆ agent)</td><td>declared here; enforced <strong>EPIC 4</strong> (4.4)</td></tr> <tr><td>dyn-region actual ⊇ spawn / tool</td><td>not built</td><td><strong>runtime</strong> (membership + bounds counters)</td><td>declared here; enforced <strong>EPIC 4</strong> (4.5)</td></tr> </tbody></table> </div> <p><strong>Clarification (spawn caps are ceiling-exempt).</strong> The <code>agent ⊇ spawn</code> link governs <em>spawn permission</em> (<code>agent.spawn</code> / <code>skill.spawn</code>) — but a spawn cap is deliberately <strong>not</strong> a raw <code>[allow]</code> ceiling entry. Root <code>[allow]</code> cannot list <code>agent.spawn</code>; it "flows through the lattice's spawn link, not a raw ceiling entry" (<code>ALLOW_CEILING_KINDS</code> in <code>tau-pkg</code>). Consequently the <code>root ⊇ agent</code> link (<code>agent.effective ⊆ root</code>, checked as "package manifest ⊆ root") <strong>excludes</strong> spawn caps from its subset check rather than demanding a matching ceiling key that by construction can never exist. Soundness is preserved by the inward link: the spawn link requires every spawned kind's caps ⊆ the agent's effective grant, and the agent's <em>non-spawn</em> effective grant is ⊆ root via <code>root ⊇ agent</code> — so a spawned kind stays transitively bounded by root. <code>Custom</code>/<code>Forward</code> caps are not spawn caps and remain subject to the raw ceiling (deny-by-default). <code>skill.spawn</code> shares the L1 exemption; a dedicated build-time skill-spawn link (analogous to L3 for <code>agent.spawn</code>) is deferred until a <code>[skill.kinds.*]</code> surface exists.</p> <h3 id="5-backward-compatibility-governed-by-default-with-explicit-opt-out"><a class="header" href="#5-backward-compatibility-governed-by-default-with-explicit-opt-out">5. Backward compatibility: governed by default, with explicit opt-out</a></h3> <p>This ADR originally framed governance as <em>opt-in</em> (an absent <code>[allow]</code> block emitting only a warning). The shipped default is stricter: <strong>D2 (ADR-0059, governance build gate, #455) makes governance the default</strong>, consistent with the Rust-like build-enforcement stance — a missing constitution is a defect, not a soft nudge. The progressive-disclosure spirit is preserved through <strong>explicit, named opt-out flags</strong> rather than a silent warning:</p> <ul> <li><strong>No <code>[allow]</code> block</strong> = <strong>hard error <code>GOV000</code></strong> at <code>tau build</code> / <code>tau run</code> / <code>tau check</code> (exit 2): "no constitution declared." A workflow does not build or run ungoverned unless the author explicitly asks.</li> <li><strong>Opt out per invocation:</strong> <ul> <li><code>--allow-ungoverned</code> — proceed despite a <em>missing</em> <code>[allow]</code> ceiling (ungoverned build/run, by explicit choice).</li> <li><code>--no-governance</code> — skip governance checking even when a ceiling <em>does</em> exist; the bundle records the governance verdict as <code>skipped</code>, so the escape is auditable in the artifact.</li> </ul> </li> <li><strong>An <code>[allow]</code> block present</strong> = strict. Anything unlisted is denied (§2's deny-by-default within <code>[allow]</code>, and §3's closed-world for references).</li> </ul> <p>Existing projects and fixtures adopt an <code>[allow]</code> block (or an explicit opt-out flag) to build; the strictness bites the moment an author writes <code>[allow]</code>, and the <em>absence</em> of one is now surfaced as an error rather than tolerated silently.</p> <h2 id="consequences-54"><a class="header" href="#consequences-54">Consequences</a></h2> <h3 id="positive-13"><a class="header" href="#positive-13">Positive</a></h3> <ul> <li>A project can express a true constitution: "no agent here may touch the network," enforced at build time, regardless of what any package requests.</li> <li>One capability vocabulary and one subset checker cover every lattice link — no second comparison code path, no coarse-vs-fine mapping to maintain.</li> <li><code>[allow]</code> reads as a reviewable constitution: a reviewer audits one section to see <em>what is permitted</em>, separate from <em>how things are wired</em>.</li> <li>The Rust-like guarantee is realized: every enforceable constraint is proven at <code>tau check</code>; runtime gating shrinks to the irreducibly dynamic case.</li> <li>EPIC 4 inherits a complete, pre-specified lattice and envelope contract.</li> </ul> <h3 id="negative--obligations"><a class="header" href="#negative--obligations">Negative / obligations</a></h3> <ul> <li><strong><code>[models]</code> folds into <code>[allow.models]</code></strong> and MCP caps move from <code>[mcp.<name>]</code> to <code>[allow.mcp.<name>]</code> — an authoring-schema change that touches ADR-0052's and β.2.2's surfaces and the philosophy examples. Because governance is opt-in (§5), this is not a forced migration, but the docs and example projects that adopt <code>[allow]</code> must use the new homes.</li> <li>The deny-by-default semantics (§2, §3) mean an author who <em>does</em> opt into <code>[allow]</code> must enumerate every capability and resource — more up-front ceremony, by design, in exchange for a provable ceiling. Story 1.6's lint (coarse ceilings such as <code>hosts = ["*"]</code>) partially offsets the temptation to over-grant.</li> <li>A new public authoring-schema surface (<code>[allow]</code>, <code>[allow.mcp]</code>, <code>[allow.tools]</code>, <code>[allow.models]</code>) is added. Per ADR-0055 it versions as the <em>governance section of the authoring contract</em>, not a separate ABI.</li> </ul> <h3 id="neutral-3"><a class="header" href="#neutral-3">Neutral</a></h3> <ul> <li>No code in this ADR. Stories 1.2 (config + registry parse / round-trip), 1.3 (elevate <code>capability_override</code> + <code>glob_subset</code> to the root ceiling), 1.4 (<code>tau check</code> failure on over-reach / unregistered reference), 1.5 (enforce the three static lattice links), and 1.6 (coarse-ceiling lint) implement it.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-44"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-44">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <div class="table-wrapper"><table><thead><tr><th>Alternative</th><th>Why rejected</th></tr></thead><tbody> <tr><td><strong><code>[allow]</code> replaces the package ceiling</strong> (packages declare nothing binding; root is the sole source of truth).</td><td>Breaks the existing <code>override ⊆ package</code> semantics and the "package author declares what the tool needs, integrator governs what's permitted" separation. The additive model preserves both and makes 1.3 <em>add a layer</em> rather than <em>rewrite one</em>.</td></tr> <tr><td><strong>Coarse category ceiling</strong> (<code>network = ["*"]</code>, <code>filesystem = ["read","write"]</code>) distinct from the fine-grained <code>Capability</code>.</td><td>Two vocabularies plus a mapping; lattice links stop being homogeneous (root⊇agent coarse-vs-fine, agent⊇tool fine-vs-fine). Conviction 3 requires uniform declaration. The coarse forms become <em>lint-detectable patterns within the same shape</em> (Story 1.6), not a separate type.</td></tr> <tr><td><strong><code>[allow.*]</code> as a thin name allow-list</strong> (registers existence only, carries no ceiling).</td><td>Cannot stop a registered MCP from declaring wider network reach than the constitution intends; the registry would not participate in the lattice. Fails EPIC 1's goal of a governed resource ceiling.</td></tr> <tr><td><strong><code>[allow.*]</code> as the canonical home, relocating concrete config (urls, bindings) into <code>[allow]</code>.</strong></td><td>Mixes governance with configuration noise; <code>[allow]</code> stops reading as a pure constitution. The chosen model keeps the <em>ceiling</em> in <code>[allow]</code> (incl. the url-as-grant for MCP) while excluding incidental config.</td></tr> <tr><td><strong>Strict deny-all when <code>[allow]</code> is absent</strong> (no escape hatch).</td><td>A <em>silent</em> strict-by-default instantly breaks every existing project and fixture. What shipped (D2 / ADR-0059) is the middle ground §5 describes: a missing <code>[allow]</code> is a hard error (<code>GOV000</code>) <strong>with an explicit per-invocation opt-out</strong> (<code>--allow-ungoverned</code> / <code>--no-governance</code>), so the strictness is the default but the migration path stays open and auditable.</td></tr> <tr><td><strong>Enforce only root ⊇ agent in EPIC 1; let EPIC 4 define the rest of the lattice.</strong></td><td>A constitutional ADR should define the whole rule once. Declaring all five links now (even with staged enforcement) prevents EPIC 4 from redesigning the envelope contract.</td></tr> </tbody></table> </div> <h2 id="references-29"><a class="header" href="#references-29">References</a></h2> <ul> <li>ADR-0055 — tau identity; <code>[allow]</code> is the governance section of the authoring contract (not a separate ABI).</li> <li>ADR-0059 — governance build gate (D2): a missing <code>[allow]</code> is a hard error (<code>GOV000</code>) with <code>--allow-ungoverned</code> / <code>--no-governance</code> opt-out (§5).</li> <li>ADR-0052 — per-agent model resolution (<code>[models]</code>, folded into <code>[allow.models]</code>).</li> <li>ADR-0032 — <code>CapabilityOverride</code> relocation to <code>tau-pkg</code>.</li> <li>ADR-0036 — capability forward-compatibility.</li> <li>ADR-0024 — multi-agent orchestration (<code>agent.spawn</code>, recursive spawn).</li> <li><code>docs/explanation/tau-philosophy.md</code> — Conviction 3 (capability-safe by construction; per-target lowering).</li> <li><code>docs/superpowers/plans/vision-roadmap.md</code> — EPIC 1 (stories 1.1–1.6), EPIC 4 (dynamic regions).</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0058-ir-structured-control-flow-blocks"><a class="header" href="#adr-0058-ir-structured-control-flow-blocks">ADR-0058: IR structured control-flow blocks</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-06-22 <strong>Deciders:</strong> tau core</p> <h2 id="context-61"><a class="header" href="#context-61">Context</a></h2> <p>The workflow IR (<code>tau-ir</code>) represents a pipeline as a flat <code>Vec<PipelineStep></code>, where each step holds a single <code>StepRun</code> leaf. This is sufficient for linear, unconditional workflows but cannot express the control-flow patterns real workflows require: conditional branching, parallel fan-out, bounded loops, and human-in-the-loop suspend/resume.</p> <p>EPIC 4 (structured control flow) extends the IR to support these patterns. The IR is a versioned public contract (ADR-0056), so any extension must preserve byte-stability for existing serialised workflows and must bump the minor version when new variants are used.</p> <p>Two design constraints follow from the existing IR shape:</p> <ol> <li><code>PipelineStep.run</code> is the single execution point. Any extension must keep it that way so the interpreter walk stays uniform — one match arm, one dispatch path.</li> <li>Conditions must reuse existing primitives. The IR already carries <code>Locus</code> (where to read a value) and <code>GoalPredicate</code> (how to test it) for verify steps. Introducing a parallel condition language would duplicate semantics and split the type-checker.</li> </ol> <h2 id="decision-50"><a class="header" href="#decision-50">Decision</a></h2> <p><code>StepRun</code> gains four recursive structured-block variants, keeping <code>PipelineStep.run</code> as the single execution point:</p> <pre><code>StepRun::Branch { on: Condition, then: Vec<PipelineStep>, otherwise: Vec<PipelineStep> } StepRun::Parallel { branches: Vec<Vec<PipelineStep>> } StepRun::Loop { body: Vec<PipelineStep>, until: Condition, max_iters: u64 } StepRun::Suspend { resume_signal: String } </code></pre> <p>A new <code>Condition</code> type reuses the existing locus/predicate vocabulary:</p> <pre><code>Condition { evaluates: Locus, predicate: GoalPredicate } </code></pre> <p>This keeps the branch/loop condition language identical to the verify-step condition language — one type-checker, one schema definition.</p> <p><code>Loop</code> reuses the <code>OnFail::Retry</code> rewind machinery (the interpreter already knows how to re-enter a step sequence from a saved snapshot) and carries a mandatory <code>max_iters: u32</code> bound. Unbounded loops are rejected at typecheck; <code>max_iters = 0</code> is a typecheck error (<code>u64</code>).</p> <p><code>Suspend</code> reuses the ADR-0053 <code>per_tool_call</code> checkpoint mechanism. The HITL round-trip is: checkpoint the run state, emit the <code>Suspend</code> event, wait for an external <code>resume_signal</code>, then seed-and-skip resume from the checkpoint. The full round-trip implementation is EPIC 4.3.</p> <p><code>Eq</code> is dropped from <code>StepRun</code>, <code>PipelineStep</code>, and <code>Pipeline</code>. The subtree now transitively holds <code>GoalPredicate::SchemaValid(serde_json::Value)</code>, which does not implement <code>Eq</code>. This mirrors the existing <code>CheckVerify</code> arm; equality on pipeline structures has no defined semantics in the IR contract.</p> <p><code>ir_format</code> bumps from <code>v2.3.0</code> to <code>v2.4.0</code> (additive minor). Serialised workflows that use none of the new variants are byte-stable: the new enum arms are never written, and existing deserialisation round-trips are unaffected.</p> <p>The published IR JSON Schema is regenerated at <code>v2.4.0</code> with <code>Branch</code>, <code>Parallel</code>, <code>Loop</code>, <code>Suspend</code>, and <code>Condition</code> definitions added. A conformance sample for <code>Branch</code> is included in the conformance kit.</p> <h2 id="consequences-55"><a class="header" href="#consequences-55">Consequences</a></h2> <p><strong>Positive:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Real workflows with conditional logic, parallel fan-out, bounded iteration, and human-in-the-loop pauses can now be expressed and type-checked at build time.</li> <li>The <code>PipelineStep.run</code> single-dispatch invariant is preserved: the interpreter gains four new match arms, but no structural change to the walk.</li> <li><code>Condition</code> reuse eliminates a parallel predicate sublanguage; the type-checker and JSON Schema share one definition.</li> <li>Additive versioning (<code>v2.4.0</code>) means no breaking change for existing serialised workflows.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Negative / obligations:</strong></p> <ul> <li><code>Eq</code> is dropped from the pipeline subtree; any downstream code that compared pipelines structurally will not compile (intentional: equality was not a defined contract).</li> <li>The interpreter (EPIC 4.2), Suspend round-trip (EPIC 4.3), <code>StepRun::Dynamic</code> capability-bounded regions (EPICs 4.4–4.5), and extended conformance kit (EPIC 4.6) are follow-on obligations. This ADR covers only the data model, typecheck, and schema.</li> <li>Nested control-flow refs and bounds (<code>max_iters > 0</code>, branch/parallel non-empty) are enforced at typecheck (tau build time), not at runtime — consistent with the Rust-like build-time enforcement principle.</li> <li>Nested-scope resolution — a <code>Loop</code>'s <code>until</code> referencing its own body's output, uniqueness of nested <code>PipelineStepId</code>s, and nested <code>${steps.<id>.output}</code> template visibility — is <strong>deferred to EPIC 4.2</strong> (which adds execution); 4.1's typecheck validates nested node references but does not yet model nested scope, so a condition that reads a <em>nested</em> step's output is currently rejected.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-45"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-45">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <p><strong>A. Separate <code>ControlFlow</code> node type instead of extending <code>StepRun</code>.</strong> Rejected. <code>PipelineStep.run</code> is the single execution point; splitting it into a union of <code>StepRun | ControlFlow</code> forces every interpreter match to handle two top-level types. One recursive enum keeps the walk uniform.</p> <p><strong>B. Flat goto/label steps.</strong> Rejected. Goto-style control flow is not statically structured, so it cannot be type-checked for termination or well-nestedness at build time. <code>max_iters</code>-bounded loops and explicit <code>Branch</code>/<code>Parallel</code> blocks give build-time verifiability; goto labels do not.</p> <p><strong>C. Unbounded loops (no <code>max_iters</code>).</strong> Rejected. An unbounded loop is a potential runaway agent. <code>max_iters</code> is mandatory and enforced at typecheck — no workflow reaches the interpreter with an uncapped loop.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0059-ir-control-flow-interpreter-semantics"><a class="header" href="#adr-0059-ir-control-flow-interpreter-semantics">ADR-0059: IR control-flow interpreter semantics</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted (Decision 4 superseded in part — see note below) <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-07-18 <strong>Deciders:</strong> tau core</p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Update (2026-08-09, EPIC 4.3):</strong> Decision 4's "loud named error" behavior for <code>Suspend</code> has been superseded. The interpreter now checkpoints the pipeline's outputs and step position and pauses, returning <code>PipelineOutcome::Suspended { run_id, resume_signal, step_id }</code> instead of erroring; <code>tau run --resume <id> --signal <name></code> restores the checkpoint and continues past the pause. <code>RuntimeError::SuspendNotImplemented</code> is retired; the remaining error case (a caller that runs a pipeline without wiring a <code>SuspensionStore</code>, e.g. the bundle-run path) returns <code>RuntimeError::SuspendUnsupported</code> instead. See <a href="decisions/../how-to/authoring-suspend.html">Author a suspend step</a> for the shipped authoring/resume surface.</p> </blockquote> <h2 id="context-62"><a class="header" href="#context-62">Context</a></h2> <p>ADR-0058 (EPIC 4.1) added four recursive structured-block variants to <code>tau-ir</code>'s <code>StepRun</code> (<code>Branch</code>/<code>Parallel</code>/<code>Loop</code>/<code>Suspend</code>) plus a reusable <code>Condition</code>, bumped <code>ir_format</code> to v2.4.0, and typechecked the blocks' <em>shape</em>. 4.1 shipped the blocks as <strong>inert data</strong>: the interpreter (<code>tau-runtime-core</code>) returns a generic <code>RuntimeError::Internal("… lands in EPIC 4.2")</code> stub whenever the pipeline walk reaches any control-flow block.</p> <p>ADR-0058 §Consequences also <strong>explicitly deferred</strong> one design hole to this story: how <em>nested</em> steps inside a block scope their ids and outputs. 4.1's typecheck validates that nested steps reference real nodes, but it <em>rejects</em> a <code>Loop.until</code> that reads its own body's output, because nested-scope visibility was not yet modeled.</p> <p>EPIC 4.2 (this ADR) resolves that deferral and specifies the execution semantics for <code>Branch</code>, <code>Parallel</code>, and <code>Loop</code>, plus the interim behavior for <code>Suspend</code>. <code>Suspend</code>'s full HITL checkpoint/resume round-trip remains out of scope — that is EPIC 4.3.</p> <h2 id="decision-51"><a class="header" href="#decision-51">Decision</a></h2> <p>Four decisions, taken together, define the interpreter walk added in EPIC 4.2.</p> <h3 id="decision-1--nested-scope-flat-global-namespace--execution-order-visibility"><a class="header" href="#decision-1--nested-scope-flat-global-namespace--execution-order-visibility">Decision 1 — nested scope: flat global namespace + execution-order visibility</a></h3> <p><strong>This resolves ADR-0058's deferred nested-scope note.</strong></p> <p>Every <code>PipelineStepId</code> in the whole pipeline tree (top-level and nested) is <strong>globally unique</strong>. There is <strong>one flat <code>OutputStore</code></strong> keyed by bare id. The template grammar is <strong>unchanged</strong> (<code>${steps.<id>.output}</code>; bare id everywhere). A reference (a <code>Condition</code>'s <code>Locus::Output</code>, or a <code>${steps.<id>.output}</code> template ref) resolves iff the referenced step <strong>executed before</strong> the reference point in the structured walk.</p> <p>"Executed before" is <em>execution-order</em>, not pure lexical order, and differs per block:</p> <div class="table-wrapper"><table><thead><tr><th>Reference site</th><th>In-scope steps</th></tr></thead><tbody> <tr><td><code>Branch.on</code></td><td>outer-earlier only (condition runs <em>before</em> <code>then</code>/<code>otherwise</code>)</td></tr> <tr><td><code>Branch.then</code>/<code>otherwise</code> step</td><td>outer-earlier + prior siblings in that arm</td></tr> <tr><td><code>Loop.until</code></td><td>outer-earlier <strong>+ the loop body's ids</strong> (until runs <em>after</em> each body pass)</td></tr> <tr><td><code>Loop.body</code> step</td><td>outer-earlier + prior body ids (+ previous iteration's outputs at runtime)</td></tr> <tr><td><code>Parallel</code> branch step</td><td>outer-earlier + that branch's own prior steps <strong>only</strong> (never sibling branches — they are concurrent)</td></tr> </tbody></table> </div> <p>A downstream step reads a block's result by <strong>bare id</strong> (<code>${steps.<inner>.output}</code>), because the store is flat and block-transparent. In a <code>Loop</code>, a body step's output key is <strong>overwritten each iteration</strong> (last-iteration-wins).</p> <h3 id="decision-2--parallel-bounded-cooperative-fork-join-nginx-model"><a class="header" href="#decision-2--parallel-bounded-cooperative-fork-join-nginx-model">Decision 2 — <code>Parallel</code>: bounded cooperative fork-join (nginx model)</a></h3> <p><code>tau-runtime-core</code> is <code>no_std</code> + <code>alloc</code> and <strong>executor-agnostic</strong> (only <code>futures-core</code> traits; it cannot spawn tasks — the same code runs in the wasm guest and on embassy). So <code>Parallel</code> concurrency is <strong>cooperative multiplexing inside the single interpreter task</strong>: each branch fires its LLM/tool request and parks on <code>.await</code>; the driver polls the next branch, firing <em>its</em> request. All requests are in flight at once, on one thread — the nginx event-loop model, which is exactly right for τ's I/O-bound agent/tool branches.</p> <ul> <li>Each branch forks a <strong>read-only <code>store.clone()</code></strong> (no <code>&mut</code> aliasing), runs via <code>run_steps</code>, and returns <code>(branch_index, produced_store)</code>.</li> <li>Branches are driven with <code>futures_util::stream::iter(futs).buffered(PARALLEL_CAP)</code> — a <strong>bounded</strong> number in flight (<code>PARALLEL_CAP = 8</code>, a hardcoded const for 4.2; "make it configurable" is a later story), and <code>buffered</code> <strong>preserves result order</strong> so the join is deterministic.</li> <li>At join, each branch's produced keys are <strong>merged back into the shared store in branch-index order</strong>. Because branches only <em>add</em> keys (Decision 1 isolates their reads to their own branch), the merge is a straight key insertion.</li> <li>Branch futures are polled in the same task → <strong>no <code>Send</code> bound</strong> is required between them, and no <code>Spawn</code> port is introduced. The interpreter stays executor-agnostic.</li> </ul> <h3 id="decision-3--loop-own-bounded-walk-hard-exhaustion-feedback-threading"><a class="header" href="#decision-3--loop-own-bounded-walk-hard-exhaustion-feedback-threading">Decision 3 — <code>Loop</code>: own bounded walk, hard exhaustion, feedback threading</a></h3> <p><strong>3a. Exhaustion is a hard error.</strong> When <code>body</code> has run <code>max_iters</code> times and <code>until</code> never held, the interpreter returns <code>RuntimeError::LoopExhausted { step, max_iters }</code> and the run aborts. A loop that cannot reach its goal within its mandatory bound is a failure, not a silent success — consistent with ADR-0058's "no runaway agents" and the no-silent-wrong-result stance.</p> <p><strong>3b. <code>Loop</code> gets its own small bounded walk</strong> and shares only the <em>primitives</em> with the existing <code>Check</code> gate-rewind — condition evaluation (<code>eval_condition</code>, the existing <code>evaluate_goal</code>, already reused by <code>Branch.on</code>) and the feedback-injection idiom. It does <strong>not</strong> literally reuse the flat top-level gate-rewind index loop, whose flat-index arithmetic (<code>gate_index</code>, <code>i = gate_idx</code>) would require projecting nested ids into the flat pipeline index — fighting Decision 1's tree walk. A <code>Check</code> <em>inside</em> a loop body still rewinds within its own body via the per-slice check logic in <code>run_steps</code>, so check-retry composes without literal reuse.</p> <p><strong>3c. Feedback threads across iterations.</strong> When iteration <em>N</em>'s <code>until</code> fails, its rationale is carried into iteration <em>N+1</em>'s body as a prior agent turn (<code>"Previous attempt rejected: <rationale>"</code>), reusing the existing <code>feedback: Option<String></code> idiom (<code>pipeline.rs</code> + <code>split_history</code> in <code>agent_loop</code>). A looping agent that is told <em>why</em> it is being asked again converges faster; a blind re-roll is much weaker and more likely to exhaust.</p> <h3 id="decision-4--suspend-loud-named-error-round-trip-deferred-to-43"><a class="header" href="#decision-4--suspend-loud-named-error-round-trip-deferred-to-43">Decision 4 — <code>Suspend</code>: loud named error (round-trip deferred to 4.3)</a></h3> <p>The full HITL round-trip (checkpoint run state → emit event → wait for <code>resume_signal</code> → seed-and-skip resume) is EPIC 4.3. In 4.2 the recursive walk reaching a <code>Suspend</code> (top-level or nested) returns <code>RuntimeError::SuspendNotImplemented { step, resume_signal }</code> and aborts. This keeps 4.1's never-silently-skip discipline while not shipping a half-built pause that looks resumable but cannot resume. The only change vs today's generic <code>Internal</code> stub is a <strong>named</strong> variant, giving 4.3 a clear seam.</p> <h2 id="consequences-56"><a class="header" href="#consequences-56">Consequences</a></h2> <p><strong>Positive:</strong></p> <ul> <li>The interpreter (<code>tau-runtime-core</code>) executes <code>Branch</code>, <code>Parallel</code>, and <code>Loop</code> for real; the recursive walk (<code>run_steps</code>) is shared by the top level and every nested body.</li> <li>No <code>ir_format</code> bump. 4.2 changes only the interpreter and the <code>tau-ir-lower</code> typecheck; the IR wire format (v2.4.0, from ADR-0058) is unchanged, and existing serialised workflows stay byte-stable.</li> <li>The nested-scope deferral from ADR-0058 is closed: <code>Loop.until</code> reading its own body's output now typechecks and executes; nested <code>PipelineStepId</code>s are uniqueness-checked across the whole tree; <code>Parallel</code> branch isolation and nested-template ref-checking are enforced at typecheck (tau build time), not runtime — consistent with the Rust-like build-time enforcement principle.</li> <li><code>Parallel</code>'s bounded cooperative fork-join gets real wall-clock concurrency for I/O-bound branches without adding an executor dependency, so the interpreter continues to run unmodified in the wasm guest and on embassy.</li> <li>A <code>Spawn</code> port is left as the deliberate future seam for compute-heavy <code>StepRun::Dynamic</code> regions (EPIC 4.4+), rather than being introduced now for a workload (I/O-bound agent/tool branches) that does not need it.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Negative / obligations:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Two new named <code>RuntimeError</code> variants (<code>LoopExhausted</code>, <code>SuspendNotImplemented</code>) replace the 4.1 generic <code>Internal(...)</code> stubs; any code matching exhaustively on <code>RuntimeError</code> must handle them.</li> <li><code>Suspend</code> still aborts the run in 4.2 — no workflow using <code>Suspend</code> can complete until EPIC 4.3 ships the checkpoint/resume round-trip.</li> <li><strong>Known limitation surfaced during implementation:</strong> under the flat-global model, a top-level step that references a <code>Branch</code> arm step which did <strong>not</strong> execute (because only one of <code>then</code>/<code>otherwise</code> runs per invocation) yields a runtime unresolved-template error at the point of reference, not a typecheck-time diagnostic — the reference is only invalid <em>conditionally</em>, depending on which arm executes. <code>Loop</code> bodies do not have this hazard: they always run at least once, so a downstream reference to a loop-body output is always safe once the loop step itself resolves. This is treated as an honest hard-error rather than silently resolving to an empty/default value; a typecheck-time warning on such conditionally-populated refs is a possible later story, not required for 4.2's DoD.</li> <li><code>Parallel</code> concurrency is capped at <code>PARALLEL_CAP = 8</code> (hardcoded); making it configurable is deferred to a later story.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-46"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-46">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <p><strong>Decision 1 — hierarchical/pathed scope.</strong> A namespace keyed by path (<code>${steps.<block>.<child>.output}</code>, ids unique only per-block) was rejected: it changes the template grammar, the <code>Locus::Output</code> shape (an IR schema bump), and the <code>OutputStore</code> keying, buying cross-block id reuse that hand-authored τ workflows do not need.</p> <p><strong>Decision 1 — block-encapsulated outputs.</strong> Making nested outputs invisible outside their enclosing block is a dead-simple lexical rule, but it makes loops/branches output-opaque, so downstream steps could not consume their results without inventing a new "block export" IR feature. Flat-global is the only option where "read a loop/branch result downstream" works with zero contract change.</p> <p><strong>Decision 2 — sequential <code>Parallel</code> (concurrency = 1).</strong> Semantically correct but makes <code>Parallel</code> pointless: two 5s LLM waits take 10s instead of ~5s.</p> <p><strong>Decision 2 — true multi-thread parallelism via a new <code>Spawn</code> port</strong> (apache prefork model). Delivers simultaneous <em>CPU</em> across branches, but forces a new port plus three host implementations (tokio real, wasm/embassy no-op — which just re-does the cooperative path anyway) and a <code>Send + 'static</code> sweep through the whole interpreter (<code>agent_loop</code> / <code>tool_dispatch</code> / <code>check</code>), for capacity that I/O-bound agent workflows do not use. If a future compute-heavy <code>Dynamic</code> region (EPIC 4.4+) needs it, that is the right place to introduce a <code>Spawn</code> port deliberately.</p> <p><strong>Decision 3 — literal reuse of the flat top-level gate-rewind loop for <code>Loop</code>.</strong> Rejected: the flat-index arithmetic (<code>gate_index</code>, <code>i = gate_idx</code>) would require projecting nested ids into the flat pipeline index, fighting Decision 1's tree walk. <code>Loop</code> gets its own small bounded walk and shares only the condition-eval and feedback primitives with <code>Check</code> gate-rewind.</p> <p><strong>Decision 3 — stop-and-continue on loop exhaustion.</strong> Rejected: shipping the last un-converged output and exiting 0 silently hides a loop that never reached its goal, violating the no-silent-wrong-result stance. Exhaustion is a hard error (<code>LoopExhausted</code>).</p> <p><strong>Decision 4 — emit a <code>RunOutcome::Suspended</code> / <code>RunEvent::Suspended</code> terminal now.</strong> Rejected: this introduces a public contract that looks resumable but is a dead end until EPIC 4.3, which would then have to reshape it. A named hard-error (<code>SuspendNotImplemented</code>) keeps the seam honest without committing to an unfinished public shape.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0060-bundles-carry-a-content-addressed-asset-store-prompts-are-assets-or-inline"><a class="header" href="#adr-0060-bundles-carry-a-content-addressed-asset-store-prompts-are-assets-or-inline">ADR-0060: Bundles carry a content-addressed asset store; prompts are assets or inline</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-07-19 <strong>Deciders:</strong> tau maintainers</p> <h2 id="context-63"><a class="header" href="#context-63">Context</a></h2> <p>Before <code>ir_format v2.5.0</code>, an <code>Agent.prompt</code> was a bare <code>String</code>. Lowering stored a <code>system_file</code> agent's prompt as the <strong>path string</strong> and the interpreter sent it verbatim as the system prompt. Two defects followed:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Non-hermetic.</strong> The bundle's IR pinned the <em>path</em>, not the <em>content</em>. The same bundle run on a different machine (or after the file changed) produced different behavior while hashing identically.</li> <li><strong>Wrong at run time.</strong> A <code>system_file</code> agent ran with a filesystem path as its system prompt instead of the file's contents.</li> </ol> <p>The bundle already recorded a per-agent <code>system_prompt_sha256</code> for reproducibility, but the prompt <em>bytes</em> never reached the IR or the interpreter. This violates tau's build-time-enforcement stance (G: "any check that can run at build time must") and its hermeticity guarantee.</p> <p><code>PromptSource</code> (untagged <code>Inline | Asset</code>, ADR predecessor <code>ir_format v2.5.0</code>) made the fix <em>expressible</em>; this ADR records how the bytes are carried and resolved.</p> <h2 id="decision-52"><a class="header" href="#decision-52">Decision</a></h2> <p>Bundles gain a <strong>content-addressed asset store</strong>: file-like resources keyed by <code>"sha256:" + 64 lowercase hex</code>, each with a <code>kind</code> tag (<code>prompt</code> today; <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> for skill bodies / templates / schemas later).</p> <ul> <li><strong>Lowering</strong> reads a <code>system_file</code> prompt's bytes at build time via an injected <code>prompt_file</code> closure (I/O stays out of the pure lowering pass), hashes them, emits <code>PromptSource::Asset("sha256:…")</code> into the IR, and collects the blob into <code>LowerOutput.assets</code> (deduped by hash). A missing or unreadable file is a <strong>hard build error</strong> (<code>LowerError::PromptFileUnreadable</code>), moving prompt-file existence from run time to build time. Paths never enter the IR.</li> <li><strong>The bundle</strong> carries the blobs in a new <code>[[assets]]</code> section (bytes hex-encoded, mirroring <code>[ir_payload]</code>), sorted by hash and hashed into the bundle self-hash via the canonical TOML. A bundle with assets declares <code>schema_version = 5</code>; older tau rejects it rather than dropping the bytes. Old bundles (no section) parse unchanged (absent ⇒ empty).</li> <li><strong>The runtime</strong> resolves <code>Asset</code> references at agent-run assembly by looking the hash up in a map the host supplies through a new <code>ToolDispatcher::assets()</code> accessor (mirroring <code>clock()</code>/<code>random()</code>/ <code>artifact_reader()</code>). Native <code>tau run --bundle</code> and <code>tau dev</code> both wire it; the default is <code>None</code> (inline-only runs behave exactly as before).</li> <li><strong>Closed-world checks</strong> at load time: every <code>Asset</code> reference resolves to a bundle asset (no dangling refs) and every asset is referenced (no orphans); each asset's bytes are re-hashed against its key (tamper-evidence the bundle self-hash alone does not provide).</li> </ul> <p>The blob type (<code>AssetBlob</code>/<code>AssetKind</code>) lives in the no_std <code>tau-ir</code> crate so the interpreter can consume the asset map without pulling the std lowering stack into a wasm guest. The bundle keeps its own opaque <code>BundleAsset</code> (<code>kind</code>/<code>bytes_hex</code>); the CLI bridges the two.</p> <h2 id="consequences-57"><a class="header" href="#consequences-57">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li><code>system_file</code> agents now run hermetically with the file <strong>content</strong> as their prompt; the bundle hash pins the content. The original bug is fixed for the native path end-to-end (<code>tau build</code>, <code>tau run --bundle</code>, <code>tau dev</code>).</li> <li><code>ir_format v2.4.0 → v2.5.0</code> (the <code>PromptSource</code> type) and bundle <code>schema_version 4 → 5</code> (the asset store) are both additive.</li> <li>New obligations: the wasm/WIT lane (embedding the asset store into the guest so <code>PromptSource::Asset</code> resolves under <code>any-wasi-strict</code>) is deferred to a follow-up PR; until then <code>tau build --wasm</code> warns rather than silently shipping an unresolvable module.</li> <li>The existing per-agent <code>system_prompt_sha256</code> is retained (a bundle reproducibility record); it is consistent-by-construction with the asset hash because both read the file through the same <code>read_prompt_file</code> helper.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-47"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-47">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>Inline the bytes into the IR <code>Agent.prompt</code> directly.</strong> Rejected: it bloats every module with duplicated prompt text, defeats cross-agent dedup, and gives file-like resources (skill bodies, schemas) no general home. The asset section is that home.</li> <li><strong>Pre-resolve <code>Asset → Inline</code> host-side before handing the module to the interpreter.</strong> Rejected: it rewrites the module, breaking the symmetry between the shipped IR bytes and their hash (and the wasm guest would receive a different module than the one that was built and verified).</li> <li><strong>Put <code>AssetBlob</code> in <code>tau-ir-lower</code>.</strong> Rejected: the no_std interpreter must consume the asset map, and <code>tau-ir-lower</code> depends on the std <code>tau-pkg</code> — that would drag std into the wasm guest. <code>tau-ir</code> is the shared no_std home.</li> <li><strong>A hash-keyed TOML map (<code>[assets."sha256:…"]</code>).</strong> Rejected in favor of a sorted <code>[[assets]]</code> array-of-tables: it matches the existing <code>[[agents]]</code>/<code>[[packages]]</code> discipline and avoids TOML quoted-key handling in the hand-rolled canonical emitter.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0061-tau-build-links-bundles-carry-a-verified-linkrecord-run-trusts-after-verify"><a class="header" href="#adr-0061-tau-build-links-bundles-carry-a-verified-linkrecord-run-trusts-after-verify">ADR-0061: tau build links; bundles carry a verified LinkRecord; run trusts after verify.</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Proposed <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-07-19 <strong>Deciders:</strong> tau core <strong>Design spec:</strong> <code>docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-19-link-phase-linkrecord-design.md</code> (not part of the published book)</p> <h2 id="context-64"><a class="header" href="#context-64">Context</a></h2> <p>Symbol binding to the installed world — "does every plugin, skill, tool, and model this IR names actually resolve against what is installed, on this platform?" — happens today at <strong>every <code>tau run</code></strong>, scattered across the run path as late <code>anyhow::bail!</code>s, and partly duplicated defensively:</p> <ul> <li>Plugin resolution from the lockfile (installed?, port match?, version satisfiable?) is checked per-LLM-backend and per-tool in <code>tau-cli</code>'s <code>plugin_loader.rs</code>.</li> <li>Package version satisfiability is re-derived in <code>tau-pkg</code>'s <code>project/agent.rs</code>.</li> <li><code>SKILL.md</code> is read and parsed <strong>on every</strong> <code>skill.<name>.spawn</code>, with no cache.</li> <li>Model aliases are resolved three times: once correctly at lowering, and twice more defensively at run — one of the run-time paths falls back to a silent <code>"unresolved"</code> sentinel.</li> </ul> <p>Worse, <code>tau run --bundle</code> re-lowers the whole project on every run using an empty MCP contract cache, which produces a <em>different</em> IR hash for MCP projects and is conservatively rejected as <code>IrSourceDivergence</code>. An MCP project therefore cannot run from its own bundle — a confirmed bug.</p> <p>This binding work is knowable statically, from the lockfile, package manifests, and on-disk <code>SKILL.md</code> files, without spawning any plugin process. Doing it once, at build time, and recording the outcome removes the repeated computation, deletes the scattered <code>bail!</code>s and the <code>"unresolved"</code> sentinel, and gives <code>run --bundle</code> something concrete to verify instead of re-deriving from scratch.</p> <h2 id="decision-53"><a class="header" href="#decision-53">Decision</a></h2> <p><code>tau-pkg</code> gains a new module, <code>tau-pkg/src/link.rs</code>, exposing:</p> <pre><pre class="playground"><code class="language-rust"><span class="boring">#![allow(unused)] </span><span class="boring">fn main() { </span>pub fn link( cfg: &ProjectConfig, module: &IrModule, lockfile: &LockFile, scope: &Scope, ) -> Result<LinkOutcome, Vec<LinkError>>; pub struct LinkOutcome { pub record: LinkRecord, pub parsed_skills: BTreeMap<String, tau_domain::SkillContent>, } pub struct LinkRecord { pub resolved_plugins: Vec<LinkedPlugin>, // name, version, binary_sha256, provides pub resolved_skills: Vec<LinkedSkill>, // name, content_sha256, parsed_ok pub model_bindings: BTreeMap<String, ModelRef>, // alias -> ModelRef pub platform: TargetTriple, pub lockfile_sha256: String, } pub enum LinkError { PluginNotInstalled { package: String }, PluginPortMismatch { package: String, found: PortKind, expected: PortKind }, VersionUnsatisfied { package: String, req: String }, SkillMissing { package: String, path: String }, SkillParse { package: String, detail: String }, } <span class="boring">}</span></code></pre></pre> <p><strong><code>link()</code> is a static linker, not a loader.</strong> It validates the package-level symbol table — every plugin the project references exists, is installed at a version satisfying the requirement, and provides the right port; every model alias resolves to a <code>ModelRef</code>; every installed skill's <code>SKILL.md</code> reads and parses — entirely from the lockfile, package manifests, and disk, with <strong>no process spawning</strong>. It runs once, after <code>lower_ir</code> and before <code>build()</code> in <code>tau build</code>'s pipeline.</p> <p>There is deliberately <strong>no <code>ModelAliasUnknown</code> variant</strong>. <code>ProjectConfig::validate()</code> already rejects an agent whose <code>model</code> is empty or names an alias absent from <code>[models]</code> (<code>ProjectConfigError::MissingAgentModel</code> / <code>ProjectConfigError::UnknownModelAlias</code>) at parse time. A <code>ProjectConfig</code> that reaches <code>link()</code> therefore cannot carry an unresolvable alias, so <code>link()</code>'s model-binding step is infallible: it only builds the <code>alias -> ModelRef</code> map. <code>LinkError</code> has exactly the 5 variants above.</p> <p><strong>Two checks stay at runtime, not because they're overlooked but because they cannot be computed statically:</strong></p> <ol> <li><strong><code>ToolId</code> -> loaded-plugin binding.</strong> There is no static <code>ToolId</code> -> package edge: <code>PluginManifest</code> carries <code>{provides, kind, bin}</code>, not tool names, so matching a workflow's <code>ToolId</code> references against a specific plugin's advertised tool names requires the plugin to actually be spawned and asked. This is the <strong>dynamic loader</strong>'s job. The cheap "5b" tool-name pre-check in the run path stays exactly where it is; <code>LinkRecord</code> carries no <code>tool_bindings</code> field and there is no <code>ToolUnbound</code> error variant.</li> <li><strong>Sandbox adapter availability and plan construction.</strong> <code>build_plan</code> lives in <code>tau-runtime-tokio</code>; <code>tau-pkg</code> cannot call it without creating a dependency cycle. Adapter availability is host-inherent — it depends on the machine actually running the bundle, which for a portable bundle is not knowable at build time on the build host. Sandbox planning and adapter probing stay a runtime concern, exactly as today. <code>LinkRecord</code> carries no sandbox fields; <code>resolved_plugins[].binary_sha256</code> plus the lockfile's existing <code>required_shapes</code> are sufficient for what the run path still needs.</li> </ol> <p><strong>Precondition:</strong> the <code>lockfile</code> argument must equal the lockfile persisted on disk at <code>scope.lockfile_path()</code>. Plugin resolution reads only the passed <code>lockfile</code>; skill resolution and <code>LinkRecord::lockfile_sha256</code> both read from disk via <code>scope</code>. A <code>lockfile</code> that has drifted from disk is undefined territory for skills specifically — a skill package listed in the passed <code>lockfile</code> but absent from the on-disk lockfile surfaces as <code>LinkError::SkillMissing</code> rather than being silently dropped. Every caller in PR 2 passes the lockfile it just loaded from <code>scope.lockfile_path()</code>, so the invariant holds in practice.</p> <p><strong>Errors are collected, never short-circuited.</strong> <code>link()</code> returns <code>Err(Vec<LinkError>)</code> containing every fault found across plugins, models, and skills, sorted by a stable key <code>(variant_rank, package_name)</code> so identical inputs yield an identical error list regardless of which caller invoked <code>link()</code> — the no-drift bar shared with <code>build</code>, <code>check</code>, and dev-<code>run</code>.</p> <h2 id="consequences-58"><a class="header" href="#consequences-58">Consequences</a></h2> <p><strong>Positive:</strong></p> <ul> <li>One implementation of "does the world satisfy the IR" replaces four scattered, partially-duplicated call sites.</li> <li>The <code>"unresolved"</code> model-alias sentinel and the redundant re-resolutions at run time become deletable (PR 2).</li> <li><code>SKILL.md</code> moves from "read + parsed on every spawn" to "read + parsed once at link time"; a corrupt skill fails the <strong>build</strong>, not a spawn mid-run.</li> <li><code>run --bundle</code> gets something to verify — bundle IR hash plus <code>LinkRecord</code> invariants (lockfile sha, per-plugin/-skill presence and sha, platform match) — instead of re-lowering the whole project, which both restores byte-for-byte trust semantics and removes the MCP empty-cache bug's root cause (fixed properly in PR 3 by re-lowering <code>verify --bundle</code>'s reproduce path with the pinned MCP resolver instead).</li> <li><code>tau check</code> gains a "link" category for free: the same <code>link()</code> function run in dry-run mode against the current installed set.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Negative / obligations:</strong></p> <ul> <li>PR 1 (this ADR + <code>link()</code> + <code>LinkRecord</code>/<code>LinkError</code> + unit tests) ships dead code: nothing calls <code>link()</code> yet. It is unit-tested in isolation (truth table: one fixture per <code>LinkError</code> variant, plus a multi-error collection test) but not wired into any command.</li> <li>PR 2 must wire the three callers — <code>tau build</code>, dev <code>tau run</code>/<code>tau chat</code>, and <code>tau check</code> — behind one no-drift test asserting identical findings for the same broken fixture across all three, embed <code>LinkRecord</code> in the bundle manifest as an additive optional field, and construct the record-seeded <code>SkillResolver</code> adapter in <code>tau-runtime-tokio</code> from <code>LinkOutcome::parsed_skills</code>.</li> <li>PR 3 must replace <code>run --bundle</code>'s re-lowering with verify-then-trust against the embedded <code>LinkRecord</code>, and fix the MCP reproduce-path bug by re-lowering with the pinned MCP resolver instead of an empty cache.</li> <li>PR 4, unrelated to linking but sequenced after it, flips the credential posture from silent ambient-env fallback to a hard startup error with an explicit <code>--allow-ambient-credentials</code> escape hatch; it gets its own ADR.</li> <li><code>tau-pkg</code> gains a dependency on <code>tau-ir</code> for <code>ModelRef</code>/<code>IrModule</code>. This is not a new cycle: <code>tau-ir</code> is the no_std base crate.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-48"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-48">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <p><strong>A. Keep binding resolution scattered at run time, just deduplicate the logic into a shared helper called from each run-time site.</strong> Rejected. This does not fix the core problem: the cost (fs reads for skills, lockfile scans for plugins) is still paid on every run, and <code>run --bundle</code> still has to re-derive the world instead of trusting a verified artifact. It also does nothing for the MCP re-lowering bug, which is caused by re-lowering at all, not by how the binding logic is organized.</p> <p><strong>B. Make <code>link()</code> a full loader — spawn plugins and bind <code>ToolId</code>s and sandbox adapters at build time, embedding a complete "world" into the bundle.</strong> Rejected. Spawning processes and probing sandbox adapters at build time requires the build host to have the same live capabilities as the eventual run host, which is false for portable bundles built on one machine and run on another. It would also pull <code>tau-runtime-tokio</code> into <code>tau-pkg</code>, creating a dependency cycle (<code>build_plan</code> lives in <code>tau-runtime-tokio</code>, which itself depends on <code>tau-pkg</code>). The static/dynamic split keeps <code>tau-pkg</code> a pure, no-process linker and leaves host-inherent decisions to the runtime loader, where they belong.</p> <p><strong>C. Record skill bodies (not just hashes) directly in the serialized <code>LinkRecord</code>.</strong> Rejected. <code>LinkRecord</code> is embedded in the bundle manifest and needs to stay small and stable; skill bodies can be large and are not needed for the manifest's own verification checks (<code>content_sha256</code> is sufficient to detect drift). Instead, <code>link()</code> returns the parsed bodies separately as <code>LinkOutcome::parsed_skills</code>, used only in-process to seed the runtime <code>SkillResolver</code>; they never travel through serialization.</p> <p><strong>D. Give <code>link()</code> a <code>ModelAliasUnknown</code> error variant to mirror the handoff's original sketch.</strong> Rejected once <code>ProjectConfig::validate()</code>'s existing guarantees were checked against the actual code: an unresolvable model alias cannot reach <code>link()</code> in the first place, because <code>ProjectConfig</code> construction already rejects it.
