Adding a dead error variant would misrepresent <code>link()</code>'s actual failure surface and invite untestable code paths.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0062-dynprocessgate-port--decouple-transports-from-the-host-runtime"><a class="header" href="#adr-0062-dynprocessgate-port--decouple-transports-from-the-host-runtime">ADR-0062: <code>DynProcessGate</code> port — decouple transports from the host runtime</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-07-19 <strong>Deciders:</strong> tau core</p> <h2 id="context-65"><a class="header" href="#context-65">Context</a></h2> <p><code>tau-mcp-tokio</code> (the MCP stdio/HTTP transport crate) needs to gate the subprocess it spawns for a stdio MCP server: it calls <code>wrap_spawn(plan, cmd)</code> on a capability gate the host supplies. To name that gate abstractly it stored <code>Arc<dyn DynProcessCapabilityGate></code> — an object-safe wrapper trait that lived in <code>tau-runtime-tokio</code>.</p> <p>Depending on <code>tau-runtime-tokio</code> for one trait + one default gate dragged the <strong>entire host runtime</strong> into the MCP transport's dependency graph: <code>tau-pkg</code>, <code>tau-plugin-protocol</code>, and all four <code>tau-sandbox-*</code> crates. A transport that only needs to call <code>wrap_spawn</code> should not compile the plugin host, the package manager, or the sandbox adapters.</p> <p>The underlying port already exists: <code>tau_ports::ProcessCapabilityGate</code> (an <code>async fn</code>-in-trait, so not dyn-compatible). The only thing missing in <code>tau-ports</code> was the <strong>dyn-compatible</strong> form and a <strong>default no-op gate</strong>.</p> <h2 id="decision-54"><a class="header" href="#decision-54">Decision</a></h2> <p>Move the object-safe process-gate surface into <code>tau-ports</code>, behind the existing <code>process</code> feature:</p> <ul> <li><strong><code>tau_ports::DynProcessGate</code></strong> — object-safe wrapper of <code>ProcessCapabilityGate</code> with boxed-future <code>wrap_spawn</code> / <code>apply_post_spawn</code>. A blanket <code>impl<T: ProcessCapabilityGate + 'static> DynProcessGate for T</code> means every sandbox adapter and the passthrough gate satisfy it for free. It deliberately does <strong>not</strong> extend <code>tau-runtime-core</code>'s <code>DynCapabilityGate</code> (the universal-methods wrapper): transports only ever call <code>wrap_spawn</code>, and keeping the port free of that super-trait keeps <code>tau-ports</code> off <code>tau-runtime-core</code>.</li> <li><strong><code>tau_ports::PassthroughGate</code></strong> — the no-isolation default gate (moved from <code>tau-runtime-tokio::process_gate::passthrough::PassthroughSandbox</code>).</li> </ul> <p><code>tau-runtime-tokio</code> keeps <code>DynProcessCapabilityGate</code> and <code>PassthroughSandbox</code> as <strong>back-compat re-export aliases</strong> of the moved items, so the resolver's <code>SandboxAdapter::Passthrough</code> variant, the adapter registry, and the CLI wiring are unchanged. The host still injects the concrete gate at <code>setup_mcp_runtime</code> time; nothing about the injection direction changes.</p> <p><code>tau-mcp-tokio</code> now depends on <code>tau-ports</code> (with <code>process</code>) <strong>only</strong>. A CI guard (<code>mcp-tokio-decoupled</code>) asserts its manifest never names <code>tau-runtime-tokio</code>.</p> <h2 id="consequences-59"><a class="header" href="#consequences-59">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li><code>cargo tree -p tau-mcp-tokio</code> no longer contains <code>tau-runtime-tokio</code>, <code>tau-pkg</code>, <code>tau-plugin-protocol</code>, or any <code>tau-sandbox-*</code> crate. The MCP transport builds against the ports layer alone.</li> <li><strong>Semver:</strong> the change to <code>tau-ports</code> (the one semver-gated crate) is purely <strong>additive</strong> — a new public trait, a new public struct, and two new re-exports, all behind the pre-existing <code>process</code> feature. No existing item changes or is removed, so the <code>ports-semver</code> lane (cargo-semver-checks vs <code>origin/main</code>) stays green; it is a minor-compatible addition.</li> <li>Decoupling surfaced one previously-implicit dependency: <code>tau-mcp-tokio</code> formats a <code>PathBuf</code> in a <code>thiserror</code> error, which needs <code>thiserror</code>'s <code>std</code> feature. It was unified in transitively via <code>tau-runtime-tokio</code>; it is now requested explicitly.</li> <li>The dyn wrapper is now defined once in the port layer rather than per host shell; a future <code>tau-runtime-embassy</code> reuses the same <code>DynProcessGate</code>.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0063-ci-tiering--thin-pre-merge-gate-nightly-authority-for-trunk-health"><a class="header" href="#adr-0063-ci-tiering--thin-pre-merge-gate-nightly-authority-for-trunk-health">ADR-0063: CI tiering — thin pre-merge gate, nightly authority for trunk health</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-07-20 <strong>Supersedes:</strong> ADR-0039 (in part — the per-PR job set of Tier 1)</p> <h2 id="context-66"><a class="header" href="#context-66">Context</a></h2> <p>ADR-0039's three-tier model still ran the full 23-job matrix plus a 15–30 min standalone coverage workflow on every PR push, again in the merge queue, and again on push to main — School-1 ("pre-merge authority") cost, while the repo already owned School-2 ("post-merge authority") machinery: nightly tier2 with auto-bisect, auto-rerun-flaky, security-daily, a merge queue, and release preflight that re-runs both tiers via workflow_call.</p> <h2 id="decision-55"><a class="header" href="#decision-55">Decision</a></h2> <p>Adopt trunk-based post-merge authority:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Tier 0 (pre-merge + merge queue + main push)</strong> — <code>ci.yml</code> shrinks to 10 fast jobs: fmt, clippy, cargo-deny, gitleaks, cargo-check (macos + windows), test-stable, doc-tests, runtime-core-no-std, ports-semver. Target ≤ ~8 min wall clock. <code>ci-summary</code> remains the only required check.</li> <li><strong>Nightly (authority)</strong> — the remaining ex-Tier-1 jobs move into <code>tier2.yml</code> (msrv-check, test-fixtures-ports, conformance, test-credential-chain, feature-flag-matrix, mock-sandbox-prod-gate, build-checks-linux, schema-conformance, wit-host-drift), covered by the nightly cron, the <code>full-matrix</code> PR label, and release preflight. The standalone coverage workflow is deleted; tier2's coverage job is the only coverage lane.</li> <li><strong>Contract</strong> — a red nightly on main is a stop-the-line event: the first action next session is fix or revert. <code>auto-bisect</code> posts the culprit commit to the rolling regression issue.</li> </ul> <p>Deliberate placements:</p> <ul> <li><code>runtime-core-no-std</code> stays pre-merge: the feature-graph/no_std-link regression class fires often and hard-blocks the wasm epic.</li> <li><code>ports-semver</code> stays pre-merge: its <code>--baseline-rev origin/main</code> compares main to itself on a nightly run and can never fail there — the check only has signal before merge.</li> <li><code>cargo-audit</code>/<code>osv-scanner</code> are deleted from the PR path outright: advisory risk is time-triggered and <code>security-daily.yml</code> already runs both every day.</li> </ul> <h2 id="consequences-60"><a class="header" href="#consequences-60">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>PR feedback drops from ~23 jobs + coverage × (push + queue + main) to 10 fast jobs per event.</li> <li>Platform-specific <em>test</em> failures (macOS/Windows nextest) and the moved contract gates are now discovered nightly, not pre-merge; cargo-check on both platforms stays pre-merge to catch the compile-level cfg-root class. Risky PRs can opt back in with the <code>full-matrix</code> label.</li> <li>Releases are unaffected: <code>release.yml</code> preflight re-runs ci.yml and tier2.yml (now including the moved jobs) on the tag.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0064-one-host-semantic--exact-hostnames--a-typed-any-no-derived-hosts"><a class="header" href="#adr-0064-one-host-semantic--exact-hostnames--a-typed-any-no-derived-hosts">ADR-0064: One host semantic — exact hostnames + a typed <code>any</code>; no derived hosts</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-07-18 <strong>Deciders:</strong> tau core</p> <h2 id="context-67"><a class="header" href="#context-67">Context</a></h2> <p>The <code>net.http</code> capability's <code>hosts</code> field had three divergent semantics live at once:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Docs</strong> claimed hosts are "exact match or glob" (<code>crates/tau-domain/src/package/capability.rs:137</code>, pre-change).</li> <li><strong>The lattice</strong> did exact string equality — <code>hosts=["*"]</code> was treated as the literal host <code>"*"</code> rather than a wildcard (<code>crates/tau-pkg/src/capability_override/subset.rs</code>, <code>string_set_subset</code>).</li> <li><strong>The runtime proxy</strong> rejected any <code>*</code> at spawn time (<code>crates/tau-sandbox-proxy/src/validate.rs</code>, invoked from the native <code>strict.rs</code> and the darwin / container / windows sandbox adapters).</li> </ol> <p>The practical consequence: a manifest authored with <code>hosts = ["*"]</code> parsed successfully, passed the capability lattice, passed <code>tau check</code>, and passed <code>tau build</code> — then <strong>deterministically failed at <code>tau run</code></strong> when the proxy rejected the wildcard. Build-accepts-but-run-rejects is exactly the false-security divergence tau's build-time enforcement principle exists to prevent.</p> <p>Two secondary defects compounded this:</p> <ul> <li><strong>No case folding.</strong> <code>API.COM</code> and <code>api.com</code> were distinct strings through the entire stack (parse, lattice, proxy), so a ceiling authored in one case did not subsume a grant authored in another.</li> <li><strong>Hand-rolled <code>derive_host</code></strong> (<code>crates/tau-pkg/src/project/allow.rs</code>) parsed <code>[allow.mcp.<name>].url</code> into a host ceiling using ad hoc string surgery — <code>https://user@evil.com/</code> derived to host <code>user@evil.com</code>, and IPv6 URLs derived to <code>"["</code>.</li> </ul> <p>Separately, the lattice's <code>methods</code> field was ignored entirely (<code>subset.rs</code>): a child capability could declare <code>methods = ["POST"]</code> against a parent that only granted <code>methods = ["GET"]</code> and the subset check would pass, because method inclusion was never checked.</p> <p>Full analysis: <code>docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-18-hostset-exact-plus-typed-any-design.md</code>.</p> <h2 id="decision-56"><a class="header" href="#decision-56">Decision</a></h2> <p>Hosts are <strong>bare lowercase hostnames</strong> or a <strong>typed any-sentinel</strong> — one semantic enforced identically from parse through the capability lattice through the runtime proxy.</p> <pre><pre class="playground"><code class="language-rust"><span class="boring">#![allow(unused)] </span><span class="boring">fn main() { </span>/// A validated bare hostname with optional port. Never a URL, glob, or scheme. pub struct HostName(String); pub enum HostSet { Any, // authored as hosts = "any" Exact(BTreeSet<HostName>), // authored as hosts = ["a.com", "b.io:8080"] } impl HostSet { /// Any ⊇ everything; Exact(p) ⊇ Exact(c) ⟺ c ⊆ p; Exact ⊉ Any. pub fn subsumes(&self, child: &HostSet) -> bool; } <span class="boring">}</span></code></pre></pre> <p><code>HostName::parse</code> case-folds (<code>A.COM</code> → <code>a.com</code>, accept-and-fold, never reject on case) and rejects anything that is not a bare hostname: <code>*</code> (with a <code>help: write hosts = "any"</code> hint), suffix globs like <code>*.a.com</code>, URLs (<code>https://...</code>), userinfo (<code>user@a.com</code>), paths, and IPv6 literals (<code>[::1]:8080</code>). <code>BTreeSet</code> gives deterministic, sorted serialization.</p> <p><code>methods</code> becomes a typed, checked field:</p> <pre><pre class="playground"><code class="language-rust"><span class="boring">#![allow(unused)] </span><span class="boring">fn main() { </span>pub enum HttpMethod { Get, Head, Post, Put, Delete, Connect, Options, Trace, Patch } Http { hosts: HostSet, methods: Option<BTreeSet<HttpMethod>>, // None = all methods } <span class="boring">}</span></code></pre></pre> <p><strong>Absent vs. empty is load-bearing and never conflated:</strong> <code>methods</code> absent → <code>None</code> → <em>all methods</em>; <code>methods = []</code> → <code>Some(∅)</code> → <em>deny all methods</em>. The old lattice code collapsed this distinction via <code>unwrap_or_default</code>, which is the same bug shape as the audit-B2 finding this ADR closes for methods.</p> <p>Three resolutions from the design brainstorm:</p> <ul> <li><strong><code>derive_host</code> is deleted.</strong> It backed only <code>[allow.mcp.<name>]</code>'s host ceiling (the <code>net.http</code> capability bridge never used it). No URL→host derivation exists anywhere in the capability stack after this change. <code>[allow.mcp.<name>].hosts</code> is now <strong>required</strong>; an MCP entry with no explicit <code>hosts</code> is a validation error.</li> <li><strong>One PR, ordered commits.</strong> The <code>Http</code> variant's field type change is atomic across the workspace — a types-only first commit does not compile standalone — so domain → consumers → docs land as one PR with logically-ordered commits, compiling green only at the end.</li> <li><strong>Typed <code>HttpMethod</code> + absent-vs-empty</strong>, as above.</li> </ul> <h3 id="consumers-updated-to-the-one-semantic"><a class="header" href="#consumers-updated-to-the-one-semantic">Consumers updated to the one semantic</a></h3> <ul> <li><strong>Lattice</strong> (<code>subset.rs</code>): the <code>Http</code> arm now calls <code>HostSet::subsumes</code> and a real methods-inclusion check; the old <code>gather_hosts</code> / string-set-subset path for hosts is gone.</li> <li><strong><code>[allow]</code> bridge</strong> (<code>allow.rs</code>): <code>derive_host</code> deleted; <code>[allow.mcp.<name>].hosts</code> required, empty/absent is an error.</li> <li><strong>Proxy</strong> (<code>tau-sandbox-proxy</code>): a typed <code>HostAllow { Any, Exact(Vec<String>) }</code> policy, with pass-all mode reachable only from <code>HostSet::Any</code>. Runtime CONNECT host matching case-folds. <code>validate_hosts</code> still rejects <code>*</code> and non-loopback IPs as defense in depth on the <code>Exact</code> path.</li> <li><strong>Sandbox adapters</strong> (native <code>strict.rs</code>, darwin, container, windows): map <code>HostSet::Exact</code> → <code>HostAllow::Exact</code> (case-folded) and <code>HostSet::Any</code> → <code>HostAllow::Any</code> before calling <code>spawn_proxy</code>.</li> </ul> <h2 id="consequences-61"><a class="header" href="#consequences-61">Consequences</a></h2> <p><strong>Positive:</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Build-accepts ⟺ run-enforces</strong>, both directions. <code>hosts = "any"</code> passes parse, <code>tau check</code>, <code>tau build</code>, and reaches the proxy in pass-all mode with no spawn-time rejection. <code>hosts = ["*"]</code> now fails at <strong>parse</strong> — it never reaches build, closing the divergence this ADR exists to fix.</li> <li>Case folding is uniform: a ceiling authored <code>API.COM</code> and a grant authored <code>api.com</code> are recognized as the same host everywhere.</li> <li><code>methods</code> inclusion is a real, checked lattice rule instead of a silently ignored field; the <code>_method_diff_ignored</code> test class flips to actually checking method subsumption.</li> <li><code>[allow.mcp.<name>].hosts</code> being required removes a whole class of URL-parsing edge cases (<code>derive_host</code>'s userinfo/IPv6 mishandling) by deleting the code path rather than hardening it.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Negative / obligations:</strong></p> <ul> <li><code>[allow.mcp.<name>]</code> entries that previously relied on <code>derive_host</code> (no explicit <code>hosts</code>) now fail validation and must be updated with an explicit <code>hosts = [...]</code> list. No such fixtures existed in-tree at time of writing; documentation examples were swept for the same pattern.</li> <li>Manifests that previously omitted <code>methods</code> and round-tripped through <code>unwrap_or_default</code> into a serialized <code>"methods": []</code> now correctly serialize with the key omitted — a byte-stability change for that specific (pre-existing bug) shape. Already-lowercase, sorted <code>Exact</code> host lists and manifests with real <code>methods</code> sets are unaffected; a golden test asserts this.</li> <li>EPIC 1.6's coarse-ceiling lint must target the typed <code>HostSet::Any</code> variant, not a string match on <code>"*"</code> — noted on that branch (<code>feat/epic-1.6-coarse-lint</code>), not implemented here.</li> </ul> <h2 id="explicitly-deferred-additive-later-not-part-of-this-adr"><a class="header" href="#explicitly-deferred-additive-later-not-part-of-this-adr">Explicitly deferred (additive later, not part of this ADR)</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>Suffix wildcards</strong> (<code>*.x.com</code>). Would require per-label glob matching in both the lattice and the proxy's CONNECT-host check; deferred until there is a concrete need.</li> <li><strong>IPv6 literal hosts</strong> (<code>[::1]:8080</code>). <code>HostName::parse</code> rejects <code>[</code> today; adding IPv6 support is additive and does not require revisiting the <code>HostSet</code>/<code>HostName</code> shape.</li> <li><strong>Runtime method enforcement.</strong> The proxy filters by host, not method; <code>methods</code> is enforced only in the build-time lattice (now <em>checked</em>, previously ignored — see Decision). This leaves methods build-checked-but-not-run-enforced, a narrower residual than the host divergence this ADR closes. Tracked as a follow-up, not part of this change.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-49"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-49">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <p><strong>A. Keep hosts as a raw <code>Vec<String></code> and special-case <code>"*"</code> at each consumer.</strong> Rejected. This is exactly the status quo that produced the three-way divergence — each consumer (lattice, proxy) would need its own special-case logic and case-folding, with no shared invariant. A typed <code>HostSet</code> makes "what counts as a host" and "what counts as any" a single, testable definition.</p> <p><strong>B. Support suffix wildcards now, alongside exact + any.</strong> Rejected for this ADR. Wildcards require resolution-time or match-time glob logic in the proxy's CONNECT-host check, which is materially more code and a larger attack surface for host-matching bugs. Exact + typed-any closes the build/run divergence completely without it; wildcards are additive later.</p> <p><strong>C. Keep <code>derive_host</code> and harden it against the userinfo/IPv6 bugs instead of deleting it.</strong> Rejected. <code>derive_host</code> is not used by the <code>net.http</code> capability bridge at all — it exists solely to backfill <code>[allow.mcp.<name>].hosts</code> from a URL. Requiring explicit <code>hosts</code> removes an entire parsing surface rather than patching it, and matches the governance principle that ceilings should be explicit, not inferred.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0065-unknown-input-policy--strict-authoring-surfaces-versioned-interchange"><a class="header" href="#adr-0065-unknown-input-policy--strict-authoring-surfaces-versioned-interchange">ADR-0065: Unknown-input policy — strict authoring surfaces, versioned interchange</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-07-19 <strong>Deciders:</strong> tau core</p> <h2 id="context-68"><a class="header" href="#context-68">Context</a></h2> <p>An audit of the frontend (D7-B, audit B2) found <strong>five inconsistent behaviors</strong> for unknown or malformed input across tau's deserialization surfaces:</p> <ol> <li>A typo'd capability kind silently became <code>Capability::Custom</code> in package manifests, but was rejected in <code>[allow]</code>.</li> <li>A wrong field on a known capability kind was silently dropped (<code>unwrap_or_default</code> conflation).</li> <li><code>#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]</code> was present on some leaf structs but absent on the top-level authoring structs (<code>UncheckedProjectConfig</code>, <code>UncheckedAgent</code>, <code>UncheckedManifest</code>, …), so unknown top-level keys were silently ignored.</li> <li>Lowering mapped an unknown <code>PromptEntry</code> to an <strong>empty prompt</strong> and an unknown determinism string to <code>Pure</code> — the most permissive class.</li> <li><code>[allow]</code> maintained its own capability-kind whitelist, free to drift from the manifest parser.</li> </ol> <p>These are all instances of the same anti-pattern: <strong>silently accepting input tau does not understand</strong>, which contradicts tau's build-time-enforcement philosophy (a check that <em>can</em> run at build time <em>must</em>).</p> <h2 id="decision-57"><a class="header" href="#decision-57">Decision</a></h2> <p><strong>One rule, split by who writes the input.</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>AUTHORING</strong> (humans: <code>tau.toml</code>, root <code>[allow]</code>, package manifests) → unknown input is an <strong>error</strong>.</li> <li><strong>INTERCHANGE</strong> (machines: lockfile, bundle, IR) → <strong>version-gated acceptance</strong>. Within an accepted format version, unknown fields are still rejected (canonical, hashed formats have no slack); a <em>newer</em> declared version is an explicit upgrade error, never silent dropping.</li> </ul> <p>This ADR is written whole, but implemented in halves:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Authoring half</strong> — implemented across D7-B PR1–PR3 (this work).</li> <li><strong>Interchange half</strong> — the version-gate-at-load for lockfile/bundle/IR — is <strong>D8's</strong> handoff. It is <em>not</em> implemented here; this ADR states the rule so D8 has a single reference.</li> </ul> <h3 id="authoring-half--what-shipped-d7-b"><a class="header" href="#authoring-half--what-shipped-d7-b">Authoring half — what shipped (D7-B)</a></h3> <p><strong>Struct strictness (PR1).</strong> <code>#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]</code> on every non-<code>flatten</code> authoring struct. Structs that use <code>#[serde(flatten)]</code> (<code>UncheckedAllow</code>, <code>UncheckedToolAllow</code>) cannot use <code>deny_unknown_fields</code>; their strictness stays in <code>validate_allow</code>.</p> <p><strong>Field-shape strictness (PR1).</strong> The hand-written <code>Capability</code> deserializer no longer conflates fields: each kind requires exactly its fields and rejects foreign or unknown fields, naming the offender and the expected shape. <code>net.http</code> requires <code>hosts</code> — either a non-empty list, or the any-host escape hatch <code>hosts = "any"</code> (typed <code>NetHosts { Any, List }</code>); the bare <code>{ kind = "net.http" }</code> form, which previously meant deny-all, is now an error.</p> <p><strong>Kind strictness + explicit <code>custom.</code> (PR2).</strong> An unrecognized capability kind is an error with a Levenshtein did-you-mean and a pointer to the escape-hatch docs. A plugin-defined capability must opt in <em>explicitly</em> via a <code>custom.</code> kind prefix → <a href="decisions/../explanation/escape-hatches.html#capability-custom"><code>Capability::Custom</code></a>. <code>[allow]</code> and package manifests share the <strong>single</strong> capability parser (Decision 4-A): typo/did-you-mean/field-shape live in one place, and <code>[allow]</code>'s deliberately narrower ceiling kind-set is a <em>post-parse</em> semantic gate — "one parser" ≠ "same accepted kinds".</p> <p><strong>Forward-vocabulary opt-in (PR2).</strong> A package manifest may declare a top-level <code>vocab_version</code> (a monotonic <code>u32</code> generation). Only when it is <em>newer</em> than this build's <code>KNOWN_VOCAB</code> do unrecognized (non-<code>custom.</code>) kinds parse — as a distinct, fail-closed <a href="decisions/../explanation/escape-hatches.html#capability-forward"><code>Capability::Forward</code></a> variant (subsumes nothing, subsumed by nothing but an exact match / an <code>Any</code> ceiling), surfaced by <code>tau check</code> as an info finding. An undeclared <code>vocab_version</code> means the current vocabulary, strict. This preserves the Phase-2 §D forward-compatibility path: an older tau can inspect/install a newer-vocab plugin fail-closed instead of hard-failing. Package manifests are the only authored artifact that travels between tau versions, so they alone get this opt-in; the root <code>tau.toml</code>/<code>[allow]</code> stay strict-current with no escape.</p> <p><strong>Lowering arms (PR3).</strong> The two silent lowering defaults become structured errors (<code>LowerError::UnsupportedPromptKind</code>, <code>LowerError::UnknownDeterminism</code>), mirrored into the drifting <code>tau-ir</code> <code>IrError</code> copy (D11 consolidation debt).</p> <h3 id="interchange-half--d8-not-implemented-here"><a class="header" href="#interchange-half--d8-not-implemented-here">Interchange half — D8 (not implemented here)</a></h3> <p>The lockfile/bundle/IR readers gain a <strong>version gate at load</strong>: a known format version parses strictly (unknown fields rejected); a newer format version is an explicit "upgrade tau" error. See D8's handoff.</p> <h2 id="consequences-62"><a class="header" href="#consequences-62">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>Positive:</strong> every unknown input on an authoring surface now fails loudly at build time with an actionable message; <code>[allow]</code> and manifests can no longer diverge on kind handling; forward-compat is explicit and fail-closed; any-host egress is a typed, honest declaration rather than a magic empty list.</li> <li><strong>Negative / migration:</strong> existing manifests/fixtures using the bare <code>net.http</code> form, an unprefixed custom kind, or an unknown top-level key now fail to parse and were migrated. The <code>NetHosts</code> change rippled through every sandbox adapter (each now folds capabilities into a proxy <code>HostPolicy</code> where <code>Any</code> = unrestricted egress).</li> <li>The former non-namespaced-<code>Custom</code> <em>warning</em> is obsolete — a <code>Custom</code> capability is namespaced by construction (<code>custom.</code> prefix), enforced at parse.</li> </ul> <h2 id="alternatives-considered-50"><a class="header" href="#alternatives-considered-50">Alternatives considered</a></h2> <ul> <li><strong>Keep the permissive Custom fallback for unknown kinds.</strong> Rejected: it is the exact silent-drop the audit flagged, and it let typos reach downstream governance errors instead of failing at the typo.</li> <li><strong>Represent any-host with a <code>["*"]</code> sentinel</strong> rather than a typed <code>NetHosts</code>. Rejected: the three enforcement layers disagreed on <code>"*"</code>, and a sentinel breaks the lattice's own subset check; a typed <code>Any</code> is correct-by-construction.</li> <li><strong>Fully collapse <code>[allow]</code> into the manifest parser.</strong> Rejected: it would widen <code>[allow]</code> to accept <code>agent.spawn</code>/<code>task_list</code>/<code>custom.*</code> as ceilings, a semantic expansion with no defined meaning; the post-parse gate preserves <code>[allow]</code>'s scope.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="adr-0066-guest-fs-effect-descriptor-resolution--preopen-plumbing-dual-cfg-absence-denial"><a class="header" href="#adr-0066-guest-fs-effect-descriptor-resolution--preopen-plumbing-dual-cfg-absence-denial">ADR-0066: Guest fs-effect descriptor resolution — preopen plumbing, dual cfg, absence-denial</a></h1> <p><strong>Status:</strong> Accepted <strong>Date:</strong> 2026-08-21 <strong>Deciders:</strong> tau core</p> <h2 id="context-69"><a class="header" href="#context-69">Context</a></h2> <p>EPIC 3.6-b routes the wasm guest's <code>fs.read</code>/<code>fs.write</code> tool effects through <code>wasi:filesystem</code>, mirroring 3.6's net mechanism. Unlike net (a single host call), fs requires a descriptor ceremony — the guest holds no ambient root on wasip2 and must resolve a requested path against a host-preopened directory before opening anything. Three sub-decisions fall out of that ceremony.</p> <h2 id="decision-58"><a class="header" href="#decision-58">Decision</a></h2> <p><strong>D2 — Both fs cfgs gate on the single <code>wasi:filesystem</code> world import.</strong> <code>fs.read</code> and <code>fs.write</code> map to the same two interfaces (<code>wasi:filesystem/types</code></p> <ul> <li><code>/preopens</code>); the world text cannot distinguish them. <code>build.rs</code> therefore sets both <code>tau_cap_fs_read</code> and <code>tau_cap_fs_write</code> whenever <code>wasi:filesystem</code> is present. Read-vs-write is enforced at runtime by the host preopen perms (<code>DirPerms::READ</code> vs <code>DirPerms::all()</code> from <code>PreopenAccess</code>), not the cfg — a write to a read-only preopen fails at the host <code>open-at</code>. The two-cfg naming is kept for per-effect symmetry and future interface divergence.</li> </ul> <p><strong>D3 — Preopen-relative resolution is descriptor plumbing, not a cap gate.</strong> The guest computes reachability solely from the host's <code>get-directories()</code> list. A matching preopen → strip the guest-path prefix, pass the remainder straight to the host <code>open-at</code> (the guest does NOT reject/normalize <code>..</code>; the host rejects escapes at the descriptor boundary). No matching preopen → the guest holds no descriptor and cannot fabricate one. This is WASI's capability-security model: absence of a preopen is absence of capability. The enforcement point is the host's preopen set (its <code>WasiCtx</code>), which the host populates only from granted caps — preserving 3.4's "no in-guest cap gate" invariant.</p> <p><strong>D4 — Ungranted-path denial is guest-observed absence, not a host error-code.</strong> Net's denial is a host hook returning a <code>wasi:http</code> error-code (<code>HttpRequestDenied</code>), asserted exactly. Fs's no-preopen denial produces no host error-code by construction — the guest never calls the host for a path it holds no descriptor for. So the round-trip asserts an exact, stable guest-authored marker (<code>FsAccessDenied</code>). The enforcement stays 100% host (what the host placed in <code>get-directories</code>); only the marker string is guest-emitted.</p> <h2 id="consequences-63"><a class="header" href="#consequences-63">Consequences</a></h2> <ul> <li>A future divergence of the read/write WIT surface would let D2 split the cfgs; until then they move in lockstep.</li> <li>Tests asserting fs denial key on <code>FsAccessDenied</code> (guest constant), whereas net keys on the host <code>HttpRequestDenied</code> — an intentional, documented asymmetry, not an inconsistency.</li> <li>The positive/connected fs path is offline-untested by design (as net); the host-side <code>wasi_fs_enforcement.rs</code> fs-probe test covers the granted read.</li> </ul> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="phase-0-retrospective"><a class="header" href="#phase-0-retrospective">Phase 0 retrospective</a></h1> <p><strong>Phase:</strong> 0 — bootstrap + foundational sub-projects <strong>Duration:</strong> 2026-04-24 → 2026-04-28 (5 days) <strong>Status:</strong> Complete <strong>Author:</strong> Maintainer + Claude Opus 4.7</p> <p>Per PG4, phases close with a retrospective that records what shipped, what slipped, what was learned, and what changes to guidelines or plans follow. Phase 0 ran from the bootstrap commit through the merge of sub-project 5 (<code>tau-cli</code>). This document is the public artifact closing the phase.</p> <p>The mid-phase reflection at <code>docs/retrospectives/phase-0-mid.md</code> already captured patterns from sub-projects 1-4. This document supersedes it for the formal retrospective record while preserving the mid-phase memo as the in-context capture that it was.</p> <hr /> <h2 id="1-phase-0-summary"><a class="header" href="#1-phase-0-summary">1. Phase 0 summary</a></h2> <p><strong>Original goal:</strong> empty repo with green CI, full governance files, and the hexagonal workspace skeleton in place; then five foundational sub-projects (tau-domain, tau-ports, tau-pkg, tau-runtime, tau-cli) producing working, testable software on its own per the brainstorm→spec→plan→implementation cycle.</p> <p><strong>Outcome:</strong> the goal was met. Every sub-project shipped on time with ADR coverage, comprehensive tests, and CI gating. The hexagonal architecture (domain ⟶ ports ⟶ adapters) holds. The constitution and process guidelines proved load-bearing.</p> <p><strong>One unanticipated v0.1 limitation:</strong> plugin loading was deferred to Phase 1+ in sub-project 5 because the loading mechanism (dlopen, abi_stable, out-of-process IPC, WASM) was a bigger design decision than fits inside any single Phase 0 sub-project. v0.1 ships compiled-in mock plugins gated by <code>cfg(feature = "test-mock")</code> for testing; users can <code>tau install</code> source trees but the installed packages don't actually execute until Phase 1+ ships the loader. ADR-0007 §18 documents this prominently. This is the most material gap between Phase 0's intent and what was delivered.</p> <hr /> <h2 id="2-phase-0-deliverables"><a class="header" href="#2-phase-0-deliverables">2. Phase 0 deliverables</a></h2> <h3 id="sub-projects-5"><a class="header" href="#sub-projects-5">Sub-projects (5)</a></h3> <div class="table-wrapper"><table><thead><tr><th>#</th><th>Sub-project</th><th>Crate</th><th>Merge</th><th>ADRs</th></tr></thead><tbody> <tr><td>1</td><td>Pure data shapes</td><td><code>tau-domain</code></td><td>sign-off <code>2a06e18</code> (linear)</td><td>ADR-0002, ADR-0005</td></tr> <tr><td>2</td><td>Plugin trait surface</td><td><code>tau-ports</code></td><td>sign-off <code>cf29ae8</code> (linear)</td><td>ADR-0003</td></tr> <tr><td>3</td><td>Package manager</td><td><code>tau-pkg</code></td><td>sign-off <code>e7578b2</code> (linear)</td><td>ADR-0004</td></tr> <tr><td>4</td><td>Kernel</td><td><code>tau-runtime</code></td><td>squash <code>a50ed1d</code></td><td>ADR-0006</td></tr> <tr><td>5</td><td>CLI binary</td><td><code>tau-cli</code></td><td>squash <code>b82422e</code></td><td>ADR-0007</td></tr> </tbody></table> </div> <p>Plus the mid-phase reflection memo at <code>e7e798e</code> (between sub-projects 4 and 5).</p> <h3 id="adrs-6"><a class="header" href="#adrs-6">ADRs (6)</a></h3> <ul> <li><strong>ADR-0001</strong> Bootstrap decisions</li> <li><strong>ADR-0002</strong> Manifest format, capability evolution, escape-hatch policy</li> <li><strong>ADR-0003</strong> tau-ports trait surface</li> <li><strong>ADR-0004</strong> tau-pkg package manager — public API, storage layout, lockfile</li> <li><strong>ADR-0005</strong> Custom serde for <code>PackageSource</code> and <code>PackageKind</code></li> <li><strong>ADR-0006</strong> tau-runtime kernel + Tool capabilities amendment</li> <li><strong>ADR-0007</strong> tau-cli + tau-runtime amendments (capability filter, run_with_history)</li> </ul> <p>All Accepted. Two ADRs (0006 + 0007) bundle a downstream sub-project's design with an additive amendment to the upstream crate it consumes — the "bundled-amendment" pattern works when the amendment is solely motivated by the downstream consumer.</p> <h3 id="tests-workspace-wide"><a class="header" href="#tests-workspace-wide">Tests (workspace-wide)</a></h3> <ul> <li><strong>464 tests</strong> passing across <strong>60 test binaries</strong> (workspace <code>cargo test --all-targets</code>).</li> <li><strong>21 doctests</strong> passing, <strong>49 ignored</strong> (the <code>ignore</code>-marked doctests on <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> types per the established E0639 workaround).</li> <li><strong>1 ignored</strong> integration test (<code>run_kernel_errors::plugin_contract_violation</code> in tau-runtime; deferred to Phase 1's schema validation work).</li> <li><strong>Multiple proptests</strong> in tau-domain (capability parsers, manifest validation), tau-runtime (capability satisfies-relation, 256 cases × 3 properties), and tau-cli (project tau.toml round-trip, 64 cases).</li> </ul> <h3 id="ci"><a class="header" href="#ci">CI</a></h3> <ul> <li><strong>12 required status checks</strong> on <code>main</code>: rustfmt, clippy, 4× test matrix (Linux/macOS × stable/1.91), 5× per-crate no-default-features builds (tau-domain, tau-ports, tau-pkg, tau-runtime, tau-cli), and the tau-ports test-fixtures-only job.</li> <li>Windows test jobs run with <code>continue-on-error: true</code> per Constitution G15 — exercised but not gating.</li> <li>Branch protection: <code>enforce_admins=true</code>, <code>strict=true</code>, no force-push, no deletion. The maintainer follows the same gate.</li> </ul> <h3 id="workspace-structure"><a class="header" href="#workspace-structure">Workspace structure</a></h3> <p>The 8-crate skeleton from ADR-0001 is realized:</p> <div class="table-wrapper"><table><thead><tr><th>Crate</th><th>Role</th><th>Status</th></tr></thead><tbody> <tr><td><code>tau-domain</code></td><td>Pure data shapes</td><td>Shipped sub-project 1</td></tr> <tr><td><code>tau-ports</code></td><td>Plugin trait surface</td><td>Shipped sub-project 2</td></tr> <tr><td><code>tau-pkg</code></td><td>Package manager (sync)</td><td>Shipped sub-project 3</td></tr> <tr><td><code>tau-runtime</code></td><td>Kernel (async)</td><td>Shipped sub-project 4</td></tr> <tr><td><code>tau-cli</code></td><td>CLI binary</td><td>Shipped sub-project 5</td></tr> <tr><td><code>tau-app</code></td><td>Reserved for serve-mode binary</td><td>Bootstrap stub</td></tr> <tr><td><code>tau-infra</code></td><td>Reserved for shared infra</td><td>Bootstrap stub</td></tr> <tr><td><code>tau-observe</code></td><td>Reserved for observability extensions</td><td>Bootstrap stub</td></tr> </tbody></table> </div> <p>Three crates remain bootstrap stubs (<code>tau-app</code>, <code>tau-infra</code>, <code>tau-observe</code>); their roles are reserved for Phase 1+ work.</p> <hr /> <h2 id="3-what-shipped--patterns-that-worked"><a class="header" href="#3-what-shipped--patterns-that-worked">3. What shipped — patterns that worked</a></h2> <h3 id="brainstorm--spec--plan--implementation--adr-cycle"><a class="header" href="#brainstorm--spec--plan--implementation--adr-cycle">Brainstorm → spec → plan → implementation → ADR cycle</a></h3> <p>Every sub-project followed the same rhythm: maintainer-driven brainstorm producing a spec; spec derived into a plan; plan executed via subagent- driven development (or in-line execution for sub-project 1); ADR filed penultimately; sign-off commit closing the branch. The cycle is predictable, auditable, and the per-step artifacts (spec, plan, ADR) are useful long after the sub-project ships.</p> <p>Concrete: sub-project 4's branch had 21 commits squash-merged into <code>a50ed1d</code>. Sub-project 5's branch had 19 implementation commits + 4 mid-implementation fixes squash-merged into <code>b82422e</code>.</p> <h3 id="same-commit-escape-hatch-registration"><a class="header" href="#same-commit-escape-hatch-registration">Same-commit escape-hatch registration</a></h3> <p>The mechanical CI gate at <code>crates/tau-domain/tests/escape_hatch_registry.rs</code> enforces that every commit introducing an <code>Internal</code> error variant also appends an anchor to <code>docs/explanation/escape-hatches.md</code>. The discipline caught misses: two anchor registrations in sub-project 3 (<code>ScopeError::Internal</code>, <code>RegistryError::Internal</code>) were initially missed and the gate stopped them.</p> <p>Sub-project 5 deliberately added zero new <code>Internal</code> variants — the typed <code>ProjectConfigError</code> and <code>AgentResolutionError</code> taxonomies cover every codepath. The "don't ship variants without triggering codepaths" discipline (crystallized in the mid-phase memo) held end-to-end.</p> <h3 id="outcome--error-dichotomy"><a class="header" href="#outcome--error-dichotomy">Outcome / Error dichotomy</a></h3> <p>Crystallized during sub-project 4's brainstorm. Clean separation:</p> <ul> <li><code>Ok(RunOutcome::Failed)</code> for agent-level failures (capability denial, max turns reached) — the agent ran but couldn't accomplish the task.</li> <li><code>Err(RuntimeError)</code> for kernel-level errors (plugin errors, dispatch errors, contract violations) — the kernel itself broke.</li> </ul> <p>In sub-project 5 the dichotomy mapped cleanly to CLI exit codes (3 buckets: 0 / 1 / 2). CI scripts can <code>case $?</code> on this without parsing JSON — and <code>--json</code> output is there when scripts need precision.</p> <p>The pattern generalizes to any future "run something" verb (workflow runner, multi-agent orchestrator, etc.). It should propagate.</p> <h3 id="bundled-adrs-for-tightly-coupled-trait-amendments"><a class="header" href="#bundled-adrs-for-tightly-coupled-trait-amendments">Bundled ADRs for tightly-coupled trait amendments</a></h3> <p>ADR-0006 covered the kernel design + the additive <code>Tool::capabilities()</code> amendment to ADR-0003. ADR-0007 covered tau-cli + two additive amendments to tau-runtime (capability filter, <code>run_with_history</code>).</p> <p>The bundling works when:</p> <ul> <li>The amendment is solely motivated by the downstream consumer.</li> <li>The downstream sub-project ships the amendment as part of its work.</li> <li>The amendment is additive (no breaking changes to existing callers).</li> </ul> <p>If a future amendment doesn't satisfy these — say, a tau-pkg change motivated by both tau-cli and a hypothetical Phase 1+ workflow runner — it gets its own ADR.</p> <h3 id="toml-round-trip-for-testing-non_exhaustive-types"><a class="header" href="#toml-round-trip-for-testing-non_exhaustive-types">TOML round-trip for testing <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> types</a></h3> <p>Every sub-project after sub-project 1 leaned on this pattern:</p> <pre><pre class="playground"><code class="language-rust"><span class="boring">#![allow(unused)] </span><span class="boring">fn main() { </span>#[derive(serde::Deserialize)] struct CapWrapper { cap: Capability } let wrapped: CapWrapper = toml::from_str( r#"cap = { kind = "fs.read", paths = ["/tmp/**"] }"# ).unwrap(); <span class="boring">}</span></code></pre></pre> <p>Cleaner than threading constructors. More readable than mutating defaults. Should remain the v0.1 idiom for testing <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> types in cross-crate contexts.</p> <h3 id="hand-authored-fixture-pattern-lockfile--manifest"><a class="header" href="#hand-authored-fixture-pattern-lockfile--manifest">Hand-authored fixture pattern (lockfile + manifest)</a></h3> <p>Sub-project 5's tests for <code>cmd::run</code> and <code>cmd::chat</code> initially planned to use git fixtures (<code>file://</code> URLs cloned via subprocess). The implementer pivoted to hand-authoring <code>.tau/tau-lock.toml</code> + <code>.tau/packages/<name>/<version>/tau.toml</code> directly. Faster (no git binary invocation per test), more deterministic, no bare-repo HEAD quirks. The git-fixture pattern remains the right choice for <code>tau install</code> integration tests where the install pipeline IS what's under test.</p> <h3 id="subagent-driven-development-for-plan-execution"><a class="header" href="#subagent-driven-development-for-plan-execution">Subagent-driven development for plan execution</a></h3> <p>Sub-projects 4 and 5 were executed via the <code>subagent-driven-development</code> skill. Per-task implementer subagents with controller review. The controller (this conversation) caught:</p> <ul> <li>Spec/reality mismatches (e.g., <code>tau_pkg::list</code> returns <code>Vec<LockedPackage></code>, not <code>Vec<InstalledPackage></code> as sub-project 5's spec hypothesized).</li> <li>Mid-implementation deviations that needed bundling (8 tau-domain / tau-ports constructors in sub-project 4 Task 10).</li> <li>Cross-platform foot-guns (CRLF, hardcoded <code>/tmp</code> paths).</li> </ul> <p>The skill's two-stage review (spec compliance + code quality) was not formally invoked per task — the controller reviewed each implementer's report directly. This worked for the maintainer-driven workflow but should be revisited if the team scales beyond one maintainer.</p> <hr /> <h2 id="4-what-slipped--recurring-foot-guns-and-surprises"><a class="header" href="#4-what-slipped--recurring-foot-guns-and-surprises">4. What slipped — recurring foot-guns and surprises</a></h2> <h3 id="non_exhaustive-cross-crate-construction"><a class="header" href="#non_exhaustive-cross-crate-construction"><code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> cross-crate construction</a></h3> <p>The most repeated pattern across the phase. Specs assumed struct-literal construction would work; it doesn't across crate boundaries on <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> types. Concrete instances:</p> <ul> <li>Sub-project 4 Task 10: 8 mid-implementation constructors landed in tau-domain and tau-ports (<code>Message::new</code>, <code>AgentStatus::failed</code>, <code>PackageId::new</code>, <code>CompletionRequest::new</code>, <code>LlmProviderMessage::{user,assistant,tool_result}</code>, <code>ToolUse::new</code>, <code>TokenUsage::new</code>, <code>SessionContext::new</code>).</li> <li>Sub-project 5 Task 9: spec assumed <code>Scope::resolve_project_only</code>, <code>InstalledPackage</code> shape, <code>PackageSource::Git { url }</code> — none matched reality.</li> </ul> <p>The mid-phase memo crystallized the spec-phase pre-flight checklist. Sub-project 5 still hit it because the spec was written <em>before</em> the checklist was crystallized. Phase 1 specs should run the checklist explicitly.</p> <h3 id="async-fn-in-trait-is-not-dyn-compatible"><a class="header" href="#async-fn-in-trait-is-not-dyn-compatible"><code>async fn in trait</code> is not dyn-compatible</a></h3> <p>Sub-project 4's spec wrote <code>Arc<dyn LlmBackend></code> directly. Doesn't compile. The <code>DynLlmBackend</code> / <code>DynTool</code> / <code>DynStorage</code> wrapper-trait shim with blanket impls (~250 lines) is the standard idiomatic workaround. Removable when tau-ports gains a <code>trait_variant</code>-generated dyn variant.</p> <p>This was the single largest mid-implementation invention of the phase. It cost about 4 hours of design + implementation. A spec-phase pre-flight that asked "are async traits involved? are they dyn-compatible?" would have caught it.</p> <h3 id="file-git-clone-ci-failures-across-3-oses"><a class="header" href="#file-git-clone-ci-failures-across-3-oses"><code>file://</code> git clone CI failures across 3 OSes</a></h3> <p>Sub-project 3 hit three distinct issues:</p> <ol> <li>git 2.38+'s <code>protocol.file.allow=user</code> default silently blocking <code>file://</code> clones (CVE-2022-39253 mitigation).</li> <li>Bare repo <code>HEAD</code> not pointing at <code>main</code> after <code>clone --bare</code>.</li> <li>Windows path-to-URL conversion producing backslashes.</li> </ol> <p>Each surfaced only after CI ran on the relevant OS. The fixes are now captured (passing <code>-c protocol.file.allow=always</code>, explicit <code>symbolic-ref HEAD refs/heads/main</code>, <code>url::Url::from_file_path</code> for forward-slash). Phase 1 specs touching git fixtures should reference sub-project 3's Task 14 explicitly.</p> <h3 id="spec-drift-between-summary-tables-and-per-task-detail"><a class="header" href="#spec-drift-between-summary-tables-and-per-task-detail">Spec drift between summary tables and per-task detail</a></h3> <p>Sub-project 4 plan §Task 20 (final verification) expected <code>tests/proptest_capability_satisfies.rs</code> as a file; sub-project 4 Task 17 correctly chose in-module proptests instead (Option B for <code>pub(crate)</code> access). The deviation was correct but had to be rationalized at sign-off rather than caught earlier.</p> <p>Plan-writing skill should cross-reference the summary table against per-task detail. Tackled mechanically by the writing-plans skill's self-review step ("type consistency"). Sub-project 5 had fewer such surprises; the skill is improving.</p> <h3 id="plugin-loading-deferred-to-phase-1"><a class="header" href="#plugin-loading-deferred-to-phase-1">Plugin loading deferred to Phase 1+</a></h3> <p>Not an unanticipated foot-gun so much as a scope decision that should have been made earlier. Sub-projects 1-4 produced libraries; sub-project 5 was the first that needed real plugin loading to be useful. The deferral was the right call (plugin loading is a meaningful design decision deserving its own ADR), but it means Phase 0 ships a CLI that can install but not actually run anything outside the test-mock.</p> <p>This is <strong>the</strong> most material gap in Phase 0's deliverables.</p> <h3 id="windows-snapshot-tests--fixed-pre-retro-merge"><a class="header" href="#windows-snapshot-tests--fixed-pre-retro-merge">Windows snapshot tests — fixed pre-retro-merge</a></h3> <p>Sub-project 5's <code>help_snapshots.rs</code> snapshots passed locally on macOS but initially failed on Windows. Two normalizations resolved them end-to-end (both shipped before this retrospective merged):</p> <ol> <li><strong>CRLF → LF</strong> (commit <code>bd47d77</code>) — Windows writes <code>\r\n</code>, snapshots were recorded with <code>\n</code>.</li> <li><strong><code>tau.exe</code> → <code>tau</code></strong> (commit <code>8f614b6</code> on this retro branch) — clap derives the binary name from <code>argv[0]</code>, so help text shows <code>Usage: tau.exe init</code> on Windows.</li> </ol> <p>The earlier hypothesis (terminal-width-dependent text wrapping) was wrong; the wrapping is identical, only the binary-name and line-ending differ. With both normalizations in <code>capture_help</code>, the same <code>.snap</code> files are valid on every platform. All 14 CI jobs (incl. Windows stable + 1.91) green at retrospective merge time.</p> <p>This was the only outstanding non-blocking failure closing Phase 0. It's resolved; no Phase 1 work item required (originally listed as Tier 4 priority 16 — dropped).</p> <h3 id="other-minor-surprises"><a class="header" href="#other-minor-surprises">Other minor surprises</a></h3> <ul> <li>Sub-project 4 Task 5 hit <code>forbid(unsafe_code)</code> blocking <code>unsafe { env::set_var }</code> for tests; pivoted to <code>#[cfg(test)] pub(crate)</code> test-only constructors. Documented in sub-project 4's commit history.</li> <li>Sub-project 5 Task 9 added 2 extra <code>AgentResolutionError</code> variants beyond the spec text (<code>Registry</code>, <code>InvalidIdentifier</code>) for triggering codepaths the spec missed. Still satisfies "no error variants without triggering codepaths" — just additive.</li> <li>Sub-project 5 Task 13's <code>--max-turns</code> integration test had to set <code>max_turns: 1</code> rather than asserting "loop forever" because the mock backend's tool-use behaviour is single-turn-only. Not a defect, just a scope reality.</li> <li>4 mid-implementation fixes in sub-project 5 (clippy unused import, cross-platform paths, CRLF, rustfmt) added overhead between Tasks 19 and the final merge. Most were caught by remote CI rather than local — local CI was rustfmt-permissive in ways the CI's rustfmt wasn't.</li> </ul> <hr /> <h2 id="5-what-was-learned--guidelines-worth-keeping"><a class="header" href="#5-what-was-learned--guidelines-worth-keeping">5. What was learned — guidelines worth keeping</a></h2> <p>The mid-phase memo captured most of these. Sub-project 5 confirmed them and added a few. Consolidating here:</p> <h3 id="spec-phase-trait-pre-flight-checklist-now-codified"><a class="header" href="#spec-phase-trait-pre-flight-checklist-now-codified">Spec-phase trait pre-flight checklist (now codified)</a></h3> <p>Three checks every spec should run before the plan is derived:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Are all types referenced in code snippets <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code>?</strong> If yes, do public constructors exist for cross-crate use? If not, list the constructors as line items in the spec, NOT as silent discoveries during implementation.</li> <li><strong>Are async trait methods involved?</strong> If yes, will the kernel / consuming crate need dyn-compatibility? Native <code>async fn in trait</code> is not dyn-compatible; design accordingly (wrapper traits, <code>trait_variant::make</code>, or commit to monomorphic generics).</li> <li><strong>Are tests at integration-test level vs. unit-test level constrained by <code>pub(crate)</code> visibility?</strong> If yes, the spec should say which level for which test.</li> </ol> <p>These three caught us repeatedly. Phase 1 specs run them explicitly.</p> <h3 id="dont-ship-error-variants-without-triggering-codepaths"><a class="header" href="#dont-ship-error-variants-without-triggering-codepaths">Don't ship error variants without triggering codepaths</a></h3> <p>Crystallized in the mid-phase memo, validated by sub-project 5 (which shipped only error variants with concrete failure paths and zero <code>#[ignore]</code>'d "future trigger" tests beyond <code>plugin_contract_violation</code>, which has its own deferral note).</p> <h3 id="spec-language-vs-implementation-reality"><a class="header" href="#spec-language-vs-implementation-reality">Spec language vs implementation reality</a></h3> <p>Sub-project 4 specced "~45 events across 9 subsystems" for tracing vocabulary; Task 10 actually emitted ~22. Sub-project 5 specced <code>tau_pkg::list</code> returning <code>Vec<InstalledPackage></code> but it returns <code>Vec<LockedPackage></code>. Specs are estimates with error bars, not commitments.</p> <p>ADRs ratify reality, not aspiration. Implementation reports should explicitly call out where the spec's claim differs from what shipped. Sub-project 5's commit messages did this consistently.</p> <h3 id="local-ci-must-match-remote-ci"><a class="header" href="#local-ci-must-match-remote-ci">Local CI must match remote CI</a></h3> <p>Sub-project 5's last 4 fixes were all "CI caught it that local didn't":</p> <ul> <li>Clippy unused-import gated on a feature.</li> <li><code>cross_platform.rs</code> Linux paths failing on Windows.</li> <li>CRLF in snapshots.</li> <li>rustfmt's stable version more aggressive than the dev machine's.</li> </ul> <p>Mitigation for Phase 1: run <code>cargo fmt --check</code> and <code>cargo clippy --all-features -- -D warnings</code> against the <code>stable</code> toolchain explicitly before pushing, and where possible exercise the no-default-features compile path. The <code>feedback_branch_protection_workflow</code> memory captures the principle but the pre-push checklist could be tighter.</p> <h3 id="bundled-adrs-for-tightly-coupled-amendments-work"><a class="header" href="#bundled-adrs-for-tightly-coupled-amendments-work">Bundled ADRs for tightly-coupled amendments work</a></h3> <p>ADR-0006 + ADR-0007 both used the pattern. The discipline:</p> <ul> <li>The amendment must be solely motivated by the downstream consumer.</li> <li>The amendment is additive (no breaking changes).</li> <li>The bundle gets a single ADR rather than two.</li> </ul> <p>Don't bundle promiscuously — ADRs are cheap, and unrelated changes deserve separate decisions.</p> <h3 id="hand-authored-fixtures--git-fixtures-for-unit-tests"><a class="header" href="#hand-authored-fixtures--git-fixtures-for-unit-tests">Hand-authored fixtures > git fixtures for unit tests</a></h3> <p>Where the test isn't exercising the install pipeline directly, writing the lockfile + manifest TOML on disk is faster, more deterministic, and free of git-binary quirks (HEAD pointing, protocol-allow, path normalization). Reserve git fixtures for the install path.</p> <h3 id="same-commit-escape-hatch-registration-is-non-negotiable"><a class="header" href="#same-commit-escape-hatch-registration-is-non-negotiable">Same-commit escape-hatch registration is non-negotiable</a></h3> <p>Mechanical CI test enforces it; the discipline caught misses; Phase 0 ended with all anchors registered correctly. Keep it.</p> <hr /> <h2 id="6-architecture-audit--does-the-design-hold"><a class="header" href="#6-architecture-audit--does-the-design-hold">6. Architecture audit — does the design hold?</a></h2> <p>Phase 0 closes with the hexagonal architecture and 5-crate runtime surface intact. A short audit before Phase 1 priorities:</p> <h3 id="things-to-keep-as-is"><a class="header" href="#things-to-keep-as-is">Things to keep as-is</a></h3> <ul> <li><strong>Domain ⟶ ports ⟶ adapters direction.</strong> No back-edges. tau-domain knows nothing about tau-ports; tau-ports knows nothing about tau-pkg or tau-runtime; tau-runtime knows nothing about tau-cli.</li> <li><strong>Per-operation typed errors with <code>#[from]</code> composition.</strong> Established in sub-project 1, validated in 3, 4, and 5. Top-level umbrella errors rejected (ADR-0004 §12, ADR-0006 alternative F).</li> <li><strong><code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> everywhere.</strong> Cross-crate construction is the cost; forward-compat additive evolution is the benefit. The pattern works. Phase 1 keeps it.</li> <li><strong>Bundled ADRs for tightly-coupled amendments.</strong> Pattern works; keep.</li> <li><strong>3-bucket exit codes mapped to the Outcome/Error dichotomy.</strong> Works for tau-cli; should propagate to any future "run something" verb.</li> </ul> <h3 id="things-to-revisit-in-phase-1"><a class="header" href="#things-to-revisit-in-phase-1">Things to revisit in Phase 1</a></h3> <ul> <li><strong>The <code>DynLlmBackend</code> / <code>DynTool</code> / <code>DynStorage</code> shim</strong> in tau-runtime is ~250 lines of boilerplate. When tau-ports gains a <code>trait_variant</code>- generated dyn variant (or when Rust's native <code>async fn in trait</code> gains dyn-compatibility), the shim can be removed. Phase 1 candidate: <code>trait_variant::make</code> on the four port traits with an explicit <code>Send</code>-bounded variant for <code>tokio::spawn</code> use cases.</li> <li><strong>Plugin loading mechanism</strong> (the elephant in the room). dlopen vs abi_stable vs out-of-process IPC vs WASM is a large design decision needing its own ADR. <strong>First Phase 1 sub-project candidate.</strong></li> <li><strong><code>tau-app</code> / <code>tau-infra</code> / <code>tau-observe</code> reserved crates.</strong> Their roles need definition in Phase 1. <code>tau-app</code> is intended for the serve-mode binary (was in original Phase 1 preview); <code>tau-infra</code> and <code>tau-observe</code> may absorb plugin-loading + advanced tracing respectively, or may consolidate / rename based on actual Phase 1 needs.</li> <li><strong>REPL persistence.</strong> v0.1's in-memory-only approach is correct for v0.1 but Phase 1 likely wants <code>tau chat --resume <id></code>. Schema + garbage-collection policy questions.</li> <li><strong>Streaming LLM responses.</strong> <code>LlmBackend::stream</code> exists but tau-runtime doesn't invoke it. Additive <code>Runtime::run_streaming</code> lands alongside the first real LLM-backend plugin that benefits from it (latency-sensitive UX).</li> </ul> <h3 id="things-explicitly-not-to-revisit-per-constitution-ng1-ng12"><a class="header" href="#things-explicitly-not-to-revisit-per-constitution-ng1-ng12">Things explicitly NOT to revisit (per Constitution NG1-NG12)</a></h3> <p>The non-goals from Constitution §2 hold. Phase 0 didn't violate any of them. Phase 1 doesn't either: the priorities below all fit within "runtime, not framework" (NG12), "developer tool, not end-user product" (NG11), and the rest of the NG list.</p> <p>One non-goal is worth re-emphasizing: <strong>NG6 — no persistent agent memory in core</strong>. REPL persistence (<code>tau chat --resume</code>) is CLI-side state, not agent memory. Workflow runners (Phase 1+) likewise persist <em>workflow state</em>, not agent state. The line between them must stay sharp.</p> <hr /> <h2 id="7-phase-1-priorities"><a class="header" href="#7-phase-1-priorities">7. Phase 1 priorities</a></h2> <p>Concrete ordered list. The original <code>ROADMAP.md</code> Phase 1 (preview) section had four items (serve mode, sandboxing, performance budgets, cargo-audit/cargo-deny). Phase 1's actual priorities, informed by Phase 0's deliverables and deferrals, are below. They re-include the preview's four items at appropriate priority.</p> <h3 id="tier-1--unblocks-phase-1-itself"><a class="header" href="#tier-1--unblocks-phase-1-itself">Tier 1 — unblocks Phase 1 itself</a></h3> <p>These need to ship before most other work makes sense.</p> <ol> <li><strong>Plugin loading mechanism.</strong> Without it, <code>tau install</code> is a record-keeping operation. Multiple options (dlopen / abi_stable / out-of-process IPC / WASM) need an ADR-driven decision. <strong>First sub-project of Phase 1.</strong> Probable winner: out-of-process IPC over stdio (matches future serve-mode design + sandbox-friendly), but the brainstorm decides.</li> <li><strong>First real LLM-backend plugin.</strong> Likely an Anthropic / OpenAI HTTP adapter via reqwest. Validates the loading mechanism end-to-end and gives tau actual user value. Probably an out-of-tree package that <code>tau install</code> pulls in, not bundled with tau-cli.</li> <li><strong>First real Tool plugin.</strong> <code>fs-read</code> + <code>shell</code> as initial set — validates multi-plugin composition and the capability check at runtime. Exercises the tool dispatch loop with non-mock inputs.</li> </ol> <h3 id="tier-2--completes-phase-0-deferrals"><a class="header" href="#tier-2--completes-phase-0-deferrals">Tier 2 — completes Phase 0 deferrals</a></h3> <ol start="4"> <li><strong>Capability override implementation</strong> (project tau.toml <code>[agents.<id>.capabilities]</code> with intersect-only semantics). Schema slot reserved in ADR-0007 §4. Small ADR + small implementation.</li> <li><strong>Transitive dependency resolution</strong> (<code>tau install <agent></code> pulls <code>requires.tools</code> automatically). ADR-0004 §10 deferral; complements priority 1.</li> <li><strong>Schema validation for tool args</strong> (activates <code>RuntimeError::PluginContractViolation</code> and the <code>plugin_contract_violation</code> <code>#[ignore]</code>'d test). JSON Schema validation via <code>jsonschema</code> crate or hand-rolled.</li> <li><strong><code>tau update</code> / <code>tau verify</code> / <code>tau uninstall</code> subcommands.</strong> Spec §1 of sub-project 5 deferred these. Each is a smallish addition once plugin loading lands.</li> <li><strong>Streaming LLM responses</strong> (<code>Runtime::run_streaming</code> additive). Lands alongside the first LLM-backend plugin that benefits from it.</li> </ol> <h3 id="tier-3--extends-the-runtime"><a class="header" href="#tier-3--extends-the-runtime">Tier 3 — extends the runtime</a></h3> <ol start="9"> <li><strong>Multi-agent orchestration</strong> (G10's deferred half). Inter-agent message routing in tau-runtime, a multi-agent run loop, possibly a new CLI verb (<code>tau orchestrate</code>). Substantial; likely its own sub-project with its own ADR.</li> <li><strong>Workflow / pipeline runner</strong> (the maintainer's broader vision — deterministic step-by-step pipelines). New crate (<code>tau-workflow</code>?) OR new tau-runtime feature. Big design discussion: LLM-driven skill flows vs pure-deterministic runners. Own ADR.</li> <li><strong>REPL persistence</strong> (<code>tau chat --resume <id></code>, <code>tau chat --list-sessions</code>). Schema + GC policy. Mid-sized.</li> <li><strong>Sandboxing implementation</strong> (Constitution G12). The <code>Sandbox</code> trait is provisional in tau-ports; v0.1 doesn't invoke it. Real sandboxing requires OS-level work (jails, namespaces, Seatbelt) + its own ADR.</li> </ol> <h3 id="tier-4--operational-quality"><a class="header" href="#tier-4--operational-quality">Tier 4 — operational quality</a></h3> <ol start="13"> <li><strong>Performance budgets enforced in CI</strong> (Constitution QG14). G16's 100ms startup / 50MB memory budgets need automated validation. Likely a <code>criterion</code> + a CI threshold check.</li> <li><strong><code>cargo audit</code> + <code>cargo-deny</code> in CI</strong> (Constitution QG16). Standard Rust supply-chain checks.</li> <li><strong>Serve mode</strong> (JSON-RPC over stdio — Constitution G6, QG12). The second public surface alongside the embeddable Rust API. Probably lands in <code>tau-app</code>. Coordinates with priority 1's plugin-loading mechanism if it picks IPC.</li> </ol> <h3 id="out-of-scope-for-phase-1-per-constitution-ng1-ng12"><a class="header" href="#out-of-scope-for-phase-1-per-constitution-ng1-ng12">Out of scope for Phase 1 (per Constitution NG1-NG12)</a></h3> <ul> <li>Centralized package registry (NG4).</li> <li>Persistent agent memory in core (NG6).</li> <li>Hosted service (NG3).</li> <li>Identity / credentials (NG9).</li> <li>Telemetry / training data collection (NG10).</li> </ul> <p>These are forever-deferred. Phase 1 doesn't reopen them.</p> <hr /> <h2 id="8-process-changes-for-phase-1"><a class="header" href="#8-process-changes-for-phase-1">8. Process changes for Phase 1</a></h2> <h3 id="updated-workflow"><a class="header" href="#updated-workflow">Updated workflow</a></h3> <ul> <li><strong>Spec-phase pre-flight checklist is now mandatory.</strong> Specs touching cross-crate types must check <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> constructors, async dyn-compatibility, and test-visibility constraints up front.</li> <li><strong>Local pre-push CI parity.</strong> Run <code>cargo fmt --check</code> and <code>cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings</code> plus every <code>--no-default-features</code> build before pushing. The 4 mid-merge fixes in sub-project 5 wouldn't have happened with this discipline.</li> <li><strong>Spec implementation reports must call out reality vs spec.</strong> The implementer subagent already does this; Phase 1 controllers should treat these as routine, not exceptional.</li> </ul> <h3 id="constitution-amendments"><a class="header" href="#constitution-amendments">Constitution amendments</a></h3> <p>None proposed. The Constitution held up across Phase 0 without edits. PG4's retro process worked. QG18's ADR discipline worked. The G/NG partition stayed stable.</p> <p>If anything, the mid-phase memo + this retrospective demonstrate that the discipline encoded in the Constitution is load-bearing. Don't amend what's working.</p> <h3 id="plan-execution-mode-going-forward"><a class="header" href="#plan-execution-mode-going-forward">Plan execution mode going forward</a></h3> <p>Subagent-driven development worked well for sub-projects 4 and 5. Recommend keeping it as the default for plan-driven work. The two-stage review (spec compliance + code quality) was not formally invoked per task; controller-driven review served the maintainer-driven workflow. Revisit if multi-maintainer scaling becomes relevant.</p> <h3 id="memory-hygiene"><a class="header" href="#memory-hygiene">Memory hygiene</a></h3> <p>The auto-memory system has captured branch-protection workflow and plan-driven workflow as project memories. Phase 1 should add (when the relevant decisions land):</p> <ul> <li>The plugin-loading mechanism choice.</li> <li>Phase 1 sub-project ordering (after the first 1-2 ship and validate the priorities above).</li> </ul> <hr /> <h2 id="9-closing"><a class="header" href="#9-closing">9. Closing</a></h2> <p>Phase 0 produced a working, testable runtime stack from an empty repo in 5 days, on schedule, with full ADR coverage, comprehensive tests, and a clean CI gate. The hexagonal architecture holds. The constitution proved load-bearing. The brainstorm→spec→plan→implementation cycle proved repeatable.</p> <p>The single unanticipated v0.1 limitation (plugin loading deferred) is the focal point of Phase 1's first sub-project. Everything else flows from there.</p> <p>Phase 1 begins with the plugin-loading brainstorm.</p> <div style="break-before: page; page-break-before: always;"></div><h1 id="phase-0-mid-phase-reflection"><a class="header" href="#phase-0-mid-phase-reflection">Phase 0 mid-phase reflection</a></h1> <p><strong>Date:</strong> 2026-04-28 <strong>Status:</strong> Mid-phase memo (not the formal Phase 0 retrospective)</p> <p>PG4 reserves <code>docs/retrospectives/phase-NN.md</code> for phase boundaries. Phase 0 does not close until sub-project 5 (<code>tau-cli</code>) ships, so the formal retrospective lands then. This memo captures patterns and foot-guns observed across sub-projects 1-4 while the work is fresh, so sub-project 5 inherits the lessons rather than rediscovering them.</p> <p>The four sub-projects covered:</p> <div class="table-wrapper"><table><thead><tr><th>#</th><th>Sub-project</th><th>Crate</th><th>ADR</th><th>Sign-off commit</th><th>Merge style</th></tr></thead><tbody> <tr><td>1</td><td>Pure data shapes</td><td><code>tau-domain</code></td><td>ADR-0002, ADR-0005</td><td><code>2a06e18</code></td><td>linear (rebase / ff)</td></tr> <tr><td>2</td><td>Plugin trait surface</td><td><code>tau-ports</code></td><td>ADR-0003</td><td><code>cf29ae8</code></td><td>linear (rebase / ff)</td></tr> <tr><td>3</td><td>Package manager</td><td><code>tau-pkg</code></td><td>ADR-0004</td><td><code>e7578b2</code></td><td>linear (rebase / ff)</td></tr> <tr><td>4</td><td>Kernel</td><td><code>tau-runtime</code></td><td>ADR-0006</td><td><code>a50ed1d</code></td><td>squash-merge</td></tr> </tbody></table> </div> <h2 id="what-shipped--patterns-that-worked"><a class="header" href="#what-shipped--patterns-that-worked">What shipped — patterns that worked</a></h2> <h3 id="brainstorm--spec--plan--implement-cycle"><a class="header" href="#brainstorm--spec--plan--implement-cycle">Brainstorm → spec → plan → implement cycle</a></h3> <p>Each sub-project produced at least one ADR and a <code>feat/<topic></code> PR gated by CI. The cycle is predictable and auditable: spec landed first as its own commit on the feat branch, plan landed second, implementation tasks landed one commit each, ADR landed penultimate, then a sign-off commit closed the branch.</p> <p>Merge strategies varied. Sub-projects 1-3 landed via rebase / fast-forward, keeping the per-task commit history visible on <code>main</code>. Sub-project 4 was the first squash-merge: 21 commits (spec + plan + 17 implementation</p> <ul> <li>ADR + sign-off) collapsed into <code>a50ed1d</code>. Squash trades per-task visibility for <code>main</code> log readability; the per-task history is still recoverable via the merged-PR view on GitHub. Sub-project 5 should pick deliberately rather than by default.</li> </ul> <h3 id="same-commit-escape-hatch-registration-1"><a class="header" href="#same-commit-escape-hatch-registration-1">Same-commit escape-hatch registration</a></h3> <p>The mechanical CI gate at <code>crates/tau-domain/tests/escape_hatch_registry.rs</code> enforces that every commit introducing an <code>Internal</code> error variant also appends an anchor to <code>docs/explanation/escape-hatches.md</code>. The discipline pays for itself: in sub-project 3 alone, two anchor registrations (<code>ScopeError::Internal</code>, <code>RegistryError::Internal</code>) were initially missed and the gate caught both before they could ship.</p> <h3 id="outcome--error-dichotomy-1"><a class="header" href="#outcome--error-dichotomy-1">Outcome / Error dichotomy</a></h3> <p>Crystallized during sub-project 4's brainstorm. Clean separation:</p> <ul> <li><code>Ok(RunOutcome::Failed)</code> for agent-level failures (capability denial, max turns reached) — the agent ran but couldn't accomplish the task.</li> <li><code>Err(RuntimeError)</code> for kernel-level errors (plugin errors, dispatch errors, contract violations) — the kernel itself broke.</li> </ul> <p>The split makes pattern-matching at the call site clean and gives callers two different recovery strategies. The pattern should propagate to sub-project 5's CLI exit-code design.</p> <h3 id="bundled-adrs-for-tightly-coupled-amendments"><a class="header" href="#bundled-adrs-for-tightly-coupled-amendments">Bundled ADRs for tightly-coupled amendments</a></h3> <p>ADR-0006 covered both the kernel design and the additive <code>Tool::capabilities()</code> amendment to ADR-0003. The bundle is justified because the trait amendment is solely motivated by the consuming crate (tau-runtime). Future trait amendments motivated by their own sub-project should get their own ADRs.</p> <h3 id="toml-round-trip-for-testing-non_exhaustive-types-1"><a class="header" href="#toml-round-trip-for-testing-non_exhaustive-types-1">TOML round-trip for testing <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> types</a></h3> <p>Sub-project 4's capability proptests and integration tests both leaned on it: deserialize a TOML fragment to construct test capabilities, since cross-crate struct-literal construction is blocked. Pattern:</p> <pre><pre class="playground"><code class="language-rust"><span class="boring">#![allow(unused)] </span><span class="boring">fn main() { </span>#[derive(serde::Deserialize)] struct CapWrapper { cap: Capability } let wrapped: CapWrapper = toml::from_str( r#"cap = { kind = "fs.read", paths = ["/tmp/**"] }"# ).unwrap(); <span class="boring">}</span></code></pre></pre> <p>Cleaner than mutating defaults, more readable than threading constructors. Recommend explicitly for tests against <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> types in sub-project 5.</p> <h2 id="what-slipped--recurring-foot-guns"><a class="header" href="#what-slipped--recurring-foot-guns">What slipped — recurring foot-guns</a></h2> <h3 id="non_exhaustive-cross-crate-construction-1"><a class="header" href="#non_exhaustive-cross-crate-construction-1"><code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> cross-crate construction</a></h3> <p>Sub-project 4 needed 8 mid-implementation constructors landed in Task 10 because the spec assumed struct-literal construction would just work across crates: <code>Message::new</code>, <code>AgentStatus::failed</code>, <code>PackageId::new</code>, <code>CompletionRequest::new</code>, <code>LlmProviderMessage::{user,assistant,tool_result}</code>, <code>ToolUse::new</code>, <code>TokenUsage::new</code>, <code>SessionContext::new</code>. Each is a small additive API, but they were all foreseeable at spec time and missed.</p> <p><code>#[non_exhaustive]</code> blocks struct-literal construction across crate boundaries. Pattern recognition: if a spec writes a <code>Foo { a, b, c }</code> literal anywhere outside the crate that defines <code>Foo</code>, and <code>Foo</code> is <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code>, it won't compile. Spec-phase pre-flight catches it.</p> <h3 id="async-fn-in-trait-is-not-dyn-compatible-1"><a class="header" href="#async-fn-in-trait-is-not-dyn-compatible-1"><code>async fn in trait</code> is not dyn-compatible</a></h3> <p>Sub-project 4's spec wrote <code>Arc<dyn LlmBackend></code> and <code>Box<dyn Tool<Session = ()>></code> directly, but these traits use native <code>async fn in trait</code> (per ADR-0003) which is not dyn-compatible under Rust 1.93 (E0038). The straightforward translation didn't compile.</p> <p>Resolution: invented <code>DynLlmBackend</code> / <code>DynTool</code> / <code>DynStorage</code> wrapper-trait shims with boxed-future signatures and blanket impls for <code>T: LlmBackend + 'static</code> (etc.). ~250 lines of boilerplate. The shim is documented in ADR-0006 §3 and removable when tau-ports gains a <code>trait_variant</code>-generated dyn-compatible variant.</p> <p>This was also fully foreseeable at spec time and missed.</p> <h3 id="file-git-clone-ci-failures"><a class="header" href="#file-git-clone-ci-failures"><code>file://</code> git clone CI failures</a></h3> <p>Sub-project 3 hit three distinct issues, each surfacing only after the CI gate ran:</p> <ol> <li>git 2.38+'s <code>protocol.file.allow=user</code> default silently blocks <code>file://</code> clones (CVE-2022-39253 mitigation). Required passing <code>-c protocol.file.allow=always</code> in <code>Git::clone</code>.</li> <li>Test fixture's bare repo <code>HEAD</code> had to point to <code>main</code> for clone to produce a populated working tree.</li> <li>Windows tests failed because path-to-URL conversion produced backslashes; required forward-slash normalization.</li> </ol> <p>Each of these would have been catchable with a local CI rehearsal across the three target OSes (Linux, macOS, Windows). Sub-project 5 should budget for OS-specific surprises in the path-handling parts of <code>tau init</code> and <code>tau install</code>.</p> <h3 id="spec-drift-between-summary-table-and-per-task-detail"><a class="header" href="#spec-drift-between-summary-table-and-per-task-detail">Spec drift between summary table and per-task detail</a></h3> <p>The plan format mixes a summary table (file → task mapping) with per-task detail. Drift between the two is hard to spot at review time.</p> <p>Concrete example: sub-project 4 plan §Task 20 (final verification) expected <code>tests/proptest_capability_satisfies.rs</code> to exist as an integration test file, but Task 17 (proptest implementation) correctly chose in-module proptests in <code>capability.rs</code> for <code>pub(crate)</code> access. The deviation was correct but had to be rationalized at sign-off rather than caught in the plan.</p> <p>Mitigation: plan-writing skill should cross-reference the summary table against per-task detail, OR the structure-check sub-step should read "per-task placement" rather than enumerating exact file paths.</p> <h2 id="what-was-learned--guidelines-worth-crystallizing"><a class="header" href="#what-was-learned--guidelines-worth-crystallizing">What was learned — guidelines worth crystallizing</a></h2> <h3 id="spec-phase-trait-pre-flight"><a class="header" href="#spec-phase-trait-pre-flight">Spec-phase trait pre-flight</a></h3> <p>Three checks every spec should run before the plan is derived:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Are all types referenced in code snippets <code>#[non_exhaustive]</code>?</strong> If yes, do public constructors exist for cross-crate use? If not, list the constructors as line items in the spec, NOT as silent discoveries during implementation.</li> <li><strong>Are async trait methods involved?</strong> If yes, will the kernel / consuming crate need dyn-compatibility?
